decls.name: implements_famRound_of_cover
decls.docstring:
**`Algo.Implements` from one derivation per kind.**

`covers` is one predicate per kind — in practice "the node is of kind `k`", that is
`fun x => (k.proj x).isSome`.  `hcover` says every well-formed node belongs to at least one
kind, and `hkind` is the package's obligation for that kind.  Nothing else is asked, and in
particular the kinds need not be disjoint: the master round dispatches by first match, and
`hkind` is a statement about the master round, so two kinds claiming one node is harmless.

links.rationale: **`Algo.Implements` from one derivation per kind.**

decls.name: loopMatch_famRound
decls.docstring:
**A package's `Algo.LoopMatch` is the master round's.**

`R` is the package's own round, on its own instances `k.ι` and states `k.ω`.  The kind `k` is
`R` with the children pushed into the master node type along `k.e` (`hchild`); the other four
routines agree (`hwidth`, `hinit`, `hcomb`, `hfin`).  `hmiss` says the kinds in front of `k`
in the master list do not claim `k`'s nodes, so `k` is the one the dispatch selects.

*Proof.*  `Algo.loopMatch_embed` with `e := k.e` and `u := k.u`; its three hypotheses are
`Algo.A15.famChild_eq`, `famCombine_eq` and `famFinish_eq` rewritten by the five equations
above.

links.rationale: **A package's `Algo.LoopMatch` is the master round's.**

**A matching derivation may be given a larger budget.**  The budget `w` of
`Algo.LoopMatch` bounds the number of children still to come; a package proves its derivation
at its own round's width, and the master round's width may be larger.

*Proof.*  Induction on the derivation: a stop holds at every budget, and a call takes one off
both.

decls.name: mnRed
decls.docstring:
**The mathematical round of the master round**, in coset form.

* A dispatch node: one call, to the Chain Rule node on the same instance, in the
 intransitive case (Sec. 15, line 1 step 3); and the leaf answer otherwise (Eq. (58) on a
 window of at most one point).
* A Chain Rule node: the chain of Eq. (63) over the orbits of Eq. (64) when there are at
 least two of them, and one call otherwise — the very instance `Algo.chainRound` handed to
 `solve`.
* A descent node: the chain of Eq. (62) over the coset representatives of the kernel, and
 one call when there is no descent datum.

decls.name: Implements
decls.docstring:
**The raw round `R` implements the mathematical round `ρ`**: on every well-formed
instance, the fold of `R` from the empty state walks the tree `ρ` builds.

The mathematical round runs over an **arbitrary instance type** `κ` with a projection
`inst : κ → Babai.SIInstance Ω A`, not over `Babai.SIInstance Ω A` itself.  That is forced
by the Johnson parameter: it is not determined by the group, so a round has to be handed the
giant representation its parent computed, and the recursion runs over instances *with that
hint*.  The raw side needs no change: a raw
instance `ι` already carries whatever raw data the round wants, the hint included, and
`R.measure`, `R.ground` and `R.WF` are functions of the raw instance with its hint.  Taking
`κ = Babai.SIInstance Ω A` and `inst = id` gives back the unhinted reading.

links.rationale: **The raw round `R` implements the mathematical round `ρ`**: on every well-formed instance, the fold of `R` from the empty state walks the tree `ρ` builds.

decls.name: Round
decls.docstring:
**One computable round** of Procedure String-Isomorphism (Sec. 15), on raw data.

`child (I, j, s)` is the `j`-th subproblem of the instance `I`, given the state `s` folded
from the answers of the children `0, …, j-1`; `none` means that `I` has no further child.
`finish (I, s)` reads the answer of `I` off the final state.

The four legality fields are exactly what the recursion needs: the loop over the children
terminates (`child_eq_none`), and the recursion over the children terminates and stays
inside the well-formed data of a fixed domain (`child_wf`, `child_measure`,
`child_ground`).

decls.name: CostQ
decls.docstring:
**The cost data of a round whose fold state is quasipolynomially large.**

This is `Algo.Round.Cost` with one bound split into two.  `bound` is polynomial and governs
the instances and the answers; `stateBound` is quasipolynomial and governs the fold states.
The four routines are `RAM.QuasiFun`, the class of routines whose answer is only
quasipolynomially bounded (`Workspace/Machine/QuasiFun.lean`), because `combine` returns a
fold state.

`finish_le` is the clause that carries the whole design: the answer of a node is bounded by
the **polynomial** `bound`, although the state it is read off is only quasipolynomially
bounded.  For the round of Sec. 15 this says that a node returns a coset with shortened
generators, which is what `RAM.SIWorkspaceRoutine` needs at the top.

decls.name: RunCost
decls.docstring:
**What the machine packaging needs of a round**, on top of `Algo.Round.Cost`.

Three things.  The domain size must be a routine, since the number of rounds is computed from
it.  There must be a well-formedness test, because a `RAM.QuasiPolyFun` is a total function
while the bounds of `Algo.Round.Cost` hold only on well-formed instances; the loop is run zero
times on an instance that fails the test.  And the measure — the depth of the stack — must be
polynomially bounded in the domain size; for the round of Sec. 15 the measure is
`Babai.MasterStep.rank`, which is `O(log² n)` by `Babai.MasterStep.johnsonRank_le_rankBound`,
so a polynomial bound is far more than is needed.

links.rationale: **What the machine packaging needs of a round**, on top of `Algo.Round.Cost`.

decls.name: nodes_eq_count
decls.docstring:
**The recursion tree of the round is the recursion tree of Sec. 15.**

The mathematical round runs on hinted instances (`Babai.MasterStep`, the corrected paper
hinted instances), so a raw child must decode to the *lift* of the instance the tree asks
for; that is the hypothesis `hlift`.  It says no more than that the raw child carries the
hint its parent attaches to it, which is how a raw round is built.

*Proof.*  Induction on the fuel.  On the mathematical side the calls of a round against the
recursion one level down are the calls against the true oracle, because the recursion one
level down is correct at every call (`Babai.MasterStep.solve_eq_answer` and
`Babai.SIReduction.callsWith_eq_calls_of_agree`).  On the raw side
`Algo.Round.roundCalls_eq` says the children decode to those same calls, and the induction
hypothesis matches the subtrees term by term.

decls.name: RoundProgress
decls.docstring:
§11.4 and §15, **what the recursion analysis uses of one round**, at the raw nodes:

* the raw Johnson parameter is at most twice the raw window size (`Babai.MasterStep.param_le`);
* the round `ρ I` has at most `q(n)` calls (`Babai.MasterStep.calls_length_le`);
* either every child makes the progress of recurrences (ii)/(v), or the round is a Chain
 Rule round, recurrence (i): its children have strictly smaller windows and no larger
 parameter, and the windows of its calls add up to at most `n`
 (`Babai.MasterStep.decreases`).

The window of a good node is the window of the instance it decodes to (`win_eq`), which is
how the sum of the windows of the calls of `ρ I` bounds that of the raw children.

decls.name: alignDomHintAt_good_alpha
decls.docstring:
§14.1, lines 7–11, item 3 of the repair, at a node of the Master Algorithm: **the hint the
routine `Algo.masterL57Hint` attaches to the dominant-orbit call is good.**

The node has degree `n`, window `Δ` and group `G_N` (with `Δ` invariant); Procedure Align runs
on `Δ` with the action `A`, whose group is the group `G_N` induces on `Δ`.  Let line 6 find a
dominant class with nontrivial structure, `m*` above the threshold of Theorem 10.5.1 (case 3),
and let the call `W` be given on the node's domain: its group is the full preimage in `G_N` of
`G*` (the group of the machine's generators `Algo.alignPairG1`), and its window is the image in
the node's domain of an orbit `u^{G*}` of `G*` with `u` in the dominant window, of more than
`2|Δ|/3` points.  Then the hint `Algo.alignDomHintAt` has the meaning `Algo.MasterHintGood`
for `W`; its Johnson parameter is the machine's `m*`, `2m* ≤ m` (Eq. (73)), and its labels
are below `m`.

The representation is `ϕ*` composed with the restriction to `Δ`, read on the group the call
induces on its window (`Babai.restrictFactor`: the pointwise stabilizer of the window in the
call's group restricts into the pointwise stabilizer of `u^{G*}` in `G*`, which lies in
`ker ϕ*`), with `Γ*` numbered by the machine's list of its points.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 10.5.1 (Main Structure Theorem) (PDF p. 88) — §14.1, lines 7–11, item 3 of the repair, at a node of the Master Algorithm: **the hint the routine `Algo.masterL57Hint` attaches to the dominant-orbit call is good.**

decls.name: alternating_le_iff_factorial_le
decls.docstring:
**The order test.**  A subgroup of `S(Δ)` contains `A(Δ)` exactly when twice its order
reaches `|Δ|!`.

*Proof.*  If `A(Δ) ≤ K` then `|A(Δ)| ≤ |K|`, and `2|A(Δ)| = |S(Δ)| = |Δ|!` as soon as `Δ`
has two points; for `|Δ| ≤ 1` the group `S(Δ)` is trivial and both sides hold.  Conversely
`|S(Δ) : K| · |K| = |S(Δ)| ≤ 2|K|` forces the index to be one or two.  Index one gives
`K = S(Δ)`.  Index two gives `g² ∈ K` for every `g`, and every 3-cycle `c` satisfies
`c = c⁴ = (c²)²`, so `K` contains all 3-cycles, which generate `A(Δ)`.

No hypothesis on `|Δ|` is needed.

links.rationale: **The order test.**  A subgroup of `S(Δ)` contains `A(Δ)` exactly when twice its order reaches `|Δ|!`.

decls.name: chainRep_cover
decls.docstring:
**The mixed-radix representatives cover `G^{(i)}`.**  Every element of `G^{(i)}` lies in
the left coset `σ_j · G^{(i+k)}` of one of the `Algo.chainIndex` representatives.

*Proof.*  Row `i` is a transversal of `G^{(i+1)}` in `G^{(i)}`
(`Algo.rowPerms_transversal`), so `σ = τ ρ` with `τ` the `m`-th entry of row `i` and
`ρ ∈ G^{(i+1)}`; the induction hypothesis writes `ρ` with an index `j'`, and
`j = m + (row length) · j'` has the digits `m` and those of `j'`.

decls.name: eq_64_ram_spec
decls.docstring:
**Eq. (64), §11.1 ("strong descent"), what the RAM reduction computes.**  *"'Strong
descent' begins with descent to an intransitive subgroup `N ≤ G` followed by an application of
the Chain rule to the orbit partition of `N`."*  For a well-formed instance and `N ≤ G`, if
`ansQ` answers every well-formed instance:

* the reduction returns `Iso^Δ_{σG}(x, y)`;
* it descends to the `|G : N|` cosets of `N`;
* it makes at most `|G : N| · m` calls, `m` the number of `N`-orbits in `Δ`;
* each call is a well-formed instance whose window is one of the `N`-orbits in `Δ`, with a
 subgroup of `N` and the strings `x, y`.

That every orbit has `|Δ|/m` points when `G` is transitive on `Δ` and `N ◁ G` (Fact 11.1.8)
is `Algo.winOrbits_length_mul`.  The RAM running time is `Algo.eq_64_ram`.

finds no dominant color class, there is a `Babai.Line4cdData` whose round runs Procedure Align

color classes of `Ω` of line 4 (`Algo.winSet_alignRClasses_eq`), invariant under
`ϕ⁻¹(Aut(X'))`, covering `Ω`, and, with no dominant color, each of at most `4n/5` points

contains an odd permutation exactly when some cell has at least two points, or two distinct
cells have the same key and odd size.  (A cell of even size contributes nothing: its swap
with another cell of the same key is a product of evenly many transpositions.)

decls.name: four_mul_ncard_domClass_le

§14.1, line 7, **the trivial case**: when line 6 finds a dominant class but `m* < 2`, the
outcome is a colored partition and the dominant class is a single block (a Johnson scheme has

decls.docstring:
**The representative does not matter.**  If `τ` and `ν` both lie in `S` then the two
cosets `τ·⟨τ⁻¹S⟩` and `ν·⟨ν⁻¹S⟩` are the same.

*Proof.*  Each of the two generated subgroups contains the other's generating set: for `s ∈ S`,
`ν⁻¹s = (τ⁻¹ν)⁻¹(τ⁻¹s)`, and both factors lie in `⟨τ⁻¹S⟩` because `τ⁻¹ν` and `τ⁻¹s` do.  So the
subgroups are equal, and the two cosets agree because `ν⁻¹τ` lies in the subgroup.

decls.name: genGroup_map_topOf
decls.docstring:
**The top half of the point stabilizer of `u` in the graph group generates `ψ(H_u)`.**

This is the statement Definition 13.1.4 needs: the machine has generators `L` of the point
stabilizer of `u` in the extended group (which is what `Algo.rawPointStab` returns there),
and reading their top halves gives generators of the image `H_u^ψ`.

*Proof.*  As in `Algo.genGroup_map_projOf`.  Every member of `L` is of the shape
`a ⊔ ψ(a)` with `a` fixing `u` (`Algo.mem_pointStab_ext`), so its top half lies in
`ψ(H_u)`, which gives one inclusion.  For the other, an induction over the closure shows
that every element of `⟨L⟩` is of the shape `a ⊔ b` with `b ∈ ⟨topOf '' L⟩`; applying it to
`a ⊔ ψ(a)` for `a ∈ H_u`, which lies in `⟨L⟩`, and using injectivity of `⊔`, gives
`ψ(a) ∈ ⟨topOf '' L⟩`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 13.1.4 (Affected) (PDF p. 102) — **The top half of the point stabilizer of `u` in the graph group generates `ψ(H_u)`.**

decls.name: loopMatchN_alignCalls
decls.docstring:
**The transfer lemma.**  A fold of the raw round `R` that walks the coset-form tree `T`,
reading answers with `decA`, walks the aligned tree `Algo.alignRed (decJ I) T`, reading
answers with `Algo.alignDec decJ decA`.

*Proof.*  Induction on the matching derivation.  At a stop, both sides return the value of
the node, and the aligned tree returns it shifted by the representative of the node, which is
what the shifted decoder produces.  At a call, the aligned tree asks `Babai.alignInst (decJ
J)` (`Algo.alignRed_call`), which is what `Algo.ImplementsN` demands of a child `J` whose
typed instance is the aligned one.  A raw answer `a` with `alignDec decJ decA J a = (alignInst
(decJ J)).answer` has `decA a = (decJ J).answer` by `Algo.eq_answer_of_alignDec`, so the
induction hypothesis applies; and the continuation of the aligned tree at `(alignInst (decJ
J)).answer` is the continuation of `T` at `cosetRepOf (decJ J).K • (alignInst (decJ J)).answer
= (decJ J).answer`, by Eq. (59).

that matches from every state `Q` allows, matches `T.bind k`.

continuation of the call, so the same child is asked and the induction hypothesis gives the
rest.

decls.name: loopMatch_embed
decls.docstring:
**The fold of a sub-round is a fold of the master round.**

`e` embeds the instances of `R` into those of `M`, `u` embeds the fold states.  On the image
of the fixed instance `I` the master round does what the sub-round does.  Then every step of
matching between `R` and a reduction tree is a step of matching between `M` and the same
tree.

*Proof.*  Induction on the matching derivation.  At a stop, `hchild` turns `none` into
`none` and `hfin` identifies the two answers.  At a call, `hchild` turns the child `J` into
`e J`, which decodes to the same instance by `hdec`, and `hcomb` identifies the state after
the fold, so the induction hypothesis applies.

links.rationale: **The fold of a sub-round is a fold of the master round.**

decls.name: loopMatch_top2
decls.docstring:
**The fold of the window round walks the tree of Cor. 12.0.6.**

The induction is on the remaining budget `w`.  At a state `(t, i, c, acc)` the tree is the
chain of the `t`-th test with its last `k - i` orbits left, followed by the remaining tests.
There are three steps.  If the tests are exhausted both sides stop.  Otherwise the round
asks for the `i`-th orbit of `N` with `c` as its candidate set, which is what Eq. (63) asks
for; then either the chain of the test goes on with the answer as its candidate set, or the
test is *closed* — its answer is translated back by the computed lift and joined into `acc`
— and the next test is opened.  In the second case the tree of the current test has become
`done`, either because the answer was empty (Eq. (63) gives up) or because the orbits ran
out, and `Babai.SIReduction.bind` hands the accumulated value straight to the next test.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Corollary 12.0.6 (TopAction2) (PDF p. 98) — **The fold of the window round walks the tree of Cor. 12.0.6.**

decls.name: masterAdmit
decls.docstring:
The admission test of a proposed child `z.2` of the node `z.1`: the input bounds, the
same ambient degree, a smaller measure, and **an invariant window** — the child's window is
invariant under the group its generators generate (`Algo.rawIsInvariant`).

The last test is an input-validity check of the machine, not a step of the paper.  Every call
the paper's algorithm makes is a coset instance `⟨σN, Δ, x, y⟩` with `Δ` invariant under `N`
(`Babai.IsCosetInstance`), and its raw form passes the test, so on the calls of a valid
branch the test is redundant.  This is proved for every kind of child the carrier makes:
normalized window calls (`Algo.masterCheckedCall_rawIsInvariant`, with the coset property of
the calls of lines 4b, 4d, 5–7 and of the descents: `Algo.master4Tree_calls_coset`,
`Algo.top4wTree_calls_isCosetInstance`, `Algo.masterDescStrongTree_coset`), the orbit-chain
children of line 1 (`Algo.masterChainOpen_admitted` with `Algo.masterChainReturn_calls_coset`)
and the Cameron children (`Algo.masterCameronChildInput_rawIsInvariant`).  It is there so that every admitted child, whatever raw fold state produced it,
has an invariant window, which the recursion needs of every node it reaches.

decls.name: phaseMatch_cosetChain
decls.docstring:
**Luks's Chain Rule, Eq. (63), is one phase of a round of cost `Δs.length`.**

`Inv Δs C j s` is the invariant before the windows `Δs`: the chain has reached the candidate
set `C` and the fold stands at `(j, s)`.  There are two hypotheses.  `hstep` says that at a
state of the invariant with a nonempty candidate set the round's next child is exactly the
instance `⟨C, Δ, x, y⟩` of Eq. (63), and that the invariant is restored for every raw answer
that decodes to that child's answer.  `hstop` says that a state with an empty candidate set
already satisfies the invariant at the end of the chain, which is how Eq. (63) gives up.

Every round that runs a chain over a list of windows and then continues can compose this
phase with the next one by `Algo.phaseMatch_bind`, instead of proving the sequencing by an
induction of its own.

links.rationale: **Luks's Chain Rule, Eq. (63), is one phase of a round of cost `Δs.length`.**

decls.name: proposition_10_5_4
decls.docstring:
§10.5, **Proposition 10.5.4**, proved.

Quoted from the paper (version 2.5, lines 4749–4752):

> Finally, and algorithmic observation.
> **Proposition 10.5.4.** Given a giant representation `ϕ : G → S_k`, we can find the
> standard blocks in each `G`-orbit in polynomial time.
> *Proof.* Standard.

This is the statement of the former axiom `Babai.Proposition_10_5_4`, word for word.  The
routine is `Algo.tptLabels`: label a point `u` by the first point of the domain that lies in
the orbit of `u` and has the same `T` (Theorem 10.5.1 (a), computed by `Algo.rawTpoint`).
The module docstring says how each phrase of the paper is read.

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 10.5.4 (PDF p. 90) — §10.5, **Proposition 10.5.4**, proved.

**The routine computes the image.**  Paper: the images of the generators under `ψ_T`
that Procedure LocalCertificates carries from one round of the while loop to the next
(§13.1, lines 03, 04a, 07, 10).

*Proof.*  The graph group is `{a ⊔ ϕ(a) | a ∈ G}` (`Algo.mem_ext_group_iff`), so

`Algo.rawRestrictPerm_extPerm`.

proof uses the cited `Babai.cameronStructure_polyTime` (C16) for the recognition, as the paper
does ("The algorithmic part is well known: Cameron groups can be recognized and their structure
mapped out in polynomial time").

*"Let `3/4 ≤ α < 1` be a threshold parameter.  Let `X = (Ω, R)` be a `k`-ary relational

§14.1, lines 6 and 8–10: what Procedure Align has on the table while it processes the
dominant window, *except* the structure `Y` of line 7.

The fields are the Situation of Sec. 14 (*"We have a transitive group `G ≤ S(Ω)`"* with a
giant representation `ϕ : G → S(Γ)`, `|Γ| = m`), the common label size `t = t_Δ` of
Theorem 10.5.1 (c), line 6 (the dominant color class `Δ_j`, `|Δ_j| > m/2`), line 8 (`H` and

`Babai.Align_equipartition_param_halved` in case (A)).

preserves.  Everything that depends on that lives in `Babai.AlignDominantA` and
`Babai.AlignDominantB`.

decls.name: pointwiseStab_orbit_le_ker
decls.docstring:
**Case 3, second step**: the pointwise stabilizer of an affected orbit lies in the
kernel of `ϕ*`.

*Why it is true.*  Write `N` for the pointwise stabilizer of the orbit `Δ₁` in `G*`.  It is
normal in `G*`, so `ϕ*(N)` is normal in `ϕ*(G*)`, and `A(Γ*) ≤ ϕ*(G*) ≤ S(Γ*)`
(`Babai.AlignDominant.isGiantRep_phis`).  Hence `ϕ*(N) ∩ A(Γ*)` is normal in `A(Γ*)`, which
is simple for `m* ≥ 5`, so it is trivial or all of `A(Γ*)`.

* If `A(Γ*) ≤ ϕ*(N)`: pick `z ∈ Δ₁` (the orbit is nonempty, it contains `u`).  Then
 `N ≤ G*_z`, so `A(Γ*) ≤ ϕ*(G*_z)`, that is, `z` is unaffected — contradicting `haff`.
* If `ϕ*(N) ∩ A(Γ*) = 1`: both are normal in `ϕ*(G*)`, so they commute elementwise, and
 the centralizer of `A(Γ*)` in `S(Γ*)` is trivial for `m* ≥ 5`.  So `ϕ*(N) = 1`.

This statement needs no case data: it uses only that `ϕ*` is giant and `m* ≥ 5`, both of
which `Babai.AlignDominant` already gives (`m* ≥ 5` is the hypothesis `hm5`, which in the
algorithm comes from *"`m*` is not below the threshold of Theorem 10.5.1"* — for
`m* ≤ 4` the round takes case 1 instead).

*In Lean*: the group-theoretic step is
`Babai.eq_one_or_alternating_le_of_conj_mem` (`Workspace/Master/AlignDominantAux.lean`),
which rests on `Babai.isSimpleGroup_alternatingGroup` and, for the trivial-intersection
case, on `Babai.eq_one_of_commute_alternating` (the centralizer of `A(Γ*)` in `S(Γ*)` is
trivial for `m* ≥ 4`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 10.5.1 (Main Structure Theorem) (PDF p. 88) — **Case 3, second step**: the pointwise stabilizer of an affected orbit lies in the kernel of `ϕ*`.

decls.name: three_mul_ncard_orbit_ker_le
decls.docstring:
**Case 1, in case (A)**: the orbits of `ker ϕ*` on the window are at most `2n/3`.

*Why it is true* (the corrected paper Align, "Smallest change", item 1).  An element
`σ ∈ ker ϕ*` has `ϕ(σ) ∈ H` with `ψ(ϕ(σ)) = 1`, so by `psi_block` it fixes every block of
the equipartition setwise.  By Eq. (54) the label moves as `T(σ·u) = ϕ(σ)''T(u)`, so for
`u` in the window the labels along the orbit of `u` all have the same color vector
`γ ↦ |T ∩ block⁻¹(γ)|`.  The orbit therefore lies inside one color class of
`(Δ_j choose t)`, lifted to `Ω`.

A color class is small, in both of the two possible ways:

* if its color vector is not exceptional, Lemma 7.2.1 (a) (`Babai.lemma_7_2_1a`) gives
 `3·|class| ≤ 2·C(|Δ_j|, t)`;
* if it is exceptional, all `t` elements of `T` lie in one block `P`, and the class is
 `(P choose t)`.  From `m* ≥ 2` we get `2|P| ≤ |Δ_j|`, hence
 `C(|P|, t) ≤ C(|Δ_j|, t)/2` for `t ≥ 1`, which is stronger than needed.

 (This second half is a refinement of the corrected paper, which appeals to Lemma 7.2.1
 alone; Lemma 7.2.1 (a) explicitly excludes the exceptional vectors.)

Multiplying by the common size of a standard block, and using `C(|Δ_j|, t) ≤ C(m, t)`,
turns this into the bound on `Ω`.

*In Lean*: the containment of the orbit in a color class is
`Babai.AlignDominantA.tupleColor_smul_ker`.  The class is intersected with
*"all elements lie in `Δ_j`"*, which is what makes the exceptional half work: an
exceptional `T` lies in `Δ_j ∩ block⁻¹(γ₀)`, of size `blockSize`, and `2·blockSize ≤ m`
because two distinct parts are disjoint subsets of `Δ_j`.

The hypothesis `hu` cannot be dropped: outside the window the label of `u` meets
`Γ ∖ Δ_j`, where `ker ψ` is unconstrained.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Lemma 7.2.1 (PDF p. 62) — **Case 1, in case (A)**: the orbits of `ker ϕ*` on the window are at most `2n/3`.

decls.name: three_mul_ncard_unaffected_le
decls.docstring:
**Case 3, the key estimate, in case (A)**: the points of the window that `ϕ*` leaves
*unaffected* are at most two thirds of `Ω`.

*Why it is true* (the corrected paper Align, "Smallest change", item 3).  Let
`u ∈ B_T` be a point of the window, so `T = T(u) ⊆ Δ_j` and `|T| = t`.  Then
`ϕ*(G*_u) = ψ(ϕ(G_u) ∩ H)`, and Theorem 10.5.1 (a) sandwiches `ϕ(G_u)` between the pointwise
stabilizer of `T` in `A(Γ)` and the setwise stabilizer of `T` in `S(Γ)`.  So if `u` is
unaffected then `A(Γ*) ≤ ψ(H_T)`, the image of the setwise stabilizer of `T` in `H`.

An element `h ∈ H_T` maps `T ∩ block⁻¹(γ)` bijectively onto `T ∩ block⁻¹(ψ(h) γ)`, by
`psi_block` and `h '' T = T`.  So every element of `ψ(H_T)` preserves the color vector
`γ ↦ |T ∩ block⁻¹(γ)|` of Lemma 7.2.1.  Now `m* ≥ 9` (from `hvl`, the hypothesis of case 3),
so `A(Γ*)` is transitive on `Γ*`, and `A(Γ*) ≤ ψ(H_T)` forces that vector to be constant.

The `T ⊆ Δ_j` with a constant color vector form one color class of the coloring of
`(Δ_j choose t)` induced by the equipartition.  Its color vector is not exceptional: it is
constant with sum `t ≥ 1` over `m* ≥ 2` blocks, so no coordinate equals `t`.  Lemma 7.2.1
(a) (`Babai.lemma_7_2_1a`, applicable because `2t < |Δ_j|` by
`Babai.AlignDominant.two_mul_t_lt_ncard_Δj`) bounds that class by `(2/3)·C(|Δ_j|, t)`.
Multiplying by the common size of a standard block, and using `C(|Δ_j|, t) ≤ C(m, t)`,
gives the bound on `Ω`, exactly as in `Babai.three_mul_ncard_omegaCut_le`.

*In Lean*: the passage from *"`u` is unaffected"* to *"`A(Γ*) ≤ ψ(H_T)`"* is
`Babai.AlignDominant.exists_stab_label_map_eq`, the action of `ψ(H_T)` on the color vector
is `Babai.AlignDominantA.tupleColor_psi_apply`, and the transitivity of `A(Γ*)` on `Γ*` is
`Babai.exists_mem_image_eq_of_ncard_eq` on singletons.  Lemma 7.2.1 (a) is *not* transferred
to `Δ_j`: it is quoted on all of `Γ`, which is enough, because the bound is multiplied by
the common size of a standard block and `n = C(m,t)·b`.

The hypothesis `hvl` is *"`m*` is not below the threshold of Theorem 10.5.1"*, that is, the
statement that the round is in case 3 rather than case 1.  It cannot be dropped: for
`m* = 2` the group `A(Γ*)` is trivial, so **every** point is unaffected by `ϕ*` and the
conclusion fails.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Lemma 7.2.1 (PDF p. 62) — **Case 3, the key estimate, in case (A)**: the points of the window that `ϕ*` leaves *unaffected* are at most two thirds of `Ω`.

decls.name: three_mul_ncard_orbit_ker_le
decls.docstring:
**Case 1, in case (B)**: the orbits of `ker ϕ*` on the window are at most `2n/3`.

*Why it is true* (the corrected paper Align, "Smallest change", item 1).  An
automorphism of a Johnson scheme is determined by the permutation of `Γ*` it induces
(`Babai.exists_unique_perm_of_mem_aut_johnsonScheme`), so `ker ψ` acts trivially on `Δ_j`:
by `psi_label`, `ψ(h) = 1` forces `label (h d) = label d`, hence `h d = d`, for every
`d ∈ Δ_j`.

Let `σ ∈ ker ϕ*` and let `u` be in the window.  Then `ϕ(σ) ∈ ker ψ` fixes `Δ_j` pointwise,
and `T(u) ⊆ Δ_j`, so Eq. (54) gives `T(σ·u) = ϕ(σ)''T(u) = T(u)`.  The orbit of `u` under
`ker ϕ*` therefore lies inside the single standard block `B_{T(u)}`.

The standard blocks all have the same size and there are `C(m, t)` of them, with `t ≥ 1`
and `m ≥ 9`, so `C(m, t) ≥ 9` and `9·|B_T| ≤ n`; in particular `3·|B_T| ≤ 2n`.

*In Lean*: that `ker ψ` fixes `Δ_j` pointwise, hence the label, is
`Babai.AlignDominantB.Tpoint_smul_ker`, and the count of the standard blocks is
`Babai.three_mul_card_labelFiber_le` (`Workspace/Master/AlignDominantAux.lean`).

The hypothesis `hu` cannot be dropped: outside the window the label of `u` meets
`Γ ∖ Δ_j`, where `ker ψ` is unconstrained.

links.rationale: **Case 1, in case (B)**: the orbits of `ker ϕ*` on the window are at most `2n/3`.

decls.name: window_inter_unaffected_eq_empty
decls.docstring:
**Case 3, the key estimate, in case (B)**: in case (B) there is no unaffected point in
the window at all.

*Why it is true* (the corrected paper Align, "Smallest change", item 3).  Let `u` be
a point of the window with label `T = T(u) ⊆ Δ_j`, `|T| = t`.  As in case (A), if `u` is
unaffected then `A(Γ*) ≤ ψ(H_T)`.  By `psi_label`, `ψ(H_T)` is the stabilizer of `T` for
the action of `S(Γ*)` on `Δ_j = (Γ* choose t*)`, so `A(Γ*)` stabilizes the set `T` of
vertices of the Johnson scheme.

But `A(Γ*)` is transitive on `(Γ* choose t*)` (`Babai.exists_mem_image_eq_of_ncard_eq`,
applicable because `m* ≥ 2t* + 1 ≥ t* + 2`), so an `A(Γ*)`-invariant subset of `Δ_j` is `∅`
or `Δ_j`.  Both are excluded: `|T| = t ≥ 1` by `Babai.AlignDominant.one_le_t`, and
`t < |Δ_j|` because `2t < |Δ_j|` (`Babai.AlignDominant.two_mul_t_lt_ncard_Δj`).

Unlike case (A) this needs no lower bound on `m*` beyond the one the Johnson parameters
already give: `m* ≥ 2t* + 1 ≥ 5`.

*In Lean*: the passage from *"`u` is unaffected"* to *"`A(Γ*) ≤ ψ(H_T)`"* is
`Babai.AlignDominant.exists_stab_label_map_eq`, and the transitivity of `A(Γ*)` on
`(Γ* choose t*)` is `Babai.exists_mem_image_eq_of_ncard_eq`.

decls.name: Align_equipartition_card
decls.docstring:
§14.2: *"In the case of an equipartition, `Γ'` is the set of blocks of the partition,
so `|Γ'| ≤ m/2`."*

A nontrivial equipartition of `Δ` into `nb` blocks of common size `b ≥ 2` has
`nb · b = |Δ|`, hence `2·nb ≤ |Δ|`.  (Stated without division; with `|Δ| ≤ m` this is
`|Γ'| ≤ m/2`.)

decls.name: Align_johnson_card
decls.docstring:
§14.2, the Johnson case: *"so `m' < 1 + √(2m) < m/2` (for `m ≥ 12`)"*.

Stated without square roots: if `(m* − 1)² < 2m` and `m ≥ 12` then `2m* < m`.  The
threshold `12` is sharp: the real inequality `1 + √(2m) < m/2` is `m² − 12m + 4 > 0`, which
fails at `m = 11` and holds at `m = 12`.

links.rationale: §14.2, the Johnson case: *"so `m' < 1 + √(2m) < m/2` (for `m ≥ 12`)"*.

From `t* ≥ 2` and `m* ≥ 2t* + 1` (the parameters of a Johnson scheme, Def. 3.2.9) and
`C(m*, t*) ≤ m` we get `(m* − 1)² < 2 C(m*,t*) ≤ 2m` (`Babai.Align_johnson_sq_lt`), and
then `2m* < m` for `m ≥ 12` (`Babai.Align_johnson_card`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 3.2.9 (Johnson graph) (PDF p. 32) — §14.2, case (B) of line 7: **the Johnson parameter is more than halved**.

decls.name: Align_johnson_sq_lt
decls.docstring:
§14.2, the Johnson case, first step: `(m* − 1)² < 2·|Δ|`.

*"In case of a Johnson scheme `J(m', t')` (`t' ≥ 2`) with vertex set `Δ_j = (Γ' choose t')`
we have `m ≥ |Δ_j| = C(m', t') ≥ C(m', 2) > (m' − 1)²/2`."*

The middle inequality `C(m', t') ≥ C(m', 2)` holds because `2 ≤ t' ≤ m'/2`, which follows
from the parameter constraints `t' ≥ 2` and `m' ≥ 2t' + 1` of Def. 3.2.9.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 3.2.9 (Johnson graph) (PDF p. 32) — §14.2, the Johnson case, first step: `(m* − 1)² < 2·|Δ|`.

decls.name: Align_phiStar_isGiant
decls.docstring:
§14.1, line 10, the claim **"(: this is a giant representation :)"**.

Hypotheses actually needed: `ϕ` is a giant representation (`A(Γ) ≤ G^ϕ`, the standing
assumption of Sec. 14) and `ψ : H → S(Γ*)` is onto (this is what *"the natural
epimorphism"* asserts; for a nontrivial equipartition `ψ` is the induced action on the
blocks, and for a Johnson scheme `Aut(J(m*,t*)) = S_{m*}^{(t*)}` for `m* ≥ 2t* + 1` — the
cited Prop. 3.2.11, `Babai.aut_johnsonGraph` — whose natural map onto `S(Γ*)` is onto).
No lower bound on `|Γ*|` is needed.

Proof.  Every square of `S(Γ*)` is in the image: for `β = ψ(h)` with `h ∈ H`, the
permutation `h²` of `Γ` is even, so `h² ∈ A(Γ) ≤ G^ϕ`, and `h² ∈ H`; hence `h²` is in the
image of `ϕ*` and `β² = ψ(h²)` is in the image of `ϕ*` composed with `ψ`.  A `3`-cycle `c`
satisfies `c = (c²)²` (its order is `3`), so every `3`-cycle is in the image, and the
`3`-cycles generate `A(Γ*)`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Procedure Align (PDF p. 110) — §14.1, line 10, the claim **"(: this is a giant representation :)"**.

decls.name: Align_reject_struct
decls.docstring:
Procedure Align, **line 1**: *"If `X(x)` and `X(y)` are not `G^ϕ`-isomorphic then
reject isomorphism, exit."*

The rejection is correct: if there is no `G^ϕ`-isomorphism of the two structures then `x`
and `y` are not `G`-isomorphic.  Indeed a `G`-isomorphism `τ` of the strings has
`X(y) = X(x^τ) = X(x)^{τ^ϕ}` by canonicity, so `τ^ϕ ∈ Iso_{G^ϕ}(X(x), X(y))`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure Align (PDF p. 110) — Procedure Align, **line 1**: *"If `X(x)` and `X(y)` are not `G^ϕ`-isomorphic then reject isomorphism, exit."*

decls.name: Align_shift
decls.docstring:
Procedure Align, items 2–3, in the form Cor. 12.0.10 uses: **"else `y` is updated so
now `C_x = C_y = C`"**.

Given `σ ∈ G` whose image `σ^ϕ` carries the color class of `c` for `x` onto the one for
`y` (this is the `G^ϕ`-isomorphism of the two colorings that item 2 (i) produces, lifted
by item 2 (ii)), the shifted string `y' = y^{σ⁻¹}` has the same color class of `c` as `x`,
and `Iso_G(x,y)` is the paper's **right** coset `Iso_G(x,y')σ` of Eq. (57), i.e. Lean's left
translate `σ • Iso_G(x,y')`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Corollary 12.0.10 (TopAction4) (PDF p. 99) — Procedure Align, items 2–3, in the form Cor. 12.0.10 uses: **"else `y` is updated so now `C_x = C_y = C`"**.

decls.name: color_symm_of_pair
decls.docstring:
Observation 3.3.5.  If the first part has exactly the two vertices `a ≠ b`, then
`c(a,b) = c(b,a)`.

The out-degree of the color `c(a,b)` is the same at `a` and at `b`
(`Babai.BipCaseData.ncard_nbhd_eq`).  At `a` it is `1`: the only vertex of that color from
`a` is `b`, because the head of an edge of that color lies in the first part (Obs. 3.3.4)
and `c(a,a) = c(a,b)` would force `a = b` (Def. 3.1.2(i)).  So at `b` it is `1` too, and
the only candidate is `a`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 3.1.2 (Configuration) (PDF p. 29) — Observation 3.3.5.  If the first part has exactly the two vertices `a ≠ b`, then `c(a,b) = c(b,a)`.

decls.docstring:
Proposition 2.4.30 (Symmetry defect of semiregular bipartite graphs).  "The symmetry
defect of each part of a nontrivial semiregular bipartite graph is `≥ 1/2`."

Paper's proof: by taking the bipartite complement if necessary we may assume the density
is `≤ 1/2`; a vertex `x` of a set `T` of twins in `Ωᵢ` has a neighbor `y` in the other
part, and then `X(y) ⊇ T`, so `|T| ≤ deg(y) ≤ |Ωᵢ|/2`.

The passage to the bipartite complement is `isTwinSet_compl₁`/`isTwinSet_compl₂` (a set of
twins of `X` is a set of twins of `X^c`), and "density `≤ 1/2`" is the integer condition
`2 d₂ ≤ |Ω₁|` (resp. `2 d₁ ≤ |Ω₂|`), on which the proof splits.

decls.name: exists_nbr_not_complete
decls.docstring:
The step *"`Y` is not complete"* of the proof of Prop. 4.1.4, in the form in which it
is true.

The paper justifies it by *"`deg(y) ≤ n₁/2 < |Γ|`"*, but `deg₂ ≤ n₁/2` is an assumption
made inside the proof of Lemma 4.1.5 (*"by complementing if necessary"*) and is not
available in the proof of Prop. 4.1.4, where `X` is an arbitrary nontrivial semiregular
bipartite graph.  What is true, and is all the proof uses, is that the neighbor `y` of
`x` can be *chosen* so that `X[Γ, Δ_y]` is not complete: if for every neighbor `y` of `x`
every vertex of `Γ` were joined to all of `Δ_y`, then every `u ∈ Γ` would have
`N(x) ⊆ N(u)`, hence `N(u) = N(x) =: S` because `X` is semiregular; then every vertex of
`S` would have at least `|Γ| > n₁/2` neighbors and every vertex outside `S` at most
`n₁ - |Γ| < n₁/2`, so, `X` being semiregular, `S = Ω₂` or `S = ∅`, and in both cases `X`
would be trivial.  See the corrected paper. 4.1.4.

The classes `Γ` and `Δ_y` enter only through `a ∈ Γ`, `|Γ| > n₁/2` and `y ∈ Δ_y`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 4.1.4 (PDF p. 47) — The step *"`Y` is not complete"* of the proof of Prop. 4.1.4, in the form in which it is true.

decls.name: exists_prefix_nbhd
decls.docstring:
Claim 4.1.6.  "There is a prefix `P_k` of which the neighborhood `X(P_k)` has size
`n₁/3 < |X(P_k)| ≤ 2n₁/3`."

The hypotheses are those in force where the claim is stated (inside the proof of
Lemma 4.1.5): `X` is semiregular of degree `d₂` on `Ω₂` with `d₂ ≤ n₁/2` (the paper's
`deg₂ ≤ n₁/2`, obtained there from the density assumption), and every vertex of `Ω₁` has a
neighbor (`X` is nontrivial and semiregular).  Both inequalities are written without
division.

The paper's proof reads *"`|X(P_k)| ≤ |X(P_{k-1})| + deg₂ < n₂/3 + deg₂`, so we are done if
`deg₂ ≤ n₂/3`.  If `deg₂ > n₂/3` then we necessarily have `k = 1`"*; the three occurrences
of `n₂` there are typos for `n₁` (the bound concerns a subset of `Ω₁`, and `deg₂ ≤ n₁/2` is
a bound in terms of `n₁`).  See the corrected paper 4.1.6.

links.rationale: Formalizes Claim 4.1.6 (PDF p. 48) — Claim 4.1.6.  "There is a prefix `P_k` of which the neighborhood `X(P_k)` has size `n₁/3 < |X(P_k)| ≤ 2n₁/3`."

decls.name: exists_three_coloring
decls.docstring:
Proposition 4.1.4.  "Let `X = (Ω₁, Ω₂; E)` be a nontrivial semiregular bipartite graph.
Then there is a 3-coloring `f : Ω₂ → [3]` such that naive refinement of the colored
bipartite graph `(Ω₁, Ω₂; E, f)` yields a `(1/2)`-coloring of `Ω₁`: each color-subclass of
`Ω₁` has size `≤ |Ω₁|/2`."

The paper's proof: take `g` from Lemma 4.1.5 and let `h` be the coloring after naive
refinement of `(Ω₁, Ω₂; E, g)`.  If every `h`-color class in `Ω₁` has size `≤ n₁/2`, take
`f := g`.  Otherwise there is a dominant class `Γ ⊆ Ω₁` with `n₁/2 < |Γ| ≤ 2n₁/3`; pick an
edge `(x,y)` with `x ∈ Γ`, let `Δ` be the `h`-class of `y`, and let `Y = X[Γ, Δ]`.  Then
`Y` is nontrivial (it has the edge `(x,y)`, and is not complete since
`deg(y) ≤ n₁/2 < |Γ|`) and semiregular (because `h` is equitable, Obs. 4.1.1), so
Lemma 4.1.5 applied to `Y` gives `g' : Δ → {i, 3}` whose refinement `h'` has classes of
size `≤ 2|Γ|/3 ≤ 4n₁/9` inside `Γ`.  Gluing `f := g` off `Δ` and `f := g'` on `Δ` gives a
3-coloring whose refinement `h*` refines both `h` and (on `Γ`) `h'`, so its classes have
size `≤ max(n₁ - |Γ|, 4n₁/9) < n₁/2`.

Two places need more than the printed text.  *"`Y` is not complete"* is
`exists_nbr_not_complete` (the paper's reason is not available here; see its docstring).
*"On `Γ`, the coloring `h*` is a refinement of `h'`"* is proved without transferring the
whole refinement process to `Y`: already after *one* round, the color of `u ∈ Γ` under `f`
determines the pair of numbers that one round of refinement of `(Γ, Δ; g')` gives `u`,
because the number of neighbors of `u` in `Δ` of `g'`-color `3` is the number of its
neighbors of `f`-color `3`, and the number of its neighbors in `Δ` is the same for all
`u ∈ Γ` by stability of `h` (Obs. 4.1.1).

decls.name: isTwin_iff
decls.docstring:
Observation 2.4.28 (Twins in bipartite graphs).  "Let `X = (Ω₁, Ω₂; E)` be a bipartite
graph and `x ≠ y` two non-isolated vertices.  Then `x` and `y` are twins if and only if
(a) `x, y` belong to the same part `Ωᵢ`, and (b) they have the same neighborhood in the
other part: `X̃(x) = X̃(y)` (where `X̃` denotes the symmetrization of `X`, see
Def. 2.4.16)."

The observation splits into four Lean statements.  Part (a) says that two non-isolated
vertices in different parts are never twins, in either order: `not_isTwin_inl_inr` and
`not_isTwin_inr_inl`.  Part (b) is stated once for each part: `isTwin_iff` for two
vertices of `Ω₁` and `isTwin_inr_iff` for two vertices of `Ω₂`.  Since all edges of `X`
point from `Ω₁` to `Ω₂`, the symmetrization neighborhood `X̃(x)` of a vertex `x ∈ Ω₁` is
its set of out-neighbors and that of a vertex `x ∈ Ω₂` is its set of in-neighbors.

decls.name: refineA_injective_of_no_twins
decls.docstring:
Observation 4.1.3.  "Let `X = (Ω₁, Ω₂; E)` be a bipartite graph.  If there are no twins
in `Ω₁` then individualizing each element of `Ω₂` completely splits `Ω₁`."

Individualizing every element of `Ω₂` is the coloring `f = id : Ω₂ → Ω₂`; "completely
splits `Ω₁`" is that the resulting coloring of `Ω₁` is injective.  (Observation 2.4.28(b),
`Babai.BipGraph.isTwin_inl_iff_aux`, identifies twins in `Ω₁` with equality of
neighborhoods.)

links.rationale: Formalizes Observation 4.1.3 (PDF p. 47) — Observation 4.1.3.  "Let `X = (Ω₁, Ω₂; E)` be a bipartite graph.  If there are no twins in `Ω₁` then individualizing each element of `Ω₂` completely splits `Ω₁`."

decls.name: d'
decls.docstring:
§9.7, Case 3.  The arity at which the Design Lemma is applied to `H`:
`d' = min(d₁, n₂ − d₁)`.

§9.7 writes `d₁`, and applies the Design Lemma (Theorem 8.1.2) to *"`H`, viewed as a
`d₁`-ary relational structure"*, without checking Theorem 8.1.2's hypothesis
`d₁ ≤ n₂/2`, which need not hold.  The **bipartite complement** `H^c = {V₂ ∖ E | E ∈ 𝓔}`
is `(n₂ − d₁)`-uniform, simple, and has the same automorphism group, hence the same
twins and the same symmetry defect, as `H`; and a canonical object on `V₂` for `H^c` is
one for `H`.  So Case 3 may be run on whichever of `H`, `H^c` has the smaller rank, and
that rank is `d'`.  See the entry *"§9.7 Case 3: `d₁ ≤ n₂/2` is not checked"* in
the corrected paper.

Since `d' ≤ d₁`, the branch costs only drop.

decls.name: nbhd_injective
decls.docstring:
§9.7.  *"This hypergraph has no multiple edges because there are no twins in `V₁`."*
Two different points of `V₁` have different neighborhoods.

The reason is the Claim of step 8 of §9.4 (`Babai.claim_9_4_step8`), which is Theorem 3.4.11
(*"no twins in primitive color"*) applied to the constituent `Rᵢ` of the link: `X₁` is a
UPCC, hence primitive (the field `upcc₁` of `Babai.IsBipartiteCase`), and the constituent is
nontrivial — it is nonempty because `Babai.BlkCaseObj.linkColor` is a color that occurs on
`V₁ × V₂`, and it is not complete because the link is nontrivial (the field
`link_nontrivial`), i.e. a second color occurs there.  The form of Theorem 3.4.11 that is
used is `Babai.PartitionStructure.nbr_ne_of_primitive`, which is literally *"distinct
vertices of the tail class have distinct `R_k`-neighbourhoods"*.

Note that the field `noTwins₁` of `Babai.IsBlockDesignCase` is **not** enough: it says that
no two points of `V₁` are twins for the whole coloring `c`, while what is needed here is
that no two of them have the same neighborhood in the **single** constituent
`Babai.BlkCaseObj.linkColor`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 3.4.11 (No twins in primitive color) (PDF p. 37) — §9.7.  *"This hypergraph has no multiple edges because there are no twins in `V₁`."* Two different points of `V₁` have different neighborhoods.

decls.name: nbhd_ncard_uniform
decls.docstring:
§9.7.  *"`H` … is uniform of rank `d₁`"*: all the neighborhoods `X(v)`, `v ∈ V₁`, have
the same size.

This is the semiregularity of the constituent `Rᵢ` of the link that step 8 of §9.4 picks
out: `Rᵢ` is a constituent of the coherent configuration `X` of step 3 of §9.4 (the field
`coherent` of `Babai.IsBipartiteCase`), and by Obs. 3.3.5 (degree awareness,
`Babai.PartitionStructure.outDegC_eq_of_vcolor_eq`) the out-degree in a fixed color depends
only on the vertex color, which is the same for all the vertices of `V₁`.

(The statement is not vacuous in the degenerate cases: for `d₁ = 0` it says that all
neighborhoods are empty, and for `V₁` a single point it is trivial.)

decls.name: numBlocks_ne_two_mul_d₁
decls.docstring:
§9.7, Case 1, entry 41 of the corrected paper.  `n₂ ≠ 2d₁`.

The boundary `n₂ = 2d₁` is the one case in which neither the labels `X(v)` nor their
complements satisfy the constraint `2t + 1 ≤ k` of Def. 3.2.9, so that
`Babai.isJohnsonColoring_of_labels` does not apply.  It is excluded by the primitivity of
`X₁`: the scheme `J(2d₁, d₁)` is imprimitive, its constituent `|S ∖ T| = d₁` being the
perfect matching `S ↔ V₂ ∖ S`; that relation is *"`u` and `v` have no common neighbour"*, an
intersection number of the coherent configuration `X`, hence a union of constituents of
`X₁`, each of them a non-empty subgraph of a perfect matching — contradicting the
primitivity of `X₁`.

The proof runs the argument of entry 41 inside the coherent configuration `X` of step 3 of
§9.4, where *"the number of common neighbours"* is an intersection number
(`Babai.PartitionStructure.ncard_inter_nbr_eq_interNum`) and so depends on a pair of
vertices of `V₁` only through its color.  Write `L = X(x₀)` for the label of one point `x₀`
of `V₁`.  Case 1 makes `V₂ ∖ L`, which has `n₂ − d₁ = d₁` blocks, again a hyperedge, say
`X(y₀)`; and `x₀ ≠ y₀` because `L` is not empty.  Let `ℓ` be the color of `(x₀, y₀)` in
`X₁`.  Every `ℓ`-edge `(u,v)` then has `|X(u) ∩ X(v)| = |X(x₀) ∩ X(y₀)| = 0`, so
`X(u) = V₂ ∖ X(v)`, because both have `d₁ = n₂/2` blocks.  *"Same or complementary label"*
is an equivalence relation, so by the weak connectivity of the `ℓ`-constituent — `X₁` is a
UPCC, hence primitive, and `ℓ` is off-diagonal — every point of `V₁` has label `L` or
`V₂ ∖ L`.  The labels are distinct (`Babai.BlkCaseObj.nbhd_injective`), so `V₁` has at most
two points, while a UPCC has at least three vertices
(`Babai.BipCaseData.three_le_ncard_part₁`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 3.2.9 (Johnson graph) (PDF p. 32) — §9.7, Case 1, entry 41 of the corrected paper.  `n₂ ≠ 2d₁`.

decls.name: upccBip_defect₁
decls.docstring:
§9.8, step 3.  **The symmetry defect of `V₁` in the returned graph is at least
`1/2`.**  (Claim of §9.8, version 2.5, lines 4333-4336.)

A set of twins of `V₁` has one `f`-color (`Babai.VColBipBlk.isTwin_iff`), so it lies
either inside `R_m⁻(B₀)` or inside its complement in `V₁`.  In the first case its members
have the same `m`-neighborhood among the blocks of `R_ℓ(B₀)`, so it has at most
`|R_m⁻(B₀)|/2 ≤ n₁/2` points (`Babai.BlkCaseObj.upccStep2_local_twins`).  In the second
case it has at most `n₁ - |R_m⁻(B₀)| ≤ n₁/2` points, because `m` is dominant at `B₀`.

decls.name: upccStep2Out

§9.8, step 3.  **The outcomes of step 3**: one returned graph per individualized
vertex `x ∈ V₂` at which the link has a dominant color.

`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.of_outcomes_sub` asks that *every* member of the family be a
solution, and the symmetry defect of the returned graph is `≥ 1/2` exactly when the link
has a dominant color at the individualized vertex; so the family of the individualized
vertices is filtered by that condition, which is a condition on the object alone and is
therefore invariant under isomorphisms.  (By the semiregularity of the constituents of the
link the condition in fact holds at every vertex of `V₂` as soon as it holds at one, but
the filter avoids the appeal to §3.4.)

decls.name: Cat
decls.docstring:
§6.  A *category* in the sense of the paper: a concrete, faithful Brandt groupoid whose
points all lie in the ambient type `Ω`.

*"The objects `X` have an underlying set `□(X)` and the morphisms are mappings between the
objects (bijections in our case) ... every morphism is invertible ... `□` is faithful,
i.e., if objects `X` and `Y` have the same underlying set `□(X) = □(Y)` and the identity
map on this set is a morphism between `X` and `Y` then `X = Y`."*

The underlying set of an object is the index `s : Set Ω` of the type `Obj s` it lives in.

links.rationale: §6.  A *category* in the sense of the paper: a concrete, faithful Brandt groupoid whose points all lie in the ambient type `Ω`.

decls.name: sub
decls.docstring:
§6.  The category whose objects on `s` are the objects of `K` on a **subset** of `s`,
with the bijections of `s` that carry one subset onto the other by a morphism of `K`.

A canonical embedding satisfies `□(F(X)) ⊆ □(X)` with `□(F(X))` varying with `X`, so this
is the category in which an outcome of a step of §9 lives when it is an object on a subset
of the input's vertex set (the bipartite graph `X̄` of Lemma 9.3.1, the Johnson scheme of
Theorems 9.2.1–9.2.3).  The projection `Babai.Cat.subProj` back to `K` is a canonical
embedding, which is what makes `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.of_outcomes_sub` a special case of
`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.of_outcomes_emb`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Lemma 9.3.1 (UPCC-to-bipartite) (PDF p. 73) — §6.  The category whose objects on `s` are the objects of `K` on a **subset** of `s`, with the bijections of `s` that carry one subset onto the other by a morphism of `K`.

decls.name: IsEquipartitionOn
decls.docstring:
Procedure Align, line 7 (A): the structure `X` gives a **nontrivial equipartition** of
the color class `Δ ⊆ Γ`.

The equivalence relation is `X.ecol γ δ = 0` (line 7 (A): *"let `Y` be this equivalence
relation on `Δ_j`"*); `Γ*` is its set of blocks.  *Nontrivial* means the blocks are
neither singletons nor all of `Δ`; *equipartition* means they all have the same size.  The
size is stated as `b`, so `|Γ*| · b = |Δ|`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure Align (PDF p. 110) — Procedure Align, line 7 (A): the structure `X` gives a **nontrivial equipartition** of the color class `Δ ⊆ Γ`.

decls.name: IsJohnsonOn
decls.docstring:
Procedure Align, line 7 (B): the color class `Δ ⊆ Γ` **is the vertex set of a Johnson
scheme** `J(m*, t*)` with `t* ≥ 2`.

*"identify `Δ_j` with `Δ_j = (Γ* choose t*)` where `|Γ*| = m*`"*: there is a bijection `e`
of `Δ` with the `t*`-subsets of `[m*]` under which the pair coloring of `X` is the Johnson
coloring `|S ∖ T|` of Def. 3.2.13.  The parameter constraints of Def. 3.2.9 are `t* ≥ 2`
and `m* ≥ 2t* + 1`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 3.2.9 (Johnson graph) (PDF p. 32) — Procedure Align, line 7 (B): the color class `Δ ⊆ Γ` **is the vertex set of a Johnson scheme** `J(m*, t*)` with `t* ≥ 2`.

`V` (the paper: "The naive refinement process clearly terminates in `k ≤ n-1` rounds"),

canonical.  `stableRefine_isStable` shows that the result is stable, so this is the
paper's `X*`.

decls.name: Corollary_12_0_10
decls.docstring:
§12, **Corollary 12.0.10** (TopAction4).

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a transitive permutation group and `ϕ : G → S(Γ)` a giant
> representation where `|Γ| = m ≥ max{16, 4 + 2 log₂ n}`.  Let `x, y : Ω → Σ` be strings.
> Assume `Γ` has a canonical coloring with respect to `x` with a color class `C` of size
> `|C| > m/2` such that the restriction of `Aut_G(x)^ϕ` to `C` is a giant (includes
> `A(C)`).  Then we can find `Iso_G(x,y)` by recursively calling `≤ 6k` instances of String
> Isomorphism with window size `≤ n/k` for some `|C| ≤ k ≤ n`, plus a number of instances
> of total size `≤ n` and maximum size `≤ 2n/3`.
>
> *Proof.*  Since `m ≥ max{9, 2 log₂ n}`, by the Main Structure Theorem (Theorem 10.5.1)
> `Ω` can be divided into standard blocks on which `G` acts as a Johnson group. […]  Let
> `C_x = C`.  By canonicity, there is a corresponding color class `C_y ⊆ Γ` (which may be
> empty).  Apply items 1 to 6 of Procedure Align (Sec. 14.1) with `X(x) := C_x` and
> `X(y) := C_y`. […]  Now we process `Ω(C)` via Cor. 12.0.8.  This can be done because
> `|C| > m/2 ≥ max{8, 2 + log₂ n}`.  Then proceed to the remaining color classes in
> accordance with the Chain Rule.  The bound `2n/3` on the length of the remaining color
> classes comes from Lemma 7.2.1.

The hypotheses are transcribed as follows.  `m ≥ max{16, 4 + 2 log₂ n}` is `Babai.HugeM`;
"`Γ` has a canonical coloring with respect to `x`" is `Babai.IsCanonicalColoring` (the
fragment of Section 6 that the proof uses, see `Workspace/TopAction/Align.lean`), with `C`
the class of the color `c` for `x`; `|C| > m/2` is `m < 2|C|`.

"The restriction of `Aut_G(x)^ϕ` to `C` is a giant (includes `A(C)`)" is `hgiantC`: it asks
that the *restriction map* `(Aut_G(x)^ϕ)_C → S(C)` have image containing `A(C)`, i.e. that
for every `α ∈ A(C)` — written here as an even permutation of `Γ` fixing `Γ ∖ C`
pointwise, which is the same thing — there be a `β ∈ Aut_G(x)^ϕ` with `β|_C = α|_C`.  The
element `β` may move `Γ ∖ C` arbitrarily.  The window-size bounds are stated without
division: `k·|Δ| ≤ n` for the first family, `3·|Δ| ≤ 2n` for the second, and the total size
of the second family is at most `n`.

**The reduction.**  The statement is about the *named* reduction
`Babai.topAction4Reduction`, built from the paper's steps, not about an existentially
quantified one:

* Procedure Align lines 1–3 with `X(z) = C_z`: if `|C_x| ≠ |C_y|` the answer is `∅`
 (`Babai.Align_reject`); otherwise the aligning `σ` of line 2 exists
 (`Babai.exists_alignColorElt`: `A(Γ) ≤ G^ϕ` is transitive on the subsets of a given
 size), `y' = y^{σ⁻¹}` has `C_{y'} = C_x` and `Iso_G(x,y) = Iso_G(x,y')σ`
 (`Babai.Align_shift`), and `Iso_G(x,y') = Iso_{G₁}(x,y')` for the group
 `G₁ = ϕ⁻¹((S(Γ))_C) = G_C` of line 2 (iv) (`Babai.stabOn`).
* Lines 4–6: the coloring `(C, Γ ∖ C)` of `Γ` lifts to the coloring of `Ω` whose classes
 are `Ω_j = {u | |T(u) ∩ C| = j}` (`Babai.omegaCut`), with `Ω_t = Ω(C)`.  The Chain Rule
 starts with `Ω(C)`, which is processed by the window version of Cor. 12.0.8
 (`Babai.Corollary_12_0_8_window` about `Babai.windowTopAction3Reduction`, with the giant
 representation `Babai.phiCFin` of the group induced on the window), and continues over
 `Ω_0, …, Ω_{t−1}`.
* The `2n/3` bound on the remaining classes is Lemma 7.2.1 (a) multiplied by the common
 size of the standard blocks (`Babai.three_mul_ncard_omegaCut_le`), except for the class
 `Ω_0 = Ω(Γ ∖ C)`, whose color vector is exceptional for Lemma 7.2.1 and which is bounded
 instead by `|Γ ∖ C| ≤ m/2` (`Babai.two_mul_ncard_omegaCut_zero_le`).

**How many instances the second family has.**  The paper bounds the second family by its
total size only.  Sec. 15 also needs their number, so the conclusion records
`rest.length ≤ t` — the Chain Rule visits each of the classes `Ω_0, …, Ω_{t−1}` at most
once — and `t ≤ n`, which follows from `4t < m` (Theorem 10.5.1 (a)) together with
`m < 2|C| ≤ 2k ≤ 2n`.  These are extra true clauses; nothing in the paper's conclusion is
dropped.

decls.name: Corollary_12_0_6
decls.docstring:
§12, **Corollary 12.0.6** (TopAction2).

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a transitive permutation group and `ϕ : G → S(Γ)` a giant
> representation, where `|Γ| = m > max{8, 2 + log₂ n}`.  Given these data and the strings
> `x, y : Ω → Σ`, we can achieve the following by recursively calling `≤ 6k` instances of
> String Isomorphism with window size `≤ n/k` for some `m ≤ k ≤ n`, at polynomial cost per
> instance:
> (i) decide whether `ϕ` maps `Iso_G(x,y)` onto a giant coset, i. e.,
>     `Iso_G(x,y)^ϕ ≥ A(Γ)τ` for some `τ ∈ S(Γ)`;
> (ii) if the answer is affirmative, find `Iso_G(x,y)`.
>
> *Proof.*  First assume `G^ϕ = A(Γ)`.  Apply Prop. 12.0.5 to `H := A(Γ)` with `S` a pair
> of generators of `H`.  This reduces our questions to three instances of `N`-isomorphism
> where `N = ker(ϕ)`.  Now `N` is intransitive with `k` orbits for some `k ≤ n`.  Each
> orbit has equal length (because `N ◁ G`) so Luks's Chain Rule performs the desired
> reduction, calling `3k` instances of window size `n/k`.  We need to justify the
> inequality `k ≥ m`. […]  Now if `G^ϕ = S(Γ)` then apply Luks descent, reducing
> `G`-isomorphism to two instances of `G₁`-isomorphism where `G₁ = ϕ⁻¹(A(Γ))`.

The hypothesis `|Γ| = m > max{8, 2 + log₂ n}` is `Babai.LargeK m n`.  The window-size
bound `≤ n/k` is stated without `Nat` division, as `k · |Δ| ≤ n`.  The value of the
reduction is `none` when the answer to (i) is "no" and `some Iso_G(x,y)` when it is "yes".
The RAM round is `Algo.top2Round` (`Workspace/Algo/TopWindowRound.lean`,
`Algo.implements_top2Round`).

The statement is about the **named** reduction `Babai.topAction2Reduction`, built from the
paper's two cases, and `k = Babai.orbCount ϕ` is the number of orbits of `N = ker(ϕ)`, as
in the proof.  (An earlier version of this file stated the corollary as
`∃ k R, … R.run = …`, which `R := .done answer` satisfies with no calls at all; that form
carries no call accounting.  With a named reduction the trivial witness is not available:
`run_topAction2Reduction` is a theorem about `topAction2Reduction`.)

Ingredients: `Babai.giantAReduction` (Prop. 12.0.5 with `H = A(Γ)` and the two generators
`Babai.altGens`, each of the three `N`-instances expanded by the Chain Rule
`Babai.chainOverOrbits` over the `k` orbits of `N`); `Babai.strIso_descent` (Luks descent
with the two coset representatives `1` and `σ₀ = Babai.oddRep ϕ`);
`Babai.mapsOntoGiantCoset_iff_branches` for the correctness of the descent branch;
`Babai.orbCount_spec` for `m ≤ k ≤ n` and the common orbit length `n/k`.

One step of the paper's proof is replaced: the proof cites Lemma 10.3.1 for "`Ω` is
affected", but that lemma is stated (in the paper and here) for an epimorphism onto
`A(Γ)`, so it does not apply when `G^ϕ = S(Γ)`.  We use the paper's Theorem 10.3.5
instead; see `Babai.affected_of_transitive_giant` and the corresponding the corrected paper
entry.

decls.name: Corollary_12_0_6_orbit_count
decls.docstring:
Proof of Cor. 12.0.6: `N = ker(ϕ)` is intransitive, it has `k` orbits for some
`m ≤ k ≤ n`, and all its orbits have the common length `n/k`.

> Now `N` is intransitive with `k` orbits for some `k ≤ n`.  Each orbit has equal length
> (because `N ◁ G`) …  We need to justify the inequality `k ≥ m`.  Lemma 10.3.1 … says
> that `Ω` is affected.  Then the Affected Orbit Lemma (Cor. 10.3.7) asserts that each
> orbit of `N` has length `≤ n/m`.

The conclusion `(orbit N u).ncard * k = n` is the paper's "each orbit has length `n/k`",
stated without `Nat` division.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Lemma 10.3.1 (PDF p. 85) — Proof of Cor. 12.0.6: `N = ker(ϕ)` is intransitive, it has `k` orbits for some `m ≤ k ≤ n`, and all its orbits have the common length `n/k`.

decls.name: Corollary_12_0_8
decls.docstring:
§12, **Corollary 12.0.8** (TopAction3).

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a transitive permutation group and `ϕ : G → S(Γ)` a giant
> representation, where `|Γ| = m > max{8, 2 + log₂ n}`.  Given these data and the strings
> `x, y : Ω → Σ`, we can achieve the following by recursively calling `≤ 6k` instances of
> String Isomorphism with window size `≤ n/k` for some `m ≤ k ≤ n`, at polynomial cost per
> instance:
> (i) decide whether `ϕ` maps `Aut_G(x)` onto a giant, i. e., `Aut_G(x)^ϕ ≥ A(Γ)`;
> (i) if the answer is affirmative, find `Iso_G(x,y)`.
>
> *Proof.*  To answer (i), apply Cor. cor:topaction with `y = x`.  Assume the answer is
> affirmative.  If `Iso_G(x,y)^ϕ` is a giant coset, we are done by Cor. 12.0.6.  We claim
> that if `Iso_G(x,y)^ϕ` is not a giant coset then `x` and `y` are not `G`-isomorphic. […]

Two printing slips in version 2.5, logged in the corrected paper (kind "typo/cross-reference"):
the broken cross-reference "Cor. cor:topaction" is Cor. 12.0.6, and the second item, again
labelled "(i)", is (ii).

Note that applying Cor. 12.0.6 with `y = x` answers (i): `Iso_G(x,x) = Aut_G(x)` and a
giant coset `A(Γ)τ` contained in `Aut_G(x)^ϕ`, a group, forces `A(Γ) ≤ Aut_G(x)^ϕ`
(`Babai.mapsOntoGiantCoset_self_iff`).  The two applications share the value of `k`, since
`k` depends only on `G` and `ϕ` (`Babai.orbCount`), not on the strings.

**Call bound.**  The printed bound `≤ 6k` is kept.  The paper's *route* does not give it:
it makes two applications of Cor. 12.0.6, each costing `6k` in the case `G^ϕ = S(Γ)`
(`3k` for Prop. 12.0.5 plus the Chain Rule, doubled by the Luks descent), so it gives
`12k`.  The second application is avoidable, because step (i) already returns
`Aut_{G₁}(x)`; `Babai.topAction3Reduction` follows the repaired route (`3k + 2k = 5k`
calls) described above it and in the the corrected paper Cor. 12.0.8.  Only the
proof changes; the statement is as printed.

links.rationale: Formalizes Corollary 12.0.8 (TopAction3) (PDF p. 98) — §12, **Corollary 12.0.8** (TopAction3).

decls.name: Corollary_12_0_8_giant_coset
decls.docstring:
The step of the proof of Cor. 12.0.8:

> We claim that if `Iso_G(x,y)^ϕ` is not a giant coset then `x` and `y` are not
> `G`-isomorphic.  Indeed, if `x ≅_G y` then `Iso_G(x,y) = Aut_G(x)σ` where `σ` is any
> element of `Iso_G(x,y)`.  It follows that `Iso_G(x,y)^ϕ = Aut_G(x)^ϕ σ̄` is a giant coset
> (where `σ̄ = σ^ϕ`).

Stated in the contrapositive-free direction: if `Aut_G(x)^ϕ` is a giant and `x` and `y` are
`G`-isomorphic, then `Iso_G(x,y)^ϕ` contains a giant coset.

decls.name: Corollary_12_0_8_window
decls.docstring:
§12, **Corollary 12.0.8 on a window**.

Let `Δ ⊆ Ω` be `K`-invariant, let `K̄ = K^Δ ≤ S(Δ)` be transitive on `Δ` and let
`ϕ : K̄ → S(Γ)` be a giant representation with `|Γ| = m > max{8, 2 + log₂ |Δ|}`.  Then the
same `≤ 6k` instances of window size `≤ |Δ|/k`, for some `m ≤ k ≤ |Δ|`, decide whether `ϕ`
maps `Aut_{K̄}(x|_Δ)` onto a giant and, if so, find `Iso^Δ_K(x,y)`.

This is Cor. 12.0.8 (`Babai.Corollary_12_0_8`) read on `Δ` and transported to `Ω`: the
window sizes and the number of calls are unchanged by the transport
(`Babai.SIReduction.calls_window`, `Babai.windowSize_windowInstance`), and the value computed
is transported by `Babai.wIso_eq_windowPreim`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Corollary 12.0.8 (TopAction3) (PDF p. 98) — §12, **Corollary 12.0.8 on a window**.

decls.name: exists_isBase_card_le
decls.docstring:
**[DiM, Thm. 3.3B]** (Bochert 1889), first statement.  A primitive group `G ≤ Sym(n)`
which does not contain `Alt(n)` has a base of size at most `n/2`.

Proof of [DiM]: let `Σ` be a base of minimal size and suppose `|Σ| > n/2`.  Then
`Δ := Ω \ Σ` is not a base, so some `x ≠ 1` has support inside `Σ`; pick `a ∈ supp(x)`.
`Σ \ {a}` is not a base, so some `y ≠ 1` has support inside `Δ ∪ {a}`; as `Σ` is a base,
`a ∈ supp(y)`.  Hence `supp(x) ∩ supp(y) = {a}` and `G` contains a 3-cycle
(Exercise 1.6.7), so `G ≥ Alt(n)` by Theorem 3.3A (Mathlib's
`Equiv.Perm.alternatingGroup_le_of_isPreprimitive_of_isThreeCycle_mem`).

links.rationale: **[DiM, Thm. 3.3B]** (Bochert 1889), first statement.  A primitive group `G ≤ Sym(n)` which does not contain `Alt(n)` has a base of size at most `n/2`.

decls.name: observation_8_1_3
decls.docstring:
**Observation 8.1.3**, §8.1.

> Let `DL(α)` be the statement of the Design Lemma for a particular `α ≥ 1/2`.  If
> `1 > α' ≥ α ≥ 1/2` then `DL(α')` follows from `DL(α)`.

The bound `α' < 1` is not used by the proof and is omitted (for `α' ≥ 1` the hypothesis
`defect ≥ 1 − α'` holds for every structure, and the proof goes through unchanged).

*Proof* (the paper's).  Let `U` be a largest symmetric subset of `Ω` and `β = |U|/n`;
the hypothesis of `DL(α')` is `β ≤ α'`.  *Case 1*, `β ≤ α`: apply `DL(α)`.  Outcome (a)
stays (a); (b) and (c) stay (b) and (c) if the dominant class `C` has `|C| > α'n`; if
`αn < |C| ≤ α'n`, the coloring `(C, Ω ∖ C)` gives outcome (a) of `DL(α')`.  *Case 2*,
`α < β ≤ α'`: the coloring `(U, Ω ∖ U)` gives outcome (a) of `DL(α')`.

Here `β > α` is read as "some twin equivalence class is `α`-dominant" (the twin classes are
the maximal symmetric subsets, Obs. 2.3.12), and `U` is that class; the two-class colorings
are `Babai.DesignAbstract.bigTwinColor` and `Babai.DesignAbstract.midClassColor`, and they
are canonical because `U` and `C` are (`Babai.DesignAbstract.obsAssign_canonical`).  In a
case (a) the string is the one `DL(α)` returns, or the empty string in Case 2 (no
individualization is needed there).  The paper's "(case (a) or (b) holds for `DL(α')`)"
for an outcome (b) with `αn < |C| ≤ α'n` is outcome (a), as for (c).

links.rationale: Formalizes Observation 8.1.3 (PDF p. 65) — **Observation 8.1.3**, §8.1.

decls.name: observation_8_1_3_kWL
decls.docstring:
**Observation 8.1.3**, §8.1, for the objects of the paper.

> If `1 > α' ≥ α ≥ 1/2` then `DL(α')` follows from `DL(α)`.

`DL(α)` is supplied by the `k`-WL objects (`theorem_8_1_2_DL`); the objects of `DL(α')` are
the ones the paper's proof builds from them (`obsAssign α α' (kwlAssign α)`: the two-class
colorings `(U, Ω ∖ U)` and `(C, Ω ∖ C)`, or else the `k`-WL objects unchanged).  They are
canonical and reach an outcome of Theorem 8.1.2 for `α'` on every structure with
`2 ≤ k ≤ n/2` and symmetry defect `≥ 1 − α'`.

decls.name: theorem_8_1_2_imp_8_1_5
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 8.1.2 ⇒ Theorem 8.1.5**, the first half of the "Proof of equivalence", §8.1.

> Outcome (a) is identical with outcome (i).  In case (b), let `c'` denote the given
> canonical coloring of `Ω`, `C` the dominant `c'`-class, and `E` the equivalence relation
> on `C` corresponding to the given equipartition. […] The structure `Y = (C,d)` is clearly
> a non-clique coherent configuration on `C`.  In case (c), let `C` be the dominant color
> class and `Y = (C,d)` be the given UPCC.  Let us now define the coherent configuration
> `X' = (Ω, c'')` required by (ii). […] It is easy to see that `X*` is coherent; `C` is its
> dominant color class; and `X*[C] = Y` is not a clique.

Proved with the repaired `c''` (`Babai.DesignAbstract.glue`, diagonal separated; see its
docstring and the corrected paper, "Proof of equivalence 8.1.2 ⇒ 8.1.5").  The paper's
`X*[C] = Y` holds up to the names of the colors: `X*[C]` has the classes of `Y`.

decls.name: theorem_8_1_5_kWL
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 8.1.5** (Design lemma, rephrased), §8.1, for the objects of the paper.

*"Let `1/2 ≤ α < 1` be a threshold parameter.  Let `X = (Ω, R)` be a `k`-ary relational
structure with `n = |Ω|` vertices, `2 ≤ k ≤ n/2`, and symmetry defect `≥ 1 − α`.  Then in
time `n^{O(k)}` we can find a value `ℓ ≤ k − 1` and a string `x⃗ = x₁ … x_ℓ ∈ Ω^⟨ℓ⟩` of `ℓ`
distinct vertices such that by individualizing each `x_j` we obtain either*

*(i) a canonical coloring of `Ω` with no dominant color, or*

*(ii) a canonical (classical) coherent configuration `X*` on vertex set `Ω` such that the
subconfiguration induced on the dominant vertex-color class of `X*` is not a clique.*

*Canonicity in the above statements is relative to `x⃗`."*

The objects are the ones of the paper's "Proof of equivalence" (8.1.2 ⇒ 8.1.5) built from
the `k`-WL objects of Theorem 8.1.2: the coloring `c'` of `X_x⃗`, and `X* = (Ω, c'')`
(`gluedAssign α (kwlAssign α)`, with the repaired `c''` of the corrected paper, "Proof of
equivalence 8.1.2 ⇒ 8.1.5").  Canonicity is the first conjunct; outcomes (i) and (ii) are
`Outcome815`.  The running-time clause is pending.

The direct form with `X* = (X_x⃗)^{(2)}` is `Babai.KAryRelStruct.theorem_8_1_5`.

decls.name: DesignOutcomes
decls.docstring:
§8.1, Theorem 8.1.2, in the form §9 consumes it: the outcome is *either* a colored
partition of the vertex set *or* a UPCC canonically embedded on the dominant color class.

Outcomes (a) and (b) of Theorem 8.1.2 are both a canonical coloring of `Ω`, which becomes
a colored partition of `Ω` (in case (b) the dominant class carries the canonical
equipartition); they are the first summand.  Outcome (c) is the second summand: the UPCC
on the dominant class.

*The coloring of outcome (c).*  Theorem 8.1.2 (c) returns the coloring of `Ω` as well as
the UPCC.  §9 does not use it: in the proof of Theorem 9.2.3 the partition of `Ω` outside
the dominant class is rebuilt from scratch by the transfer of Lemma 9.3.1
(`Babai.extendPartition`), which puts `Ω \ C` into a single block of a new color.  So the
second summand carries only the UPCC.

nontrivial irreflexive biregular digraph is `≥ 1/2`."

Prop. 2.4.11 gives `|A| ≤ n/2`.

Proposition 2.4.11 (Independent sets in biregular digraphs).  "Let `X = (Ω, E)` be a
non-empty biregular digraph.  Then `X` has no independent set of size greater than `n/2`
where `n = |Ω|`."

all edges emanating from `A`, so `d(n - |A|) ≥ d|A|`.

decls.name: cases
decls.docstring:
§6.  **A canonical case distinction.**  Let `P` be a property of the objects of `C`
that is invariant under isomorphism.  If the full subcategory of the objects satisfying `P`
and the full subcategory of those not satisfying it each admit a reduction finding an
object with the *same* property `Good`, then `C` does, at the larger of the two costs.

The proof normalizes the two reductions (`FindsAtMultCost.exists_normal`), so that their
tuples live on `□X`, and glues them: the category of versions of the glued reduction is the
disjoint union of the two categories of versions, and the version of `X` decides which
branch `X` is in.  (The two branches must land in the same output category `K`; in §9 this
is the category of "a colored partition or a Johnson scheme".)

decls.name: strongInduction
decls.docstring:
§6, §9.5.  **A reduction may call itself on strictly smaller instances.**

Let `m` be a measure on the objects of `C` that is invariant under isomorphism (`hm`) and
bounded by `N₀` (`hbd`).  Suppose that for every `N`, a reduction on the full subcategory of
the objects of measure `< N` yields a reduction on the full subcategory of the objects of
measure exactly `N`, at the same cost and for the same property found (`step`).  Then the
reduction exists on all of `C`.

This is the form of `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases` that §9.4 needs: Procedure Bipartite
Split-or-Johnson reduces Theorem 9.2.2 to itself on instances on which the measure of
progress of §9.5 has dropped, so the reduction being proved must be available inside its
own proof, on the smaller instances only.

The proof is the induction on `N` of the statement "the reduction exists on the objects of
measure `< N`".  The step splits the objects of measure `< N+1` into those of measure `= N`
and those of measure `< N` — a canonical case distinction, since `m` is an isomorphism
invariant — and applies `step N` to the first part and the induction hypothesis to the
second (`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases`).  The base case is the empty category.

decls.name: exists_nontrivial_skeleton
decls.docstring:
Proposition 2.5.10.  "Let `H` be a nontrivial `d`-uniform simple hypergraph with `n`
vertices and `m` edges, where `d ≤ n/2`.  Then there exists `t ≤ min{d, 1 + log₂ m}` such
that the `t`-skeleton `H^(t)` is nontrivial."

Paper's proof: choose `t = d` if `d ≤ 1 + log₂ m`, otherwise `t = 1 + ⌊log₂ m⌋`.  For
independently uniformly random vertices `x₁,…,x_t`, the probability that all belong to a
fixed edge `E` is `(|E|/n)^t ≤ 1/2^t`, so the probability that they all belong to some
edge is less than `m/2^t < 1`; hence `H^(t)` is not complete, and it is not empty since
`t ≤ d`.

decls.docstring:

BIBD with parameters `(v, b, r, k, λ)` we have `b ≥ v`."

decls.name: fisher_classical
decls.docstring:
Theorem 3.4.27 (Fisher's inequality), the classical statement that the paper recalls:
for a BIBD (so `λ ≥ 1`) with parameters `(v, b, r, k, λ)` we have `b ≥ v`.

The paper gives no reference key: "We recall Fisher's inequality for BIBDs (balanced
incomplete block designs)."  The classical statement allows repeated blocks, which is what
`Hypergraph` records (`b` counts a multiset of edges).

Proof (the standard linear-algebra argument).  Let `N` be the `v × b` incidence matrix
over `ℚ`, `N(x,i) = 1` if `x ∈ Eᵢ` and `0` otherwise.  Then `(N Nᵀ)(x,y)` is the number of
blocks containing both `x` and `y`, so `N Nᵀ = (r − λ)I + λJ`.  For every `z : V → ℚ`,
`zᵀ (N Nᵀ) z = (r − λ)∑ z(x)² + λ (∑ z(x))²`, and `r > λ` (`lam_lt_r`), so `N Nᵀ` sends no
nonzero vector to `0`; hence `det(N Nᵀ) ≠ 0` and `rank(N Nᵀ) = v`.  Since
`rank(N Nᵀ) ≤ rank N ≤ b`, we get `v ≤ b`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Definition 3.4.26 (PDF p. 41) — Theorem 3.4.27 (Fisher's inequality), the classical statement that the paper recalls: for a BIBD (so `λ ≥ 1`) with parameters `(v, b, r, k, λ)` we have `b ≥ v`.

decls.name: skeleton_defect
decls.docstring:
Lemma 2.5.12 (Skeleton defect lemma).  "Let `H = (V, E)` be a nontrivial, regular,
`d`-uniform simple hypergraph with `n` vertices and `m` edges where `d ≤ n/2`.  Let
`(7/4) log₂ m ≤ t ≤ (3/4) d`.  Then the symmetry defect of the `t`-skeleton `H^(t)` is
greater than `1/4`."

The upper bound on `t` is stated here in the slightly more general form
`t ≤ ⌈(3/4) d⌉`; the printed hypothesis is the corollary
`Babai.Hypergraph.skeleton_defect_of_le`.  The generalization is free: the proof uses the
upper bound only to choose a `t`-subset of `S ∩ E` where `|S ∩ E| ≥ (3/4) d`, and `|S ∩ E|`
is an integer, so `|S ∩ E| ≥ ⌈(3/4) d⌉ ≥ t`.  It is what §9.7, Case 3b needs: there
`t = ⌈(7/4) log₂ n₁⌉` and only `(7/4) log₂ n₁ < (3/4) d₁` is available, which gives
`t ≤ ⌈(3/4) d₁⌉` but not `t ≤ (3/4) d₁` (see the corrected paper entry on §9.7 Case 3b).

Paper's proof: let `S` be a set of twins in `H` and suppose `|S| ≥ 3n/4`.  By
Prop. 2.5.11 there is an edge `E` with `|S ∩ E| ≥ (3/4)d ≥ t`; a `t`-subset `T ⊆ S ∩ E`
lies in `E^(t)`, and since `S` is a set of twins, all of `S choose t` lies in `E^(t)`.
Every edge of `H` contains at most `d choose t` of these `t`-sets, so
`m ≥ binom(|S|,t)/binom(d,t) > (3n/(4d))^t ≥ (3/2)^t > m`, Eq. (15), a contradiction.

Reading of the paper's proof: the proof must start from a
set `S` of twins **of `H^{(t)}`**, not of `H`.  The conclusion bounds the symmetry defect
of `H^{(t)}`, so the set to be bounded is a twin set of `H^{(t)}`; and the only place `S`
is used as a set of twins is the step `binom(S,t) ⊆ E^{(t)}`, which needs
`S(S) ≤ Aut(H^{(t)})` (Obs. 2.3.12).  Since `Aut(H) ≤ Aut(H^{(t)})`, a twin set of `H` is
a twin set of `H^{(t)}`, so the paper's phrasing is the weaker special case and the rest
of the argument goes through verbatim.

decls.name: twins_complete_not_twins_incidence
decls.docstring:
Remark 2.5.7.  "Note that twins in `H` are not necessarily twins in the incidence
graph `X(H)`.  For instance, if `H` is the complete `d`-uniform hypergraph where
`1 ≤ d < |V|` then all vertices are twins in `H` but there are no twins in `X(H)`."

The content of the remark is the contrast between the two conjuncts: any two distinct
vertices `x ≠ y` are twins in `H`, yet they are *not* twins in the incidence graph
`X(H)`, because with `1 ≤ d < |V|` some `d`-set contains `x` and not `y`.  The side
conditions are exactly the paper's `1 ≤ d < |V|`: for `d = 0` and for `d = |V|` the
hypergraph has a single edge and the two vertices *are* twins in `X(H)`.

hypergraph is simple; that is `no_twins_indices_completeUniform` below, a corollary of
`incidence_twins_iff`, not the point of the remark.

decls.name: IsCameronGroup
decls.docstring:
§11.2, **Definition 11.2.2**.

> `G ≤ S_n` is a *Cameron group* with parameters `s, t ≥ 1` and `k ≥ max(2t, 5)` if for
> some `s, t ≥ 1` and `k > 2t` we have `n = (k choose t)^s`, the socle of `G` is
> isomorphic to `A_k^s`, and `(A_k^(t))^s ≤ G ≤ S_k^(t) ≀ S_s` (wreath product, product
> action), moreover the induced action `G → S_s` on the direct factors of the socle is
> transitive.

Transcribed literally, including the two overlapping conditions on `k`: the paper states
both `k ≥ max(2t,5)` and `k > 2t` (together they say `k ≥ 5` and `k > 2t`, so one of the
two halves of `k ≥ max(2t,5)` is redundant).  We keep both, as printed.

The containments `(A_k^(t))^s ≤ G ≤ S_k^(t) ≀ S_s` identify the domain `Ω` (of size
`n = (k choose t)^s`) with `(Fin k choose t)^s`; the identification is the bijection `e`.

decls.name: IsCase3Output
decls.docstring:
§13.2, case (3): what the Claim delivers for a family of inputs `y : I → (Ω → Σ)`
(the paper's case is `I = Fin 2`, `y = ![x₁, x₂]`).

A family of `t`-ary relational structures `𝔷_i` on the sets `D_i`, with

* symmetry defect `≥ |D_i| − t + 1`, and `> m/2` in the form `m < 2·sd(𝔷_i)`;
* canonicity: every `G`-isomorphism `σ : x_i → x_j` induces a bijection `D_i → D_j`
 (namely the restriction of `σ^ϕ`, which exists by `Babai.canonical_fixedGamma`) and that
 bijection is an isomorphism `𝔷_i → 𝔷_j`.

This last clause is the paper's "canonically embedded … structure": the `D_i` are
canonical subsets of `Γ` and the structures on them commute with the isomorphisms of the
inputs.

decls.name: isPrimitive_onBlocks
decls.docstring:
§11.2 (the sentence after the proof of Theorem 11.1.9): for a minimal system of
imprimitivity, "`Ḡ` is a primitive group".

The proof: for a block of imprimitivity `𝒞 ⊆ ℬ` of the block action, the union `⋃ 𝒞` is a
block of imprimitivity of `G` inside `Δ` (using that the blocks of `ℬ` are pairwise
disjoint), so by maximality it is a single block or all of `Δ`, i.e. `𝒞` is a singleton or
all of `ℬ`; and `|Ḡ| ≥ 2` because `ℬ` has at least two blocks and `G` is transitive on
them.

The hypothesis `[Finite Ω]` is the paper's standing assumption "All groups in this paper
are finite" (§2.2): the paper's primitivity asks for `|Ḡ| ≥ 2`, and `Nat.card` of an
infinite group is `0`, so without finiteness the conclusion would fail for a purely
Lean-side reason.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 11.1.9 (Imprimitive Luks reduction) (PDF p. 92) — §11.2 (the sentence after the proof of Theorem 11.1.9): for a minimal system of imprimitivity, "`Ḡ` is a primitive group".

decls.name: IsMultiplyTransitive
decls.docstring:
§2.2.2.  "`G ≤ S(Ω)` is *`t`-transitive* if its induced action on the set of
`n(n-1)⋯(n-t+1)` ordered `t`-tuples of distinct elements is transitive."

The ordered `t`-tuples of distinct elements are `Fin t ↪ Ω`, and "transitive" is the
paper's notion (`Babai.IsTransitiveAction`: exactly one orbit).  In particular, if `G` is
`t`-transitive then such tuples exist, so `t ≤ |Ω|` (`Babai.le_card_of_multiplyTransitive`);
this is what distinguishes the notion from Mathlib's
`MulAction.IsMultiplyPretransitive`, which holds vacuously for `t > |Ω|`.  The bridge is
`Babai.isMultiplyTransitive_iff`.

"`G` is *doubly transitive*" (§2.2.2) is the case `t = 2`.

decls.name: JohnsonCaseData
decls.docstring:
§15, what lines 1–3 leave on the table.

Line 1 (Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, Sec. 11.3) ends in the Johnson case (Def. 11.4.1):
the instance is with respect to a group `K`, the window `Δ` is `K`-invariant, the group
`G = K^Δ` induced on the window is transitive, and `G` has a system `ℬ` of imprimitivity on
which it acts as a Johnson group `S_m^{(t)}` or `A_m^{(t)}`.  Line 3 adds the giant
representation `ϕ : G → S(Γ)`, `Γ` of size `m`, which the paper says is *"inferred from
`G`"*.

Two fields record facts that hold in the Johnson case but that this development does not
derive from the others, and that the construction of the data must therefore supply:

* `two_blocks` — the block system is nontrivial, which is what makes line 2 an
 *imprimitive* Luks reduction; in the Johnson case the number of blocks is `C(m,t) ≥ 2`;
* `window_large` — the window has at least `64` points.  This is not an extra hypothesis
 on any theorem: line 2 of Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (Sec. 11.3) reads *"if `|G| < C₀`
 for some absolute constant `C₀` then compute `Iso_G(x,y)` by brute force, exit"*, so an
 instance that reaches line 2 of Sec. 15 has a window above any fixed absolute size.  It
 is what turns the test of line 2, `m > ℓ = (log n)³`, into the numeric hypotheses of
 Theorem 10.5.1 and Cor. 12.0.10 (`Babai.hugeM_of_line2`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 10.5.1 (Main Structure Theorem) (PDF p. 88) — §15, what lines 1–3 leave on the table.

decls.name: Johnson_eq_Cameron_s_one_statement
decls.docstring:
§11.2, after Definition 11.2.2:

> Note that for `k ≥ 5` the Johnson groups `S_k^(t)` and `A_k^(t)` are exactly the Cameron
> groups with `s = 1`.

The paper asserts this without proof and never uses it, so it is recorded as a statement
only.

The Johnson groups are meant in the range of §2.2.1, "the Johnson groups `S_k^(t)` and
`A_k^(t)` for `t ≥ 1` and `k ≥ 2t + 1`", which is also the range of the parameters in
Definition 11.2.2.  Outside it the sentence is false for a reason that has nothing to do
with the paper: for `t = 0` the domain `Fin k choose 0` is a single point, so *every*
subgroup equals `S_k^(0) = A_k^(0) = 1` while no group is a Cameron group with `t = 0`
(Definition 11.2.2 asks `1 ≤ t`); and for `k = 6`, `t = 3` the group `S_6^(3)` is not a
Cameron group with these parameters either (Definition 11.2.2 asks `2t < k`).  Carrying
the two constraints is therefore a matter of stating the paper's sentence in the range it
is about.
