coherent configuration."*  Every coherent refinement of `X` refines `F3(X)`; together with

refinement (`isWLStable_iff_isCoherent`, i.e. axiom (iii) of Def. 5.2.2), and that is what

the `(n+1)`-st.  Indeed the color of the `n`-th round is a function `G` of the color of

of the `n`-th round around `u⃗` is the image under `i⃗ ↦ G ∘ i⃗` of the corresponding tuple
for `Y`, and equal fiber sizes for the `Y`-tuples — which is axiom (iii) for `Y` — give

*"Now `supp(y⃗) ∩ {u,v} ≠ ∅` (since otherwise we would have `y⃗ τ = y⃗`), so without loss of
generality we may assume `u ∈ supp(y⃗)`. … Again by the axioms of configurations we may
assume that (u) `u = y_q` if `v ∉ supp(y⃗)`, and (uv) `u = y_{q-1}` and `v = y_q` if
`v ∈ supp(y⃗)`.  Let `ℓ = max{i | yᵢ ∉ {u,v}}` … Let `x⃗ = y₁ … y_ℓ`.  So
`supp(x⃗) ∩ {u,v} = ∅`.  In Case (u) we have `y⃗ = x⃗u` and in Case (uv) we have
`y⃗ = x⃗uv`."*

*"Claim 8.3.3. (a) In Case (u) we have `c_x⃗(u) ≠ c_x⃗(v)`.  (b) In Case (uv) we have
`c_x⃗(uv) ≠ c_x⃗(vu)`.  Proof. (a) By definition, `c_x⃗(u) = c(x⃗u) = c(y⃗) ≠ c(y⃗ τ) =

c_x⃗(vu)`."*

decls.name: claim_8_4_1
decls.docstring:
Claim 8.4.1, Eq. (48).  *"Let `x⃗ ∈ Ω^{⟨≤k-1⟩}` be a non-empty string with parent `y⃗`,
so `x⃗ = y⃗z` for some `z ∈ Ω`.  Then `C(x⃗) = C(y⃗) \ {z}`."*

Paper's proof: *"We have `ℓ(y⃗) = ℓ(x⃗) - 1 ≤ k-2`.  Therefore, by item (B) above, `C(y⃗)`
induces a clique in the `2`-skeleton `X_y⃗^{(2)}`.  We have `|C(y⃗)| > αn ≥ n/2`, so by the
'Large clique lemma' (Lemma 3.4.25), `C(y⃗)` is a twin equivalence class in `X_y⃗^{(2)}`.
In particular, for all `u ∈ C(y⃗) \ {z}`, the color `c_y⃗(zu)` is the same (independent of
`u`); call this color `i_z`.  So for all `u ∈ C(y⃗) \ {z}`, we have
`c_x⃗(u) = c_y⃗(zu) = i_z`, independent [of] `u`.  It follows that `i_z` is the dominant
vertex-color in `X_x⃗` and Eq. (48) holds."*

The last step uses Eq. (47): `C(x⃗)` is contained in `C(y⃗)` and misses `supp(x⃗) ∋ z`, so
`C(x⃗) ⊆ C(y⃗) \ {z}`; since `C(y⃗) \ {z}` lies in the single vertex-color class `i_z` of
`X_x⃗` and `C(x⃗)` is a non-empty vertex-color class of `X_x⃗`, the two coincide.

decls.name: imprimitive_or_uniprimitive
decls.docstring:
§8.1, second half of the "Proof of equivalence": the dichotomy that turns outcome (ii)
of Theorem 8.1.5 into outcome (b) or (c) of Theorem 8.1.2.

*"In case (ii), let `X* = (Ω, c'')` be the coherent configuration obtained.  If `X*` has no
dominant vertex-color class, we are in case (a).  Otherwise, let `C` denote the dominant
vertex-color class of `X*`.  If `X*[C]` is a UPCC, we are in case (c).  Otherwise, `X*[C]`
is imprimitive; the connected components of its first disconnected non-diagonal
constituent form the required canonical equipartition (Prop. 3.4.4)."*

Here `X* = Y^{(2)}` and `C` is the dominant class of `Y`, which is a vertex-color class of
`X*` (`skel2_vertexClass_eq`), hence a stable set, so `X*[C]` is a homogeneous coherent
configuration (Obs. 3.3.2).  Since `X*[C]` is not a clique and `|C| ≥ 2`, its rank is
`≥ 3` (`three_le_rank_induced`); so `X*[C]` is a UPCC as soon as it is primitive, and
otherwise one of its off-diagonal constituents is disconnected and Prop. 3.4.4 applies
(`homogeneous_disconnected_weakComponents`).

links.rationale: Formalizes Theorem 8.1.2 (Design lemma) (PDF p. 65) — §8.1, second half of the "Proof of equivalence": the dichotomy that turns outcome (ii) of Theorem 8.1.5 into outcome (b) or (c) of Theorem 8.1.2.

the same vertex color; since `Φ` is a union of vertex-color classes, either all of them lie
in `Φ`, in which case both counts equal the corresponding counts for `X`, or none does, in
which case both counts are `0`.

only on the vertex color.

decls.name: procedure
decls.docstring:
Procedure "Design Lemma" (§8.2).

```
Input: a k-ary structure X = (Ω, R) with symmetry defect ≥ 1 − α where 1/2 ≤ α < 1.
Output: (i) or (ii) of Theorem 8.1.5.
01 apply k-WL to X       (: henceforth we assume X is k-ary coherent :)
02 for ℓ = 0 to k − 1
03   for x⃗ ∈ Ω^⟨ℓ⟩
04     if each vertex-color class in the restriction X_x⃗ has size ≤ αn
05     then return the vertex-coloring, exit           (: goal (i) achieved :)
06     else (: we have a unique vertex-color class C(x⃗) of size > αn :)
07       if ℓ ≤ k − 2 and the 2-skeleton (X_x⃗)^{(2)} does not induce
         a clique configuration on C(x⃗) then
08         return X* := (X_x⃗)^{(2)}, exit              (: goal (ii) achieved :)
```

Line 01 is `Babai.KAryRelStruct.kWL`, applied by the theorems of `Main.lean`; the
procedure below is lines 02–08, run on the `k`-ary coherent configuration produced by
line 01.  It returns the length `ℓ` and the string `x⃗` at which lines 05 or 08 fire; the
objects returned there, the vertex-coloring of `X_x⃗` and the configuration
`X* = (X_x⃗)^{(2)}`, are functions of `x⃗` (`restrTo`, `skel2`), and which of the two fired
is recorded by `Returns`.  The outer loop of line 02 is the search for the *least* `ℓ`;
the paper prescribes no order on `Ω^⟨ℓ⟩` for the inner loop of line 03, and the choice of
`x⃗` among the strings of length `ℓ` at which the procedure returns is immaterial for
Thm. 8.2.1, so it is made by `Exists.choose`.

Proposition 5.2.6 (c).  "If `X` is a `k`-ary coherent configuration then `X_x⃗` is a
`(k-ℓ)`-ary coherent configuration."

The paper gives no proof ("*** PROVE! ***").  Proof supplied: the conditions
`c_x⃗(y⃗ ᵗ(z)) = i_t` (`t ∈ [k-ℓ]`) are the conditions `c((x⃗y⃗)^{ℓ+t}(z)) = i_t` on the last
`k-ℓ` coordinates of `x⃗y⃗`, so the count is the sum, over all color vectors `i⃗'` of the
first `ℓ` coordinates, of the intersection numbers `γ(i⃗'i⃗, c(x⃗y⃗))` of `X`; each term
depends on `y⃗` only through `c(x⃗y⃗) = c_x⃗(y⃗)`.  See the corrected paper, "hole in 2.5",
§5.2.1.

decls.name: skeleton_isCoherent
decls.docstring:
Proposition 5.2.3 (Skeleton 2).  "For `ℓ ≤ k`, the `ℓ`-skeleton `X^{(ℓ)}` of a `k`-ary
coherent configuration `X` is an `ℓ`-ary coherent configuration."

Paper's proof: "By Prop. 5.1.11, we only need to verify item (iii) in Def. 5.2.2.  We claim
that `X^{(ℓ)}` has intersection numbers `γ^{(ℓ)}(i⃗ j)` each of which is a sum of a subset
of the intersection numbers of `X`. … Let `x⃗ ∈ Ω^ℓ` with `c^{(ℓ)}(x⃗) = j`. … We need to
show that the number `γ^{(ℓ)}(i⃗ j)` of those `z ∈ Ω` for which
`(∀t ∈ [ℓ])(c^{(ℓ)}(x⃗ ᵗ(z)) = i_t)` does not depend on the specific choice of `x⃗` except
for the assumption that `c(x⃗) = j`. … For `t ≤ ℓ-1` … `pad(x⃗ ᵗ(z)) = (pad(x⃗))ᵗ(z)` …
This is not true for `t = ℓ`, however.  Instead we have `c(pad(x⃗ ℓ(z))) = i_ℓ` if and only
if for some `s ≥ ℓ` we have `f_s(c((pad(x⃗))ˢ(z))) = i_ℓ`."

(The proof as printed reads "for some `s ≥ ℓ`", while the summation condition of
Claim 5.2.4 reads "`f_s(i'_s) = i_ℓ` for `s ≥ ℓ`", i.e. for *all* `s ≥ ℓ`.  The two agree:
`idx_tauS_subst_pad` shows that `f_s(c((pad(x⃗))ˢ(z))) = c(pad(x⃗ ℓ(z)))` for every
`s ≥ ℓ`, so one `s` gives all of them.  We use the "for all" form, which is what makes the
sum of Claim 5.2.4 correct.)

decls.name: skeleton_isConfiguration
decls.docstring:
Proposition 5.1.11 (Skeleton 1).  "For `1 ≤ ℓ ≤ k`, the `ℓ`-skeleton `X^{(ℓ)}` of a
`k`-ary configuration `X` is an `ℓ`-ary configuration."

Paper's proof: "Let `x⃗, y⃗ ∈ Ω^ℓ` and assume `c^{(ℓ)}(x⃗) = c^{(ℓ)}(y⃗)`.  In other words
this means `c(pad(x⃗)) = c(pad(y⃗))`.  Therefore `ρ(pad(x⃗)) = ρ(pad(y⃗))`.  Restricting these
equivalence relations to `[ℓ]` we obtain `ρ(x⃗) = ρ(y⃗)`, verifying (i) in Def. 5.1.8.  Let
now `τ ∈ 𝔐_ℓ`.  To verify item (ii) we need to show that `c^{(ℓ)}(τ(x⃗)) = c^{(ℓ)}(τ(y⃗))`.
We know that `c(pad(x⃗)) = c(pad(y⃗))`.  Therefore, applying item (ii) to `X` we obtain that
`c((pad(τ))(pad(x⃗))) = c((pad(τ))(pad(y⃗)))`.  By Obs. 5.1.14 we infer that
`c(pad(τ(x⃗))) = c(pad(τ(y⃗)))`.  According to Def. 5.1.7, the left-hand side is equal to
`c^{(ℓ)}(τ(x⃗)) while the right-hand side is equal to `c^{(ℓ)}(τ(y⃗))`, as desired."

(The printed proof cites "Def. 5.4.1" for the last step; Def. 5.4.1 belongs to the
subsection marked "OLD — REMOVE THIS SUBSECTION", and the definition meant is the revised
Def. 5.1.7.  See the corrected paper.)

decls.name: theorem_8_2_1
decls.docstring:
Theorem 8.2.1.  *"Under the conditions of Theorem 8.1.5, Procedure 'Design Lemma'
terminates, achieving goal (i) or (ii) of Theorem 8.1.5."*

Paper's proof: *"After line 01 we assume that `X` is a `k`-ary coherent configuration.
Assume for a contradiction that the algorithm fails.  It follows that for all
`x⃗ ∈ Ω^{⟨≤k-1⟩}` (A) … and (B) …  But Claim 8.4.2 creates a contradiction between the
'Non-clique lemma' (Lemma 8.3.1) and our items (A) and (B) above.  Indeed, let
`x⃗ ∈ Ω^{⟨≤k-1⟩}` be a string of which the existence is guaranteed by Lemma 8.3.1.  Now
option (a) of Lemma 8.3.1 says `C \ supp(x⃗)` is not homogeneous under `c_x⃗`, but this is
contradicted by item (A), given Claim 8.4.2.  But then option (b) of Lemma 8.3.1
contradicts item (B), given Claim 8.4.2.  So no such `x⃗` can exist, a contradiction."*

decls.name: vcolor_eq_of_color_eq

Let `x⃗ = x₁ … x_k` and `y⃗ = y₁ … y_k` be strings in `Ω^k`.  If `c(x⃗) = c(y⃗)` then for each
`i ∈ [k]` we have `c(xᵢ) = c(yᵢ)`."

Paper's proof: "Let `τᵢ ∈ 𝔐_k` be defined as the constant map to `i`, i.e. `τᵢ(j) = i` for

`c(xᵢ) = c^{(1)}(xᵢ) = c(τᵢ(x⃗)) = c(τᵢ(y⃗)) = c^{(1)}(yᵢ) = c(yᵢ)`."

decls.name: wlStep_isConfiguration
decls.docstring:
§5.4.1.  *"This gives a refined coloring that defines a new configuration `X'`."*

Axiom (i) of Def. 5.1.8 for `c'` holds because `c'` refines `c` and `ρ(x⃗)` is already
determined by `c(x⃗)`.  For axiom (ii), let `c'(x⃗) = c'(y⃗)` and `τ ∈ 𝔐_k`.  The first
component of `c'(τ(x⃗))` is `c(τ(x⃗))`, which equals `c(τ(y⃗))` by axiom (ii) for `c`.  For
the counting component, write `D_{x⃗}(z) = (c(x⃗ ᵗ(z)) | t ∈ [k])`; the hypothesis says that
the fibers of `D_{x⃗}` and of `D_{y⃗}` have equal sizes.  By `Str.exists_subst_idx` there
are, for each `j ∈ [k]`, an index `m_j` and a `σ_j ∈ 𝔐_k` depending only on `τ` and `j`
with `(τ(w⃗)) ʲ(z) = σ_j(w⃗ ^{m_j}(z))` for all `w⃗` and `z`; hence, by Remark 5.1.9,
`D_{τ(w⃗)}(z)_j = η(σ_j)(D_{w⃗}(z)_{m_j})`.  So `D_{τ(w⃗)} = F ∘ D_{w⃗}` for a map `F` of
color tuples that does not depend on `w⃗`, and the fibers of `F ∘ D_{x⃗}` and `F ∘ D_{y⃗}`
again have equal sizes (`Babai.ncard_fiber_comp_congr`).

The counting is by `Set.ncard`, so `Ω` is assumed finite here, as it is in the paper.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 5.1.8 (Configuration) (PDF p. 52) — §5.4.1.  *"This gives a refined coloring that defines a new configuration `X'`."*

decls.name: remark_8_1_4
decls.docstring:
Remark 8.1.4, §8.1.  *"Let `X*` denote the UPCC obtained in case (c).  If we can
compute `Aut(X*)` then we achieve a major reduction in `Aut(X)` because
`|Aut(X*)| ≤ exp(Õ(√n))` [Ba81].  … Direct computation of `Aut(X*)` can be done in
`exp(Õ(n^{1/3}))` (Sun–Wilmes).  … Rather than relying on the Sun–Wilmes theorem …, we
shall further reduce the UPCC case to Johnson schemes (Split-or-Johnson routine, Sec 9) at
a quasipolynomial multiplicative cost."*

The remark states no mathematical claim that is used: it compares two routes to `Aut(X*)`
and announces §9.  The bound `|Aut(X*)| ≤ exp(Õ(√n))` for a UPCC is Thm. 3.2.4 of §3
([Ba81]), already recorded there; the Sun–Wilmes bound is cited but never used (the paper
explicitly declines to rely on it).  The reference *"(cf. ****)"* for the claim that the
automorphism group of the Johnson scheme `J(k,t)` is the Johnson group `S_k^{(t)}` is a
hole in version 2.5; the intended item is Prop. 3.2.11 (§3.2), `Aut(J(Γ,t)) = S^{(t)}(Γ)`
for the Johnson *graph*, whose metric scheme is the Johnson scheme (Def. 3.2.13).  See
the corrected paper.

decls.name: theorem_8_1_2
decls.docstring:
Theorem 8.1.2 (Design lemma), §8.1.

*"Let `1/2 ≤ α < 1` be a threshold parameter.  Let `X = (Ω, R)` be a `k`-ary relational
structure with `n = |Ω|` vertices, `2 ≤ k ≤ n/2`, and symmetry defect `≥ 1 − α`.  Then in
time `n^{O(k)}` we can find a value `ℓ ≤ k − 1` and a string `x⃗ = x₁ … x_ℓ ∈ Ω^⟨ℓ⟩` of `ℓ`
distinct vertices such that by individualizing each `x_j` we obtain either*

*(a) a canonical coloring of `Ω` with no dominant color, or*

*(b) a canonical coloring of `Ω` and a nontrivial canonical equipartition of the dominant
color class, or*

*(c) a canonical coloring of `Ω` and a canonically embedded uniprimitive coherent
configuration (UPCC) whose vertex set is the dominant color class.*

*Canonicity in the above statements is relative to `x⃗`."*

The canonical coloring is in all three cases the vertex-coloring of the restriction
`X_x⃗` of `kWL(X)` (canonical by `restrTo_canonical` and `vcolor_canonical`); the dominant
color class is `dominantClass` (canonical by `dominantClass_canonical`), and the UPCC of
(c) is the subconfiguration of `X* = (X_x⃗)^{(2)}` induced on it (canonical by
`skel2_canonical`).

The running-time clause is pending; see the corrected paper.

The proof is the paper's "proof of equivalence" in §8.1, second half: outcome (i) of
Thm. 8.1.5 is outcome (a), and in case (ii) one splits according to whether the induced
subconfiguration `X*[C]` on the dominant class `C` is uniprimitive — outcome (c) — or
imprimitive, in which case *"the connected components of its first disconnected
non-diagonal constituent form the required canonical equipartition (Prop. 3.4.4)"* —
outcome (b).  The dichotomy is `KAryPartStruct.imprimitive_or_uniprimitive`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Theorem 8.1.2 (Design lemma) (PDF p. 65) — Theorem 8.1.2 (Design lemma), §8.1.

decls.name: theorem_8_1_5
decls.docstring:
Theorem 8.1.5 (Design lemma, rephrased), §8.1.

*"Let `1/2 ≤ α < 1` be a threshold parameter.  Let `X = (Ω, R)` be a `k`-ary relational
structure with `n = |Ω|` vertices, `2 ≤ k ≤ n/2`, and symmetry defect `≥ 1 − α`.  Then in
time `n^{O(k)}` we can find a value `ℓ ≤ k − 1` and a string `x⃗ = x₁ … x_ℓ ∈ Ω^⟨ℓ⟩` of `ℓ`
distinct vertices such that by individualizing each `x_j` we obtain either*

*(i) a canonical coloring of `Ω` with no dominant color, or*

*(ii) a canonical (classical) coherent configuration `X*` on vertex set `Ω` such that the
subconfiguration induced on the dominant vertex-color class of `X*` is not a clique.*

*Canonicity in the above statements is relative to `x⃗`."*

Here the coloring of (i) is the vertex-coloring of the restriction `X_x⃗` of the `k`-ary
coherent configuration `kWL(X)`, and the configuration of (ii) is `X* = (X_x⃗)^{(2)}`; the
disjunction (i) ∨ (ii) is `Returns` (§8.2, lines 04–08).  Canonicity relative to `x⃗` is
`restrTo_canonical`, `vcolor_canonical` and `skel2_canonical`; that the objects named in
(i) and (ii) correspond is `noDominantColor_canonical` and `dominantClass_canonical`.
The `2`-skeleton is a classical coherent configuration by `skel2_isCoherent`.

The running-time clause is pending; see the corrected paper.

decls.name: Line57Shape
decls.docstring:
§15, lines 5–7 on the window: **the data the round after AggregateCertificates runs
on**.

* `align S` is the round of Procedure Align on the data `S` (`Babai.AlignShape`).  It is
 what outcomes (1), (2b) and (3) of Theorem 13.2.1 lead to: the canonical versions of the
 structure, then lines 1–11 of Sec. 14.1.
* `rejectDefect ϕ ts h` is the exit of outcome (3) at the second string: the set `D(z)` of
 fixed points of `F(z)^Γ` is a canonical invariant of the string, so `|D(y)| ≠ |D(x)|`
 means `Iso_G(x,y) = ∅` (`Babai.strIso_eq_empty_of_ncard_fixedGamma_ne`).
* `rejectCase ϕ ts hx hy` is the exit of outcome (2b) at the second string: the case test of
 Theorem 13.2.1 is canonical too (`Babai.case2b_test_strAct`), so a string that fails it
 while `x` passes it is not `G`-isomorphic to `x`.
* `rejectGuide hset ht htm hW h` is the exit of the local guide in outcome (3): some class
 of `∼` meets `y` and not `x` (`Babai.GuideClassMissing`), an invariant that differs for the
 two inputs, so `Iso_G(x,y) = ∅` (`Babai.strIso_eq_empty_of_guideClassMissing`). Version 2.5
 has no exit here; the original's proof of the Local guide proposition does
.

The two reject constructors **carry their test**, so the answer `∅` cannot be given where
the test does not hold.  Both tests read the second string alone against the first, and are
computed from `F(z)^Γ`, which the aggregation of line 5 has already produced.

The situation of the Local guide proposition: a category `C` whose objects `X_i` have
underlying sets `Ω_i`, a category `L` whose objects `X_i(L)` are indexed by the pairs

underlying sets, they contain the identities, and they are closed under inverse and
composition.  Since the objects of `C` have different carriers and the objects of `L` are

rather than through `Babai.Cat`; see the module docstring.

decls.name: MakesProgress
decls.docstring:
§11.4, recurrences (ii) and (v): the progress one *shrinking* call makes.  Either the
window drops to `4n/5`, or it does not grow and the Johnson parameter is at least halved.

Sec. 14.2 Eq. (73) writes `2n/3` for the first alternative.  The constant here is `4/5`
instead.  The reason is the `t = 1` case of Eq. (72): a dominant color class of a colored
`α`-partition can be a single block, and then Lemma 7.2.1 (b) gives only
`|Ω(Δ)| ≤ α·n`, with `α = 4/5` the threshold of Theorem 13.2.1.  So `4/5` is what the
window alternative can promise at line 5, and `2/3` is not.  Recurrences (i), (ii) and (v)
of Sec. 11.4 resolve for any fixed constant below `1`, so only this constant moves; see
the corrected paper entry on Sec. 15 lines 5–7a and Sec. 14.2 Eqs. (72)–(73).

decls.name: MasterStep
decls.docstring:
§15: one round of Procedure String-Isomorphism, together with the three properties its
analysis uses: correctness of the round, the progress it makes, and the number of instances
it produces.

The round runs on a type `ι` of **hinted** instances: an element of `ι` is a String
Isomorphism instance `inst i` together with whatever lines 1–3 have already found for it
(in `Workspace/Master/Sec15.lean` this is an optional `Babai.JohnsonCaseData`).  A round
attaches such a hint to each of its calls through `lift`, which is what Sec. 14.2 does when
it measures the pair `(G, ϕ)` and what line 11 of Procedure Align does when it hands `ϕ*`
down *"for recursive processing of the corresponding window"*.  The hint does not touch the
instance: `lift_inst` says `inst (lift i J) = J`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Procedure String-Isomorphism (PDF p. 113) — §15: one round of Procedure String-Isomorphism, together with the three properties its analysis uses: correctness of the round, the progress it makes, and the number of instances it produces.

decls.name: round_recurrence
decls.docstring:
**The one-round recurrence**: the number of instances a round produces, plus what each
of them costs, is at most what the instance costs.

*Proof.*  Two cases, the two forms of `Babai.MasterStep.decreases`.

*Shrinking round.*  If there are no calls there is nothing to prove.  Otherwise the window
is nonempty, so `johnsonRank I ≥ 3` (`Babai.MasterStep.three_le_johnsonRank`), and every
call `J` has `n_J ≤ n` and `johnsonRank J < johnsonRank I`, so
`T(J) ≤ n² B^{johnsonRank I - 1} =: c`.  There are at most `q = B - 1` calls, so the left
side is at most `q + q c`, and `c ≥ B² ≥ B > q` gives `q + q c ≤ c + q c = B c = T(I)`.

*Chain Rule round.*  Every call has `johnsonRank J ≤ johnsonRank I`, so
`∑ T(J) ≤ B^{johnsonRank I} ∑ n_J²`.  The windows are strictly smaller than `n = k + 1` and
add up to at most `n`, so `∑ n_J² ≤ k · n`.  There are at most `q < B ≤ B^{johnsonRank I}`
calls, and `B^{johnsonRank I} (n + k n) = B^{johnsonRank I} n² = T(I)`.

links.rationale: **The one-round recurrence**: the number of instances a round produces, plus what each of them costs, is at most what the instance costs.

decls.name: solve_eq_answer
decls.docstring:
§15, **correctness**: `f` levels of recursion return the true answer as soon as `f`
exceeds the measure of the instance.

*Proof.* Induction on `f`.  There is nothing to prove for `f = 0`, since `rank I < 0` is
impossible.  For `f + 1`, every instance `J` the round asks under the true oracle has
`rank J < rank I ≤ f` (`Babai.MasterStep.rank_lt`), so by the induction hypothesis the
recursion one level down answers all of them correctly.  Hence the round, run against the
recursion, takes the same path as under the true oracle
(`Babai.SIReduction.callsWith_eq_calls_of_agree`) and returns `(M.step I).run`, which is
`I.answer` by `round_correct`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure String-Isomorphism (PDF p. 113) — §15, **correctness**: `f` levels of recursion return the true answer as soon as `f` exceeds the measure of the instance.

decls.name: MultTransOn
decls.docstring:
§13.2, case (2b): **`H` is `d`-transitive on the subset `C`** — every injective `d`-tuple
of points of `C` is carried to every other by an element of `H`.

This is `Babai.IsMultiplyTransitive` for the group induced on `C`, written with tuples in
`Γ` so that a conjugation of `H` moves it by a computation
(`Babai.multTransOn_map_conj`).

The clause `d ≤ C.ncard` is not decoration.  Without it the quantifier over injective
`d`-tuples in `C` is **vacuously true** for every `d > |C|`, so the set of `d` would be
unbounded and `sSup` of an unbounded set of naturals is `0`.  That is exactly the
degenerate-case trap of `Babai.IsTransitiveAction` versus `MulAction.IsPretransitive`:
the paper's "`F^C` is `d`-transitive" asserts that the action on injective `d`-tuples has
*exactly one* orbit, which forces such a tuple to exist.  With the clause,
`Babai.multTransOn_iff_isMultiplyTransitive` is a clean bridge to
`Babai.IsMultiplyTransitive` of the induced group `F^C`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 13.2.1 (AggregateCertificates) (PDF p. 108) — §13.2, case (2b): **`H` is `d`-transitive on the subset `C`** — every injective `d`-tuple of points of `C` is carried to every other by an element of `H`.

decls.name: Observation_12_0_4
decls.docstring:
§12, **Observation 12.0.4**.

> Let `S` be a set of generators of the group `G`.  Then `S ∪ {1}` is a set of coset
> generators of `G`, i. e., no proper subcoset of `G` contains `S ∪ {1}`.

Stated inside an arbitrary ambient group: the smallest subcoset containing `S ∪ {1}` is
the subgroup generated by `S`.  The paper's form is the special case where the ambient
group is `G = ⟨S⟩` itself (`Babai.Observation_12_0_4_paper`).

decls.name: PGammaL
decls.docstring:
`PΓL(V)`, the projective semilinear group of `V` over `K`: the group of permutations
of the projective space `ℙ K V` induced by the semilinear bijections of `V`.

A *semilinear bijection* is an additive bijection `f : V ≃+ V` together with a field
automorphism `σ : K ≃+* K` such that `f (c • v) = σ c • f v` for all `c`, `v`; such an `f`
maps lines through the origin to lines through the origin, so it induces a permutation of
`ℙ K V`, and the generating set below consists of exactly those induced permutations.
`PΓL` is generated by (indeed equal to) this set.

decls.name: IsPrimitive
decls.docstring:
Definition 3.2.1 (UPCC).  "`X` is *primitive* if it is homogeneous and all
constituents other than the diagonal are connected."

For a homogeneous configuration every off-diagonal constituent has `Ω(k) = Ω`
(`vertexClass_tailColor_subset_effVertex`), so the constituent `X_k = (Ω(k), R_k)` and
the extended constituent `(Ω, R_k)` coincide and we may phrase connectivity for the
latter.  "Connected" is read as weakly connected (Def. 2.4.21); by Prop. 3.4.1 this is
the same as strongly connected for a homogeneous constituent.

decls.name: constituent_homogeneous_or_bipartite
decls.docstring:
Corollary 3.3.7 (Constituents: homogeneous or bipartite).  "For `k ≤ r`, the
constituent digraph `X_k = (Ω(k), R_k)` is either
(i) (homogeneous case) a biregular digraph with vertex set `Ω(k) = Ωᵢ` for some vertex
color `i` (in particular, all vertices of `X_k` have the same color), or
(ii) (bipartite case) a semiregular bipartite graph of the form `(Ωᵢ, Ω_j; R_k)` for some
distinct vertex colors `i` and `j` (so `R_k ⊆ Ωᵢ × Ω_j`; in particular, the vertices have
two colors)."

Paper's proof: "The first case arises when the tail and the head of an edge of color `k`
have the same color, `i`; this is in particular the case when `k` is a diagonal color.
The second when the color of the tail is `i` and the color of the head is `j ≠ i`.
Biregularity and semiregularity follow from Obs. 3.3.5."

decls.name: exists_mid_of_undirected_constituent
decls.docstring:
**The diameter-2 fact** used in the proof of Lemma 9.3.1 (§9.3, version 2.5, lines
4058–4061), proved here rather than cited from `[Ba81, Prop. 4.10]` (entry C7 of
`CITED.md`).

*"Let `(x, z) ∈ R₂` and let `y ∈ V` be such that `(x, y) ∈ Rᵢ` and `(z, y) ∈ R_j` where
`i, j ≥ 3`."*  The hypotheses are the ones the argument uses: `X` is a UPCC (Def. 3.2.1:
homogeneous, all off-diagonal constituents connected, rank `≥ 3`) and the constituent
`c₂` is undirected (`c₂⁻ = c₂`), which in the paper follows from `d₂ ≥ n/2`.
"`i, j ≥ 3`" is rendered as "off-diagonal and `≠ c₂`", which is what it means in a
homogeneous configuration.

decls.name: exists_nondominant_offDiagonal
decls.docstring:
§9.8, step 3 of Procedure Reduce-by-UPCC: *"let `ℓ` be the first non-dominant
off-diagonal color in `X₂`"*, and the Claim's justification of its existence: *"we need
'uni' (not a clique) to guarantee that a non-dominant off-diagonal color `ℓ` exists in
`X₂`."*

*"Uni"* enters as `3 ≤ rank`: in a homogeneous structure exactly one color is diagonal, so
rank `≥ 3` gives at least **two** off-diagonal colors, and two disjoint relations cannot
both have more than half of the `n²` edges.  (Rank `2`, the clique configuration, has a
single off-diagonal color, which carries all `n² − n` off-diagonal edges and is dominant as
soon as `n ≥ 3`; this is exactly the case the paper has to exclude.)

decls.name: exists_walkNum
decls.docstring:
Proposition 3.3.11 (Counting walks).  "For every string `I = i₁…i_t` of colors and
color `k` there exists a number `p(I,k)` such that for any `x, y ∈ Ω` satisfying
`c(x,y) = k`, the number of walks of length `t` of color composition `I` from `x` to `y`
is `p(I,k)`."

The proof follows the paper: induction on `t`, with `p(Λ,k) = 1` iff `k` is diagonal,
`p(i₁,k) = 1` iff `i₁ = k` (`numWalks_singleton`), `p(i₁i₂,k) = p^k_{i₁,i₂}`
(`numWalks_pair`), and for the inductive step Eq. (18)

decls.name: homogeneous_components_equipartition
decls.docstring:
Proposition 3.4.4 (Homogeneous connected components).  "If `X_k` is a homogeneous
constituent digraph in color class `Ωᵢ` then the components of `X_k` equipartition `Ωᵢ`."

Paper's proof: "Let `x ∈ Ωᵢ` and let `Y(x)` denote the set of vertices of the component
of the constituent `X_k` that contains `x`.  Then `Y(x) ⊆ Ωᵢ` and `Y(x)` consists of
those vertices that are accessible from `x` along a sequence of edges of color `k`.
Using the notation of Cor. 3.3.12, this means that `Y(x) = (k*)(x)` where
`k* = {Λ, k, kk, kkk, …}`.  It follows by the Accessibility Theorem (Thm. 3.3.14) that
`|Y(x)| = |(k*)(x)|` only depends on `k` and `c(x)`."

decls.name: isPrimitive_of_coarser

**Primitivity survives a coarsening of the coloring.**  If the color classes of `Y'`
are unions of color classes of a primitive `Y` — across a renaming `e` of the points — and
`Y'` is homogeneous, then `Y'` is primitive.

This is the argument behind *"`X₁` remains a UPCC by Claim above"* in step 8 of §9.4, for
the primitivity half: an off-diagonal color of `Y'` contains an off-diagonal color of `Y`,
whose constituent is a connected spanning subgraph, so the constituent of `Y'` is connected
too.  (Uniprimitivity itself does **not** survive coarsening: the rank can drop to `2`.
That is why the paper re-runs the Claim of step 6.)

decls.name: large_clique_twinClass
decls.docstring:
Lemma 3.4.25 (Large clique lemma).  "Let `X = (Ω, c)` be a coherent configuration.
Let `Ω₁, …, Ω_s` be the vertex-color classes.  Assume `|Ω₁| > |Ωᵢ|` for all `i ≥ 2` and
`Ω₁` induces a clique configuration in `X`.  Then `Ω₁` is a twin equivalence class
in `X`."

Paper's proof: "Let `C = Ω₁`.  First we prove that all links between `C` and the other
colors is trivial.  Given that `X[C]` is a clique, this immediately implies that `C` is a
twin equivalence class in `X`.  We need to prove that for all `x ∈ Ω \ C` and all
`y, z ∈ C` we have `c(x,y) = c(x,z)`.  For a contradiction assume this is false and let
`ℓ` be a color and `x ∈ Ω \ C` such that `c(x,y) = ℓ` for some but not all `y ∈ C`.  In
other words, `1 ≤ deg⁺_ℓ < |C|`. … the hypergraph `H = (C, {R_ℓ(u) | u ∈ B})` is
`k`-uniform with `k = deg⁺_ℓ` … `r`-regular with `r = deg⁺_{ℓ⁻}` … for `v, w ∈ C`,
`v ≠ w` we have `|B_v ∩ B_w| = p^m_{ℓ⁻,ℓ}` … hence `H` is a possibly degenerate BIBD with
`λ = p^m_{ℓ⁻,ℓ}`.  The number of vertices of this design is `|C|` and the number of (not
necessarily distinct) blocks is `|B|`.  Hence, by Fisher's inequality, `|C| ≤ |B|`, a
contradiction."

decls.name: localColoring_isEquitable
decls.docstring:
Proposition 3.4.17 (Equitability of local colorings).  "Each local coloring of a
coherent configuration is equitable."

Paper's proof: "Let `x ∈ Ω` and consider the `x`-local coloring `c_x`.  The color classes
are the sets `Rᵢ(x)` for `i ∈ [r]`.  Consider the extended constituent `X̂_k = (Ω, R_k)`.
We need to prove that `c_x` is an equitable coloring for `X̂_k`.  Let `ℓ, m ∈ [r]` be (not
necessarily distinct) colors.  We need to show that for `u ∈ R_ℓ(x)`, the quantities
`|R_k(u) ∩ R_m(x)|` and `|R_{k⁻}(u) ∩ R_m(x)|` do not depend on the particular choice
of `u`, only on the colors `k, ℓ, m`.  Indeed, `|R_k(u) ∩ R_m(x)| = p^ℓ_{m,k⁻}` and
`|R_{k⁻}(u) ∩ R_m(x)| = p^ℓ_{m,k}`."

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 3.4.17 (Equitability of local colorings) (PDF p. 39) — Proposition 3.4.17 (Equitability of local colorings).  "Each local coloring of a coherent configuration is equitable."

decls.name: ncard_accessSet_eq
decls.docstring:
Theorem 3.3.14 (Accessibility).  "Let `S ⊆ [r]*` be a (not necessarily finite) set of
finite strings of colors.  Let `x, y ∈ Ω` have the same color: `c(x) = c(y)`.  Then
`|S(x)| = |S(y)|`."

Paper's proof: "Let `i = c(x) = c(y)`.  Let `J = J(S)` be the accessibility set of `S`.
Then `|S(x)| = ∑_{j∈J} deg⁺_j(x)`.  Let `J' ⊆ J` consist of those `j ∈ J` for which the
tail of an edge of color `j` has color `i` (see Obs. 3.3.4).  So
`|S(x)| = ∑_{j∈J'} deg⁺_j = |S(y)|` by the Degree-awareness lemma (Obs. 3.3.5)."

decls.name: no_twins_in_primitive_color
decls.docstring:
Theorem 3.4.11 (No twins in primitive color).  "Let `Ωᵢ, Ω_j` be two distinct
vertex-color classes in the coherent configuration `X = (Ω, c)`.  Consider the bipartite
constituent `X_k = (Ω(k), R_k)` where `R_k ⊆ Ωᵢ × Ω_j`.  Assume `X_k` is non-trivial
(non-empty and not complete).  Assume further that the induced subconfiguration `X[Ωᵢ]`
is primitive.  Then there are no `X_k`-twins in `Ωᵢ`."

Paper's proof: "Assume for a contradiction that `x, y ∈ Ωᵢ` (`x ≠ y`) are twins for `X_k`.
Let `c(x,y) = ℓ`.  By Lemma 3.4.10 it follows that every pair `(x',y') ∈ R_ℓ` are twins.
Now the twin-or-equal relation is an equivalence relation, so the transitive closure of
`R_ℓ` is a subset of the twin-or-equal relation.  But `X[Ωᵢ]` is primitive, so `R_ℓ` is
(strongly) connected and therefore its transitive closure is `Ωᵢ × Ωᵢ`.
We have shown that `Ωᵢ` is a single twin equivalence class.  This means the set `R_ℓ(x)`
is the same for all `x ∈ Ωᵢ`; let us call this set `W ⊆ Ω_j`.  Now `W ≠ ∅` and `W ≠ Ω_j`
since in either of these cases, `X_k` would be trivial.  Let `u ∈ W` and `v ∈ Ω_j \ W`.
Then `deg⁻_k(u) = |Ωᵢ| ≠ 0` and `deg⁻_k(v) = 0`, contradicting the semiregularity
of `X_k`."

(The paper writes `R_ℓ(x)` where it means `R_k(x)`; `ℓ` is the color of the pair `(x,y)`
inside `Ωᵢ`, while the neighbourhoods that are being compared are the `R_k`-ones.  The
argument uses connectivity only through the equivalence relation "same `R_k`-neighbourhood",
which is symmetric, so weak connectivity of `R_ℓ` suffices.)

configuration.  Let `i, j` be diagonal colors, `ℓ ≠ m` off-diagonal colors, and `x ∈ Ωᵢ`
such that `R_ℓ(x) ⊆ Ωᵢ` and `R_m(x) ⊆ Ω_j`.  Assume `|Ω_j|/2 < |R_m(x)| < |Ω_j|`.  Assume
further that the induced subconfiguration `X[Ωᵢ]` is primitive.  Then the
`x`-`(m,ℓ,m)`-local constituent `Y = X_m[R_ℓ(x), R_m(x)]` is nontrivial."

Paper's proof: "`Y` is semiregular by Prop. 3.4.17.  Let `u ∈ R_ℓ(x)`; so `u ∈ Ωᵢ`.
Therefore `deg⁺_m = |R_m(u)| = |R_m(x)| > |Ω_j|/2`, hence `R_m(x) ∩ R_m(u) ≠ ∅`.  Let
`w ∈ R_m(x) ∩ R_m(u)`.  That means `(u,w) ∈ R_m` hence `Y` is not empty.
What we need to prove is that `Y` is not complete.  Suppose for a contradiction that it
is.  So for `u ∈ R_ℓ(x)` we have `R_m(u) ⊇ R_m(x)`.  But `deg⁺_m = |R_m(u)| = |R_m(x)|`
and therefore `R_m(u) = R_m(x)`.  This means `u` and `x` are twins, contradicting the
'no twins in primitive color' theorem (Theorem 3.4.11), given our assumption that
`X[Ωᵢ]` is primitive."

Two hypotheses are added relative to the paper; both are recorded in the corrected paper.
* `hlne : (R_ℓ(x)).Nonempty`.  The paper's proof opens with "Let `u ∈ R_ℓ(x)`"; without
 this the statement is false (if `R_ℓ(x) = ∅` the inclusion `R_ℓ(x) ⊆ Ωᵢ` is vacuous and
 `Y` is the empty bipartite graph, hence trivial).
* The appeal to Theorem 3.4.11 is replaced by `nbr_ne_of_primitive`, which is what the
 proof of Theorem 3.4.11 establishes and which, unlike Theorem 3.4.11 as stated, also
 covers the case `i = j` that the hypotheses of Theorem 3.4.19 allow.

decls.name: ofDigraph_isCoherent_iff
decls.docstring:
Observation 3.3.3.  "For a graph `X`, the configuration `X(X)` defined in
Example 3.1.7 is coherent if and only if `X` is strongly regular, including the case when
`X` is a clique."

Route.  Write `c` for the three-valued coloring (`Babai.PartitionStructure.digraphColor`)
and `N(x,y,a,b)` for the number of `z` with `c(x,z) = a` and `c(z,y) = b`.  For the
direction from coherence to strong regularity, the degree, the number of common
neighbours of an adjacent pair and the number of common neighbours of a non-adjacent pair
are all of the form `N(x,y,1,1)`, which coherence says depends only on `c(x,y)`.  For the
converse, the nine numbers `N(x,y,a,b)` satisfy a linear system whose solution is
determined by `c(x,y)` and by `n, k, λ, μ`: the row `a = 1` sums to `k`, the column
`b = 1` sums to `k`, all nine sum to `n`, the row `a = 0` and the column `b = 0` are
`0/1` vectors read off `c(x,y)`, and `N(x,y,1,1)` is `k`, `λ` or `μ`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Observation 3.3.3 (PDF p. 33) — Observation 3.3.3.  "For a graph `X`, the configuration `X(X)` defined in Example 3.1.7 is coherent if and only if `X` is strongly regular, including the case when `X` is a clique."

decls.name: twinAwareness_extConstituent
decls.docstring:
Lemma 3.4.13.  "Let `k ∈ [r]` be a color.  Then for all pairs `x, y ∈ Ω`, `x ≠ y`, the
color `c(x,y)` determines whether `x, y` are twins in the extended constituent
`(Ω, R_k)`."

Paper's proof: "If `c(x) ≠ c(y)` then `x, y` are not twins; and this relation only depends
on `c(x,y)` by vertex-color awareness (Obs. 3.3.4).  Assume now that `c(x) = c(y) = i`.  If
`Ωᵢ ⊄ Ω(k)` then `x, y` are twins in `(Ω, R_k)` because they are isolated.  Finally assume
`Ωᵢ ⊆ Ω(k)`.  In this case, `x, y` are twins in the extended constituent `(Ω, R_k)` if and
only if they are twins in the constituent `X_k`.  So if `X_k` is homogeneous, the result
follows from Lemma 3.4.12; and if `X_k` is bipartite, the result follows by applying
Lemma 3.4.10 to `k` or to `k⁻`."

Here it is the case `K = {k}` of Theorem 3.4.14, whose proof is the counting argument of
Lemma 3.4.12 carried out for the extended constituent directly; see the section
introduction.

links.rationale: Formalizes Lemma 3.4.13 (PDF p. 38) — Lemma 3.4.13.  "Let `k ∈ [r]` be a color.  Then for all pairs `x, y ∈ Ω`, `x ≠ y`, the color `c(x,y)` determines whether `x, y` are twins in the extended constituent `(Ω, R_k)`."

Formalizes Theorem 3.4.14 (Twin awareness 3) (PDF p. 38) — Lemma 3.4.13.  "Let `k ∈ [r]` be a color.  Then for all pairs `x, y ∈ Ω`, `x ≠ y`, the color `c(x,y)` determines whether `x, y` are twins in the extended constituent `(Ω, R_k)`."

`R_k(x) = R_k(y)`.  The latter is equivalent to saying that `p^ℓ_{k,k⁻} = p^i_{k,k⁻}`.
This equality depends only on the colors involved."

decls.name: twinAwareness₂
decls.docstring:
Lemma 3.4.12 (Twin awareness 2).  "Let `Ωᵢ` be a vertex-color class in the coherent
configuration `X = (Ω, c)`.  Consider the homogeneous constituent digraph
`X_k = (Ωᵢ, R_k)` where `R_k ⊆ Ωᵢ × Ωᵢ`.  Then for all pairs `x, y ∈ Ωᵢ`, `x ≠ y`, the
color `c(x,y)` determines whether `x, y` are twins in `X_k`."

Paper's proof: "Let `c(x,y) = ℓ`.  Case 1: `ℓ ∉ {k, k⁻}`.  In this case, `x, y` are twins
in `X_k` if and only if `R_k(x) = R_k(y)` which is again equivalent to saying that
`p^ℓ_{k,k⁻} = p^i_{k,k⁻}`.  Case 2: `ℓ ∈ {k, k⁻}`.  In this case, if `k ≠ k⁻` then `x` and
`y` are not twins.  Assume now `k = k⁻ = ℓ`.  In this case, `x, y` are twins in `X_k` if
and only if `R_k(x) \ {y} = R_k(y) \ {x}` which is equivalent to saying that
`p^k_{k,k} = p^i_{k,k} − 1`."

The Case 1 criterion fails for the diagonal color `k = i` (see the section introduction and
the corrected paper); the statement is proved here from Lemma 3.4.13, whose proof is the same
counting argument applied to the neighbourhoods outside the pair `{x,y}`.

decls.name: twinAwareness₃
decls.docstring:
Theorem 3.4.14 (Twin awareness 3).  "Let `K ⊆ [r]` be a set of colors.  Consider the
configuration `Y = (Ω, ⋃_{k ∈ K} R_k)`.  Then for all pairs `x, y ∈ Ω`, `x ≠ y`, the color
`c(x,y)` determines whether `x, y` are twins in `Y`."

Paper's proof: "`x, y` are twins in `Y` if and only if they are twins in the extended
constituent `(Ω, R_k)` for each `k ∈ K`.  So the result follows from Lemma 3.4.13."

That reduction is not used here: the counting argument behind Lemma 3.4.12 works verbatim
for a union of colors, so the union is treated directly and Lemma 3.4.13 is the case
`K = {k}`.  (The reduction the paper uses would require that an automorphism of the union
of the `R_k` preserves each `R_k` separately, which is not immediate.)

decls.name: two_mul_ncard_le_of_clique
decls.docstring:
§9.7, Case 3a2, the step with mathematical content.  **A clique of blocks is at most
half of them.**  *"`U` was a clique in `Y` and therefore `|U| ≤ |W|/2 ≤ n₂/2` by
Prop. 2.4.11."*  (Version 2.5, lines 4285-4294.)

Let `P` be a homogeneous coherent configuration of rank at least `3` on the set of blocks,
and let `D` be a set of at least two blocks all of whose *ordered pairs of distinct
members* carry one and the same color of `P`.  Then `2|D| ≤ n₂`.

The proof is the paper's.  A homogeneous configuration has one diagonal color, so of its
`≥ 3` colors at least two are off-diagonal.  `D` uses only the one color `c₀` off the
diagonal, so no edge of any other off-diagonal color `c₁` has both ends in `D`, that is,
`D` is independent in the constituent `c₁`.  That constituent is a non-empty biregular
digraph on the whole set of blocks
(`Babai.PartitionStructure.extConstituent_isBiregular_of_isHomogeneous`), so Prop. 2.4.11
applies.

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 2.4.11 (PDF p. 22) — §9.7, Case 3a2, the step with mathematical content.  **A clique of blocks is at most half of them.**  *"`U` was a clique in `Y` and therefore `|U| ≤ |W|/2 ≤ n₂/2` by Prop. 2.4.11."*  (Version 2.5, lines 4285-4294.)

decls.name: vcolor_fst_eq
decls.docstring:
Observation 3.3.4 (Vertex-color awareness).  "The color of an edge determines the
colors of its tail and head."

Paper's proof: "Assume `c(x,y) = c(x',y') = i`.  We need to show that `c(x) = c(x')` and
`c(y) = c(y')`.  Let `c(x) = ℓ`, so `p^i_{ℓ,i} ≥ 1`.  It follows that
`(∃z')(c(x',z') = ℓ and c(z',y') = i)`.  But `ℓ` is a diagonal color, so `z' = x'` and
therefore `c(x') = c(x',x') = ℓ`.  So the color of the tail of the edge `(x,y)` is
determined by `c(x,y)`.  Now apply this fact to the color `i⁻` to see that the color of
the head is also determined."

links.rationale: Formalizes Observation 3.3.4 (Vertex-color awareness) (PDF p. 33) — Observation 3.3.4 (Vertex-color awareness).  "The color of an edge determines the colors of its tail and head."

decls.name: Proposition_11_2_4
decls.docstring:
§11.2, **Proposition 11.2.4**.

> If `G ≤ S_n` is a Cameron group with parameters `k, t, s` then `ts ≤ log₂ n`.  Moreover,
> `s ≤ log n / log k ≤ log n / log 5`.
>
> *Proof.* We have `n = C(k,t)^s ≥ (k/t)^{ts} ≥ 2^{ts}`.  Moreover, `n = C(k,t)^s ≥ k^s`.

decls.name: Proposition_11_2_5
decls.docstring:
§11.2, **Proposition 11.2.5**.

> If `G ≤ S_n` is a Cameron group with parameters `k, t, s` and `|G| ≥ n^{1+log₂ n}` then
> `k ≥ log₂ n` and `s! < n`, assuming `n` is greater than an absolute constant.
>
> *Proof.* As before, we have `n ≥ k^s`.  On the other hand
> `n^{1+log₂ n} ≤ |G| ≤ (k!)^s s! < k^{ks} s! ≤ n^k s! < n^k (log₂ n)^{log₂ n} =
> n^{k+log₂ log₂ n}`.  Therefore `k > log₂ n − log₂ log₂ n > log₂ n / log 5 ≥ s`.  Hence,
> `s! < s^s ≤ k^s ≤ n`.  Moreover, `n^{1+log₂ n} < n^k s! < n^{k+1}`, hence `k ≥ log₂ n`.

"assuming `n` is greater than an absolute constant" is the leading `∃ n₀`.  The bound on
`n` is in fact not needed: a Cameron group has `n = C(k,t)^s ≥ 5`, which is all the proof
below uses, so `n₀ = 0` works.  (The paper's chain is followed step by step: `|G| ≤
(k!)^s s!` is `Babai.card_le_of_isCameronGroup`, `(k!)^s < k^{ks} ≤ n^k` is `hfactk`,
`s! ≤ s^s ≤ (log₂ n)^{log₂ n} = n^{log₂ log₂ n}` is `hfacts`/`hLL`, and the two
conclusions come out in the paper's order: first `s ≤ log₂ n/2 < k`, hence `s! < s^s <
k^s ≤ n`, then `n^{1+log₂ n} ≤ |G| < n^{k+1}`, hence `log₂ n ≤ k`.)

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 11.2.4 (PDF p. 94) — §11.2, **Proposition 11.2.5**.

decls.name: Proposition_12_0_1_lifting
decls.docstring:
§12, **Proposition 12.0.1** (Lifting).

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` and `H ≤ S(Γ)` be permutation groups, `ϕ : G → H` a homomorphism, and
> `N = ker(ϕ)`.  Given these data, the strings `x, y : Ω → Σ` and `σ̄ ∈ H`, one can reduce,
> in polynomial time, the computation of the set `ϕ⁻¹(σ̄) ∩ Iso_G(x,y)` (set of liftings of
> `σ̄` to isomorphisms) to a single call to `Iso_N(x', y)` for some string `x'`.
>
> *Proof.*  If `σ̄ ∉ G^ϕ` then return "empty."  Otherwise let `σ ∈ ϕ⁻¹(σ̄)`. […]  Let
> `x' = x^σ`.  Then `ϕ⁻¹(σ̄) = σN` and `Iso_G(x,y) = σ Iso_G(x',y)`.  Consequently,
> `ϕ⁻¹(σ̄) ∩ Iso_G(x,y) = σ (N ∩ Iso_G(x',y)) = σ Iso_N(x',y)`.

This is the mathematical identity behind the reduction: for any lifting `σ` of `σ̄` and
`x' = x^σ`, the set of liftings of `σ̄` to isomorphisms is the paper's left coset
`σ Iso_N(x', y)`, i.e. `Babai.rightTranslate (Iso_N(x',y)) σ` (see the header).  The empty
case is `Babai.liftingSet_eq_empty`.  The single call is `Babai.liftingReduction`.  The polynomial-time
half is on the RAM in `Workspace/Algo/TopLift.lean` (`Algo.polyFun_actPreimage`,
`Algo.topLift_spec`).

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 12.0.1 (Lifting) (PDF p. 97) — §12, **Proposition 12.0.1** (Lifting).

decls.name: Proposition_12_0_5_i
decls.docstring:
§12, **Proposition 12.0.5** (TopAction1), item (i): the decision.

> (i) decide whether `ϕ` maps `Iso_G(x,y)` onto `H`;
>
> *Proof.*  Let `S' = S ∪ {1}`; so `S'` is a set of coset generators of `H`.  Apply
> Prop. 12.0.1 to each `σ̄ ∈ S'`.  If there is a `σ̄ ∈ S'` for which the algorithm returns
> the empty set (`σ̄` does not lift to an isomorphism), return the answer "no" to item (i).

`S` is the given set of generators of `H`, i.e. `⟨S⟩ = H`; since `H` is the ambient group
here, this reads `Subgroup.closure S = ⊤` in `H`.  The mathematical content is that it
suffices to test the `|S| + 1` elements of `S' = S ∪ {1}`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Proposition 12.0.5 (TopAction1) (PDF p. 97) — §12, **Proposition 12.0.5** (TopAction1), item (i): the decision.

decls.name: Proposition_12_0_5_ii
decls.docstring:
§12, **Proposition 12.0.5** (TopAction1), item (ii).

> (ii) if the answer is affirmative, find `Iso_G(x,y)`.
>
> *Proof.*  […] return the answer "yes" to item (i) and observe that `Iso_G(x,y)` is the
> right subcoset of `G` generated by the subcosets `ϕ⁻¹(σ̄) ∩ Iso_G(x,y)` (`σ̄ ∈ S'`) found
> by Prop. 12.0.1.

Here `S' = S ∪ {1}` and the subcoset generated is `Babai.subcosetClosure` (the smallest
subcoset containing the union), which for a subset of `G` is the same whether computed
inside `G` or inside `S(Ω)` since `G` itself is a subcoset.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Proposition 12.0.1 (Lifting) (PDF p. 97) — §12, **Proposition 12.0.5** (TopAction1), item (ii).

decls.name: Proposition_12_0_9
decls.docstring:
§12, **Proposition 12.0.9**.

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a permutation group and `ϕ : G → S(Γ)` a giant representation.  Let
> `C ⊆ Γ`.  Then the setwise stabilizer `G_C = {σ ∈ G | C^{σ^ϕ} = C}` can be found in
> polynomial time.
>
> *Proof.*  Let `H = (G^ϕ)_C`.  Given that `G^ϕ` is a giant, finding `H` is
> straightforward.  Now `G_C = ϕ⁻¹(H)`.

The mathematical content is the last equation, `G_C = ϕ⁻¹((G^ϕ)_C)`.  ("Finding `H`" and
the polynomial time bound are on the RAM in `Workspace/Algo/TopStab.lean`:
`Algo.polyFun_topStab`, `Algo.topStab_spec_of_wf`.)

decls.name: Remark_10_2_6_statement
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.2.6**, §10.2.

> The assumption `k > 2 + log₂ n` is tight infinitely often, as shown by the affine case of
> even dimension in characteristic 2.  In this case `G = ℤ₂^{k-2} ⋊ A_k` acts primitively
> on `n = 2^{k-2}` elements as follows: `A_k` acts on `ℤ₂^k` by permuting the coordinates;
> restrict this action to the zero-weight subspace `∑ xᵢ = 0`, and then to the quotient
> space by the one-dimensional subspace `x₁ = ⋯ = x_k` (this is contained in the
> zero-weight subspace when the dimension is even).  In this case, `k = 2 + log₂ n`, and
> `A_k` is a proper quotient of `G`.

What the remark asserts is that Lemma 10.2.5 fails at `k = 2 + log₂ n`: for even `k` there
is a primitive group of degree `2^{k-2}` with `A_k` as a *proper* quotient.  The
construction is not used anywhere in the paper, so it is recorded as a statement only.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 1.2.2 (PDF p. 13) — **Remark 10.2.6**, §10.2.
Formalizes Remark 10.2.6 (PDF p. 85) — **Remark 10.2.6**, §10.2.

decls.name: Remark_10_2_7_statement
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.2.7**, §10.2.

> Under the stronger assumption `k > (log n)^c` for some constant `c`, Pyber [Py17] gave an
> elementary proof of the conclusion of Lemma 10.2.5.

Cited, and used in no proof of the paper (it records that a CFSG-free proof exists under a
stronger hypothesis), so it gets no axiom and is recorded as a statement only.

*"Stronger"* is read as it is written: the hypothesis `k > max{8, 2 + log₂ n}` of
Lemma 10.2.5 (`Babai.LargeK`) stays, and `k > (log n)^c` is added.  Without the first
hypothesis the statement is false for every `c`: the regular cyclic group on two points
(for `c ≥ 0`) or on three points (for `c < 0`) is primitive, maps onto `A₂ = 1` by the
trivial map, which is not injective, and `(log n)^c ≤ 1 < 2 = k`.  See the corrected paper.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 10.2.7 (PDF p. 85) — **Remark 10.2.7**, §10.2.

> If `k ≥ max{9, 2 log₂ n₀}` then we can use Theorem 10.5.1 to make a more detailed
> statement.  We observe that `ker(ϕ)` fixes each standard block (setwise) (see item (e) in
> Theorem 10.5.1) so the length of each orbit of `ker(ϕ)` contained in `∆` is
> `≤ |∆| / (k choose t_Δ)`.

A sharpening of Cor. 10.3.7 that the paper does not use; stated multiplicatively to avoid

`Babai.remark_10_3_8_statement_holds`.

decls.name: Remark_10_5_2_statement
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.5.2** (Tight bound for `k`), §10.5.

> The actual condition on `k`, sufficient for most conclusions of the theorem, is that
> `k > max{8, 2 + log₂ n₀}` and `(1/2)(k choose ⌊k/2⌋) > n₀`.  … The only difference would
> be that instead of `|T(x)| < k/4` we would only get `|T(x)| < k/2`, sufficient for our
> goals.

Recorded as a statement only: it asserts that items (a)–(g) hold under the weaker
hypothesis, with `|T(x)| < k/2` in place of `|T(x)| < k/4`.  Version 2.5 uses only the
`k ≥ max{9, 2 log₂ n₀}` form.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 10.5.2 (Tight bound for $k$) (PDF p. 89) — **Remark 10.5.2** (Tight bound for `k`), §10.5.

decls.name: Remark_10_5_3_statement
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.5.3** (Multiple systems of imprimitivity), §10.5.

> The presence of multiple systems of imprimitivity with the same kernel as discussed in
> Item (g) is a real possibility.  Consider for instance the action `S_k → S_{k(k−1)}`
> defined by the action of `S_k` on the `k(k−1)` ordered pairs; let `G ≤ S_{k(k−1)}` be the
> image of this action.  Then `G` has two systems of imprimitivity on which `S_k` acts in
> its natural action (there are `k` blocks in each system), and there is a unique system of
> imprimitivity with `(k choose 2)` blocks on which the action is `S_k^(2)`.  The latter
> are the standard blocks; in this case each standard block has 2 elements.  Each of the
> three actions is faithful, so their kernel is the same, namely, the identity.

An example, used nowhere; recorded as a statement only.  Its *content* is the last
sentence — the three systems have the same kernel, namely the identity — so that is
recorded too, as the triviality of the kernel of the action on each of the three systems
(`σ` fixes every block of the system setwise only if `σ = 1`); with it, the example shows
that the hypothesis of item (g) really is satisfiable by more than one system, which is
why item (g) needs its word "another".

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 10.5.3 (Multiple systems of imprimitivity) (PDF p. 89) — **Remark 10.5.3** (Multiple systems of imprimitivity), §10.5.

decls.name: Remark_11_1_4_alignment
decls.docstring:
§11.1, **Remark 11.1.4** (Alignment).

> Applying Eq. (57) to a subgroup `K = G ≤ S(Ω)`, we see that the isomorphism problem for
> the pair `(x,y)` of strings with respect to a coset `Gσ` is the same as the isomorphism
> problem for `(x, y^{σ⁻¹})` with respect to the group `G`.  In view of Eq. (59), the same
> holds for window-isomorphism.  The shift `y ← y^{σ⁻¹}` is an important **alignment
> step** that will accompany every reduction of the ambient group `G`.

The precise content is that the two sets differ by the (bijective) translation by `σ`.

decls.name: Remark_12_0_2_constructiveMembership
decls.docstring:
§12, **Remark 12.0.2**.

> `H` does not need to be a permutation group.  What we need is that `H` permit
> *constructive membership testing*, i. e., for any list of elements `τ₁, …, τ_k, ρ ∈ H` we
> should be able to efficiently decide whether `ρ ∈ K` where `K` is the subgroup generated
> by the `τᵢ`, and if the answer is affirmative, to produce a straight-line program that
> constructs `ρ` from the `τᵢ` (see Def. 11.1.10).

The mathematical content of "constructive membership testing" is the existence of the
straight-line program (Def. 11.1.10, `Babai.IsStraightLineProgram`); efficiency is not
modelled.  The statement below is that this always holds mathematically in a finite group,
so the remark is about cost only.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 12.0.2 (PDF p. 97) — §12, **Remark 12.0.2**.

decls.name: Remark_12_0_7_as_printed
decls.docstring:
§12, **Remark 12.0.7**, *as printed*.

> If `m ≥ max{9, 2 log₂ n}` then `n/k = (m choose t)` for some `1 ≤ t < m/4` by item (e) of
> the Main Structure Theorem (Theorem 10.5.1).

Here `k` is the number of orbits of `N = ker(ϕ)` and `n/k` is their common length
(Cor. 12.0.6).  This statement is **false**; see `Babai.not_Remark_12_0_7_as_printed` for a
proved counterexample, and `Babai.Remark_12_0_7_statement` for what item (e) does give.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 12.0.7 (PDF p. 98) — §12, **Remark 12.0.7**, *as printed*.

decls.name: Remark_12_0_7_statement
decls.docstring:
§12, **Remark 12.0.7**, restated.

The remark is never used, in Section 12 or later, so it is recorded as a statement only
(as `Babai.Remark_10_3_2_statement` is in Section 10).  What is printed is false
(`Babai.not_Remark_12_0_7_as_printed`); what item (e) of Theorem 10.5.1 gives is that
`(m choose t)` divides the number `k` of `N`-orbits, hence `k ≥ (m choose t)` and the
common orbit length `n/k` divides the standard-block size `n/(m choose t)`.

A *reduction*: a decision tree whose internal nodes are calls to String Isomorphism.
`done a` returns the value `a`; `call I k` asks for the answer to the instance `I` and
continues with `k` applied to that answer.

This is what the paper's "we can achieve the following by recursively calling `N`
instances of String Isomorphism …" means, minus the running time: the calls are the
recursive instances, and the whole tree is the explicit function that turns their answers
into the answer to the original question.  The calls may be *adaptive* (the Chain Rule
chooses the next instance using the previous answer), which is why a list of instances
would not do.

decls.name: Sec15Choices
decls.docstring:
§15: **the choices one round of the Master Algorithm makes**.

Line 1 chooses the branch of Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson that applies, with the data that
branch runs on (`Babai.Line1Choice`); lines 4c–4d choose the geometric data of one round of
Procedure Align (`Babai.Line4cdChoice`).  Both are choices of *data*, as the paper's
*"find a minimal block system"* and *"apply the Extended Design Lemma"* are; the reduction
each line runs is a named function of the data.  The round, and `Babai.Theorem_1_1_1_math`
with it, is stated for **every** such structure of choices.

Lines 5–7 choose in the same way (`Babai.Line567aChoice`, `Babai.Line56a7aChoice`): one
round on the window at each outcome of Theorem 13.2.1, with a reject exit that carries its
own test.  See the corrected paper entries on Finding 1 of the audit of Secs. 14–15.

decls.name: Sec15Remaining
decls.docstring:
§15, **the branches that are not yet named reductions**: lines 4c–4d and lines 5–7a.

The tests are no longer abstract: `Babai.IsJohnson`, `Babai.param`, `Babai.TIsOne` and
`Babai.IsPrimitiveCase` are read off the hint the instance carries
(`Babai.HintedInstance`), and the data itself is available to the branches through

`Babai.line1Round` (Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, §11.3), `Babai.line2Branch` and

Procedure Align).  Lines 1, 2 and 4b prescribe it: line 1 attaches the Johnson case data of
step 7 of Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (`Babai.line1Lift`), and lines 2 and 4b shrink the
window and start again at line 1, so their calls carry nothing.

decls.name: SmallDefect
decls.docstring:
§15, **line 4b, the test**: *"if relative symmetry defect of `H(x)` is `< 1/2`"*.

This is the paper's own test, on the paper's own object: `H(x)` is the string of the window,
read through the labelling of line 4 as an edge coloring of the `t`-uniform hypergraph on
`Γ` (`Babai.hyperColoring`), its automorphism group is `Babai.colorAut`, and *"relative
symmetry defect"* is `Babai.defect` (Definition 2.3.13).

Line 4b is inside line 4, so the test carries the primitive case with it; its negation is
therefore *"`G` is primitive and the defect is `≥ 1/2`"*, which is exactly the hypothesis
line 4c is given (`Babai.largeDefectData_of_not_smallDefect`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 2.3.13 (PDF p. 20) — §15, **line 4b, the test**: *"if relative symmetry defect of `H(x)` is `< 1/2`"*.

decls.name: SmallDefectData
decls.docstring:
§15, **line 4b**: the data Cor. 12.0.10 is applied to.

Line 4b reads the strings as edge-colored `t`-uniform hypergraphs on `Γ` and tests whether
the relative symmetry defect of `H(x)` is `< 1/2`.  What Cor. 12.0.10 consumes is the
consequence of that test: a canonically defined set `C ⊆ Γ` of more than `m/2` vertices, on
which the automorphism group of `x` induces at least the alternating group.  The set is
given here as a canonical two-coloring of `Γ` together with the color `c` of `C`, which is
the shape of the `col`, `c` arguments of `Babai.Corollary_12_0_10`.

The Sec. 7 symmetry-defect argument supplies the coloring and its properties through
`Babai.smallDefect_data`, as used by `Babai.nonempty_smallDefectData` below. The remaining
fields carry the choices used by the top-action tree.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Corollary 12.0.10 (TopAction4) (PDF p. 99) — §15, **line 4b**: the data Cor. 12.0.10 is applied to.

decls.name: exists_subst_idx
decls.docstring:
The index identity behind `KAryPartStruct.wlStep_isConfiguration`: substituting a
vertex `z` in the `j`-th coordinate of `τ(x⃗)` is the *same* as applying a suitable index
transformation `σ ∈ 𝔐_k` to a substitution of `z` in a single coordinate `m` of `x⃗`, where
`m` and `σ` depend only on `τ` and `j`, not on `x⃗` or on `z`.

Two cases.  If `τ` is injective, take `m = τ(j)` and `σ = τ`: the `i`-th letter of
`σ(x⃗ ᵐ(z))` is `z` when `τ(i) = τ(j)`, i.e. when `i = j`, and `x_{τ(i)}` otherwise.  If `τ`
is not injective then, `[k]` being finite, it is not surjective, so some `m ∈ [k]` is
outside the image of `τ`; take that `m` and `σ = τ` with the value at `j` changed to `m`.
Then the `i`-th letter of `σ(x⃗ ᵐ(z))` for `i ≠ j` is `x_{τ(i)}` (as `τ(i) ≠ m`), and the
`j`-th letter is `z`.

links.rationale: The index identity behind `KAryPartStruct.wlStep_isConfiguration`: substituting a vertex `z` in the `j`-th coordinate of `τ(x⃗)` is the *same* as applying a suitable index transformation `σ ∈ 𝔐_k` ...

decls.name: idx_padMap_pad
decls.docstring:
Observation 5.1.14.  "Let `x⃗ = x₁ … x_ℓ ∈ Ω^ℓ` and `τ ∈ 𝔐_ℓ`.  Then
`(pad(τ))(pad(x⃗)) = pad(τ(x⃗))`."  (Eq. (31).)

Paper's proof: "Let `j ∈ [k]`.  Let us compare the `j`-th letter of the strings on each
side.  First assume `j ≤ ℓ`.  Then on the right-hand side we have `x_{j^τ}`.  On the
left-hand side we have `x_{j^{pad(τ)}}`.  As `j^τ = j^{pad(τ)}`, we are done.  Assume now
`j ≥ ℓ`.  Then on the right-hand side we have `x_{ℓ^τ}`.  On the left-hand side we have
`x_{ℓ^{pad(τ)}}`.  We conclude as before."

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 5.1.13 (PDF p. 53) — Observation 5.1.14.  "Let `x⃗ = x₁ … x_ℓ ∈ Ω^ℓ` and `τ ∈ 𝔐_ℓ`.  Then `(pad(τ))(pad(x⃗)) = pad(τ(x⃗))`."  (Eq. (31).)
Formalizes Observation 5.1.14 (PDF p. 53) — Observation 5.1.14.  "Let `x⃗ = x₁ … x_ℓ ∈ Ω^ℓ` and `τ ∈ 𝔐_ℓ`.  Then `(pad(τ))(pad(x⃗)) = pad(τ(x⃗))`."  (Eq. (31).)

decls.name: Theorem923Uniform
decls.docstring:
§9.2, Theorem 9.2.3 **with its constants fixed before the ground set**.

`Babai.theorem_9_2_3` fixes the ground set `Ω` first and produces `q` and `c` after it, so
the constants it hands back may change with the ground set.  Line 4c of Sec. 15 calls
Theorem 9.2.3 once per round, each time on another set `Γ = Fin m`, and the cost of a
round has to be **one** function of the window size, so the constants must be the same at
every call.  This is the uniform form, with the binder of the ground set inside the
existential; see the entry *"the absolute constants are chosen after the ground set"* in
the corrected paper.

This is **not an axiom**.  It is a hypothesis of the construction of lines 4c–4d, and it is
discharged as soon as `Babai.theorem_9_2_3` is restated in this form, which is the repair
that entry describes.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 9.2.3 (Extended Design Lemma) (PDF p. 72) — §9.2, Theorem 9.2.3 **with its constants fixed before the ground set**.

decls.docstring:
§11.1, **Theorem 11.1.9** (Imprimitive Luks reduction).

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` and let `Δ ⊆ Ω` be a `G`-invariant subset.  Let `{B₁,…,B_m}` be a
> `G`-invariant partition of `Δ`.  Let `ψ : G → Ḡ ≤ S_m` be the induced action of `G` on
> the set of blocks and let `N = ker(ψ)`.  Then finding `Iso^Δ_G(x,y)` reduces to
> `m|Ḡ| = m|G/N|` instances of finding `Iso^{B_i}_{M_i}(x, y^{σ_i})` for the blocks `B_i`
> and certain subgroups `M_i ≤ N` and `σ_i ∈ G`.
>
> *Proof.*  First descend to `N = ker ψ`.  Then consider each `B_i` to be the window in
> succession, reducing the group at each round, following the Chain Rule.  In the end,
> combine all the results into a single coset.

The identity below is the two steps of the proof: descent to `N` (Prop. 11.1.6), which
produces `|G : N| = |Ḡ|` terms indexed by `G ⧸ N` (`Babai.Theorem_11_1_9_card`), and then
the decomposition of the window `Δ = ⋃ᵢ Bᵢ` into the `m` blocks (`Babai.wIso_window_sUnion`),
which produces `m` window-isomorphism problems on the blocks inside each term — `m|Ḡ|`
subproblems in total.  The subgroups `Mᵢ ≤ N` and the shifts `σᵢ` of the paper appear when
the intersection over the blocks is computed one block at a time; that is
`Babai.imprimitive_luks_step` below.

The paper's two standing hypotheses are carried: `Δ` is a `G`-invariant subset (`hΔ`) and
`{B₁,…,B_m}` is a `G`-invariant partition of `Δ` (`hℬ`, `Babai.IsInvariantPartitionOn`).
Of the clauses of `hℬ` the identity itself uses only "`G` permutes the blocks" and
"the union of the blocks is `Δ`"; the other clauses and `hΔ` are what make the blocks
legitimate windows in the Chain Rule step (`Babai.imprimitive_luks_step`).

decls.name: Theorem_11_2_1
decls.docstring:
§11.2, **Theorem 11.2.1**.

> Let `G ≤ S_n` be a primitive group of order `|G| ≥ n^{1+log₂ n}` where `n` is greater
> than some absolute constant.  Then `G` has a normal subgroup `N` of index `≤ n` such
> that `N` has a system of imprimitivity on which `N` acts as a Johnson group `A_k^(t)`
> with `k ≥ log₂ n`.  Moreover, `N` and the system of imprimitivity in question can be
> found in polynomial time.

The mathematical half is stated here.  The algorithmic half ("can be found in polynomial
time") is on the RAM, in `Workspace/Algo/CameronNbar.lean` (`Algo.exists_polyFun_cameronNbarSpec`,
the generators of `N`), `Workspace/Algo/CameronDescent.lean` (`Algo.camRecognize_index`, the
blocks and the bounds) and `Workspace/Algo/CameronJohnson.lean` (the Johnson action); it
rests on the cited recognition of Cameron groups, `Babai.cameronStructure_polyTime`
.  "where `n` is greater than some
absolute constant" is the leading `∃ n₀`.

The paper's proof is: "The mathematical part of this result is an immediate consequence of
Cameron's classification of large primitive groups" (Theorem 11.2.3), completed by
Propositions 11.2.4 and 11.2.5.  The intermediate steps are not spelled out in the paper,
and one of them needs care: if `N` is taken to be the kernel of the action `G → S_s` on the
direct factors of the socle (index `≤ s! < n` by Prop. 11.2.5), then the group `N` induces
on the fibres of one coordinate of `(Fin k choose t)^s` only lies *between* `A_k^(t)` and
`S_k^(t)`, so it need not be `A_k^(t)`, as the conclusion demands.  The route that gives
`A_k^(t)` literally is to take `N` to be the base group `(A_k^(t))^s` of Definition 11.2.2,
which is contained in `G`, normal in `S_k^(t) ≀ S_s` and hence in `G`, and whose index in
`G` is at most `|S_k^(t) ≀ S_s : (A_k^(t))^s| ≤ 2^s s! ≤ (2s)^s ≤ C(k,t)^s = n`, the last
inequality because `2s ≤ log₂ n ≤ k ≤ C(k,t)` by Propositions 11.2.4 and 11.2.5.  The
blocks are the fibres of one coordinate, on which `(A_k^(t))^s` induces exactly `A_k^(t)`,
and `k ≥ log₂ n` is Proposition 11.2.5.

Two points of reading, both forced by the paper's own conventions.

* The system of imprimitivity is on all of `Ω` (`Δ = Set.univ`): a system of imprimitivity
 is a partition of an invariant subset (§2.2.1), and here it is a system for `N`, the
 group on which the reduction continues to run with the *same* permutation domain
 ("`N` has a system of imprimitivity"); `N` is a nontrivial normal subgroup of the
 primitive group `G`, hence transitive on `Ω`.
* "`A_k^(t)`" means a Johnson group in the range of §2.2.1, i.e. `1 ≤ t` and `2t < k`
 (which is also what Definition 11.2.2 requires of the parameters of a Cameron group).
 Without these two constraints the conclusion would be satisfied by the degenerate
 `t = 0`, `ℬ = {Ω}`, for which `A_k^(0)` is the trivial group on one block, so the
 statement would be vacuous.

decls.name: Theorem_11_2_3
decls.docstring:
§11.2, **Theorem 11.2.3** (Cameron, Maróti).

Quoted from the paper:

> **Theorem 11.2.3** (Cameron [Cam81], Maróti [Mar]).  For `n ≥ 25`, if `G` is primitive
> and `|G| ≥ n^{1+log₂ n}` then `G` is a Cameron group.

The paper gives no proof.  "Cameron group" is Definition 11.2.2, transcribed as
`Babai.IsCameronGroup` (the parameters `s, t, k` are existentially quantified here, as in
the paper's "`G` is a Cameron group").

**Citation.** `[Cam81]` = Peter J. Cameron: *Finite permutation groups and finite simple
groups*, Bull. London Math. Soc. **13** (1981), 1–22.  `[Mar]` = Attila Maróti: *On the
orders of primitive groups*, J. Algebra **258** (2002), no. 2, 631–640.  The paper gives
no theorem number in either source.

**CFSG.** The paper states in §1.2.3 and §16.1 that this result depends on the
Classification of Finite Simple Groups.

**Used where.** Theorem 11.2.1 ("The mathematical part of this result is an immediate
consequence of Cameron's classification of large primitive groups which we state below"),
hence Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (§11.3), hence line 1 of the Master Algorithm (§15).

**Consistency.**  `IsPrimitive` is the paper's primitivity (`|G| ≥ 2` and no nontrivial
blocks), not Mathlib's `IsPreprimitive`; for `n ≥ 25` the two agree.  The threshold
`n ≥ 25` and the bound `|G| ≥ n^{1+log₂ n}` are as printed, with `log₂` the binary
logarithm (`Real.logb 2`) and the power a real power (`Real.rpow`).  For `n = 25` the
bound reads `|G| ≥ 25^{1+log₂ 25} ≈ 1.6·10⁸`, which only the giants `S₂₅` and `A₂₅`
satisfy among the primitive groups of degree `25`; both are Cameron groups with
`s = t = 1`, `k = 25`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Theorem 11.2.3 (Cameron~\cite{cameron}, Mar\'oti~\cite{maroti}) (PDF p. 94) — §11.2, **Theorem 11.2.3** (Cameron, Maróti).

decls.name: Theorem_1_1_1_math
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 1.1.1** (Sec. 1.1, version 2.5, `quasi25.txt` line 1089):

> **Theorem 1.1.1.** *The String Isomorphism problem can be solved in quasipolynomial time.*

This is the **mathematical half** of that statement for the Master Algorithm of Sec. 15 with
every one of its seven lines carried out: Procedure String-Isomorphism, run with the round
`Babai.sec15Remaining`, returns `Iso_G(x,y)`, and the number of String Isomorphism instances
it generates — the size of the recursion tree, which is the number of rounds and of leaves —
is at most `exp(30 (log₂ n + 2)^{c₁+2})` for an absolute constant `c₁`.  The constant is
quantified **before** the ground set, the alphabet, the group and the two strings, so it is
one absolute constant and not a function of the input; it comes from the quasipolynomial
bound on `q` of Theorem 9.2.3 alone (`Babai.quasiPolyBound_sec15RoundCost`).

**For every choice.**  The statement holds for every `Babai.Sec15Choices`: line 1 may take
any branch of Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson that applies, with any data that branch runs on,
lines 4c–4d may run Procedure Align on any admissible geometric data, and lines 5–7 may
take any outcome of Theorem 13.2.1 that applies, with the data of that outcome.  What each
line then does with the data is a named reduction, not a choice.  The first half of the
conclusion says that there is at least one such choice (`Babai.sec15Choices`), so the
second half is not vacuous.

What the Lean statement does **not** cover is the **running time**: what is bounded here is
the number of instances the recursion generates, not the number of RAM steps.  The running
time is `Algo.theorem_1_1_1` (`Workspace/Algo/TopMasterClose.lean`), a statement about the
RAM of `Workspace/Machine/`.

**What it rests on.**  No `sorry`: outcome (2b) of Theorem 13.2.1 is proved
(`Babai.nonempty_line6aCase2bCore`, from `Babai.case2b_facts_on`), and so is the last case
of Sec. 9.7 (`Babai.case_9_7_case2_dom`).  `#print axioms Babai.Theorem_1_1_1_math` lists
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` and the four results cited from the literature
(`Babai.schreierHypothesis`, `Babai.degtrans_le_five`, `Babai.le_add_two_of_involved_GL`,
`Babai.Theorem_11_2_3`), and nothing else (Fact 10.2.2 (ii), `Babai.fact_10_2_2_ii`,
Theorem 10.2.4, `Babai.theorem_10_2_4`, and [DiM, Thms. 5.2A, 5.2B],
`Babai.dixonMortimer_5_2A` and `Babai.dixonMortimer_5_2B`, are proved).  The
algorithmic axiom `Babai.cameronStructure_polyTime` is not among them: it concerns running
time only.

`Babai.Theorem_1_1_1_math_of_sec15` is the lemma this follows from, with the constants of
Theorem 9.2.3 still hypotheses.

decls.docstring:
**Theorem 1.1.1** (Sec. 1.1), the mathematical half, for the Master Algorithm of Sec. 15
run along a **family** of choices: one choice per node, not one choice for the whole run.

The statement is `Babai.Theorem_1_1_1_math` word for word, with `Babai.sec15MasterStep Ω A ch`
replaced by `Babai.masterStepOfFamily`.  The constant `c₁` is the same one: it comes from the
quasipolynomial bound on the round cost (`Babai.quasiPolyBound_sec15RoundCost`), and the
round cost of the family is `Babai.sec15RoundCost q923 c923`, the round cost of every member
of the family.  So `c₁` is quantified before the ground set, before the alphabet and before
the family, exactly as in `Babai.Theorem_1_1_1_math`.

This is what a machine layer needs: it may pick a different branch at each node, and the
count of String Isomorphism instances is still at most `exp(30 (log₂ n + 2)^{c₁+2})`.

The first half of the conclusion is the one of `Babai.Theorem_1_1_1_math`: there is at least
one `Babai.Sec15Choices`, so families are not made of nothing.

decls.name: Theorem_1_1_1_math_of_masterStep
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 1.1.1** (Sec. 1.1, proved by the Master Algorithm of Sec. 15), the
mathematical half:

> The String Isomorphism problem for a group `G ≤ S(Ω)`, `|Ω| = n`, can be solved in
> `exp(O((log n)^c))` time for some constant `c`.

Given one round of Procedure String-Isomorphism (`Babai.MasterStep`) whose multiplicative
cost `q(n)` is quasipolynomial, `q(n) ≤ exp((log n)^{c₁})`, the procedure

* returns `Iso_G(x,y)` (Sec. 15, the output line), and
* generates at most `exp(30 (log₂ n + 2)^{c₁ + 2})` String Isomorphism instances,

so the exponent is `c = c₁ + 2`: two extra powers of `log n` for the depth of the recursion,
exactly as in `T(x) = q(x)^{O(log x)}` (Eq. (67)) composed with the Johnson recursion of
item (v) of Sec. 11.4.

What is bounded is the number of instances, i.e. the number of nodes of the recursion tree,
not the number of group operations; see the Sec. 15 entry of the corrected paper.
**This is conditional on a `MasterStep`.** It is the recursion analysis of Sec. 15 given one
round with the properties listed in `MasterStep`. Theorem 1.1.1 at the mathematical level
follows only once `masterStep_of_procedure` builds such a round from the procedures of
Secs. 11–14 (not done yet). The name `Theorem_1_1_1_math` is kept free for that
unconditional statement.

The hypothesis is `q(n) ≤ 2^{(log₂ n + 2)^{c₁}}`, which is `RAM.QuasiPolyBound q` written
out.  An earlier form of this theorem wrote `log₂ n + 1` there.  That form is empty: at
`n = 1` its right side is `2^{1^{c₁}} = 2` for every `c₁`, while the cost of one round of
Sec. 15 is at least `8`, so no round of ours could satisfy it.  See the the corrected paper
entry on the round-cost hypothesis of Theorem 1.1.1.

with every one of its seven lines carried out.

Procedure String-Isomorphism, run with the round `Babai.sec15Remaining`, returns
`Iso_G(x,y)` and generates at most `exp(30 (log₂ n + 2)^{c₁+2})` String Isomorphism

Two remarks on the form.

* The multiplicative cost `(q, c)` of Theorem 9.2.3 is a parameter here (`hq`, and
 `Babai.Theorem923Uniform` where the choices are produced).  Theorem 9.2.3 is proved

* What is counted is the number of String Isomorphism instances, not the running time.  The
 running time is `Algo.theorem_1_1_1`, on the RAM model of `Workspace/Machine/`.

decls.docstring:
Theorem 2.2.5 (a) (Wielandt).  "Let `G ≤ S_n` be `t`-transitive.  Assume `G` is not a
giant.  Then `t < 3 ln n`."

(Version 2.5 prints `t < 3 ln k` although the degree is called `n` in the same sentence;
the original source and the use of this theorem in §14 show that the degree is meant.
We write `n = |Ω|`.)

The paper gives no proof; it cites Wielandt's 1934 dissertation.  This result does not
depend on the CFSG.  It is used only in the concluding remarks (Sec. 16.1, line 5976:
"By Wielandt's 1934 result (Thm. 2.2.5) we have `d < 3 ln n`"), inside the alternative
algorithm sketched there, and on no path of the main algorithm; §14 of the original
source used it.  Recorded as a statement only, not asserted.

finite simple group is solvable) is a known consequence of the CFSG; the paper carries it
as an explicit hypothesis, and so do we.

decls.name: isTwinIn_of_nbhd_eq
decls.docstring:
Observation 2.4.28 for a vertex-colored bipartite graph: two vertices of the first part
with the same neighborhood and the same vertex color are twins.

Proof: the transposition `τ = (u,v)` preserves the two parts (`u`, `v` both lie in `V₁`),
fixes every vertex of the second part, and preserves the edges — an edge runs from the
first part to the second, so its head is fixed by `τ` and its tail is moved only between
`u` and `v`, which have equal neighborhoods.  The vertex colors are preserved because
`f(u) = f(v)`.

This is the step used in step 7 of Procedure Bipartite Split-or-Johnson (*"otherwise `V₁`
would be a twin equivalence class in `X₁₂`"*) and in §9.7 (*"This hypergraph has no multiple
edges because there are no twins in `V₁`"*).

decls.name: VColBipThr
decls.docstring:
§9.2, Theorem 9.2.2.  Vertex-colored bipartite graphs **carrying their threshold
parameter**: an object on `s` is a pair `(X, α)` of a vertex-colored bipartite graph and a
real number, and a morphism `(X, α) → (Y, β)` is an isomorphism `X → Y` of vertex-colored
bipartite graphs together with `α = β`.

Why the parameter is data of the object.  The conclusion of Theorem 9.2.2 depends on `α`,
and Lemma 9.3.1 feeds Theorem 9.2.2 an `α = βn/d₂` that depends on the *input object*.
The composition rule for canonical reductions (`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.comp`) takes one
source category for the second step, so that step cannot be stated on a category indexed
by `α` from outside.  Carrying `α` in the object solves this, and loses nothing: the
objects with a fixed value of `α` form a full subcategory with exactly the morphisms of
the printed statement, and `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.full` restricts to it (see
`Babai.theorem_9_2_2_at`).

`{z | d(x,z) = a and d(z,y) = b}` over the pairs `(a,b)` with `μ(a) = j` and `μ(b) = k`,

`(x',y')`.

decls.name: actsAsJohnsonA_descentBlocks
decls.docstring:
§11.3, steps 6–7, **the Johnson case after the Luks descent**.

Let `G` be transitive with the system `ℬ` of imprimitivity of step 4, let `N̄ ≤ G^ℬ` be the
normal subgroup of Theorem 11.2.1 and `𝒞` its system of imprimitivity on `ℬ`, on which it
acts as the Johnson group `A_k^{(t)}`.  If `G₁ = ψ⁻¹(N̄)` is transitive, then `(G₁, {⋃ C})`
is the Johnson case with the same parameters `k, t`.

The proof is the paper's: the sets `⋃ C` are a system of imprimitivity of `G₁`
(`Babai.isSystemOfImprimitivity_descentBlocks`), the map `C ↦ ⋃ C` is a bijection
(`Babai.blockUnion_injOn`), and it commutes with the two actions
(`Babai.permCongr_blockHom_descentBlocks`), so the induced group on the new blocks is the
same Johnson group.

decls.name: affected_of_transitive_giant
decls.docstring:
§12, proof of Cor. 12.0.6: "Lemma 10.3.1 … says that `Ω` is affected", for a giant
representation of a transitive group.

The Lean transcription of Lemma 10.3.1 (`Babai.lemma_10_3_1`) assumes `G^ϕ = A(Γ)`, as the
paper's Lemma 10.3.1 does; the proof of Cor. 12.0.6 cites it also in the case `G^ϕ = S(Γ)`,
where it does not literally apply.  The argument used here is instead the paper's own
Theorem 10.3.5 (Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma), which *is* stated for a giant
representation: the unaffected set `D` is `G`-invariant, so for a transitive `G` it is `∅`
or `Ω`; and if it were `Ω` then `G_(D) = 1`, whereas Theorem 10.3.5 gives `G_(D)^ϕ ≥ A(Γ)`,
impossible for `m ≥ 3`.

links.rationale: Formalizes Lemma 10.3.1 (PDF p. 85) — §12, proof of Cor. 12.0.6: "Lemma 10.3.1 … says that `Ω` is affected", for a giant representation of a transitive group.

decls.name: aggregatesToStructure
decls.docstring:
§15, **the test of line 6** at a hinted instance: *"if AggregateCertificates returns
canonically embedded `k`-ary relational structure on `Γ` with relative symmetry defect
`≥ 1/2`"*.

This is the definition meant for the field `AggregatesToStructure` of
`Babai.Sec15Remaining`.  It is a test on the instance alone — the group `G = K^Δ` and the
giant representation `ϕ` of line 3 are the ones the hint carries (`Babai.johnsonData`), the
string is the string of the window, and the test set size is the `t = O(log n)` of §13.1
(`Babai.testSetSize`).  Like `Babai.SmallDefect`, it reads the instance through the *chosen*
Johnson data, so both strings of one instance are read through the same `(G, ϕ)`.

decls.name: alignColor_cases
decls.docstring:
§14.1, **lines 4-7**: an outcome of Theorem 9.2.3 either colors `Γ` with classes of at
most `αm` vertices — and then the Chain Rule of line 5 runs on classes of `Ω` of at most
`max(2/3, α)·n` points (`Babai.ncard_omegaColorClass_le_of_alpha`) — or it has a dominant
color class (line 6) carrying an extra structure (line 7).

*Proof.*  In case (a) the trichotomy
`Babai.ColoredPartition.alphaPartition_trichotomy` leaves, for each color, either a class of
at most half of `Γ` — which is at most `αm` because `α ≥ 1/2` — or a class of at most `αm`,
or a class with two blocks; a class with two blocks that is also dominant is the second
alternative, and if there is none, every class is at most `αm`.  In case (b) the vertex set
`W` of the Johnson scheme has `|W| ≥ αm > m/2`, so its color is dominant — unless `m = 0`,
when every class is empty.

automorphism group of the colored partition (`Babai.partAut`; see the module docstring for
why `Aut(X')` and not `Aut(Y)`), and `ψ` is its action on those blocks

class is the disjoint union of its blocks, each of at least two points, and it lies inside
`Γ`.

decls.name: aut_johnsonGraph_of_one_le
decls.docstring:
Proposition 3.2.11 for all `t ≥ 1` (Def. 3.2.9 asks for `t ≥ 2`; the proof needs the
case `t = 1`, where `J(Γ,1)` is the complete graph).

Route, by induction on `t`.  For `t = 1` every permutation of the `1`-sets comes from a
permutation of `Γ`.  For the step, an automorphism of `J(Γ,t+1)` permutes the stars
(`Babai.exists_star_image`), so it induces a permutation `f` of the `t`-sets.  Two
`t`-sets lie in a common `(t+1)`-set exactly when they are adjacent in `J(Γ,t)`
(`Babai.Johnson.card_sdiff_eq_one_iff`), so `f` is an automorphism of `J(Γ,t)`, hence by
induction is induced by a permutation `π` of `Γ`.  Finally every `(t+1)`-set is the union
of its `t`-subsets, so the automorphism agrees with `π` on every vertex.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 3.2.9 (Johnson graph) (PDF p. 32) — Proposition 3.2.11 for all `t ≥ 1` (Def. 3.2.9 asks for `t ≥ 2`; the proof needs the case `t = 1`, where `J(Γ,1)` is the complete graph).
