decls.name: fixes_of_fixes_omegaOf
decls.docstring:
§12, proof of Cor. 12.0.10: **an element of `G_C` that fixes `Ω(C)` pointwise has a
`ϕ`-image that fixes `C` pointwise.**  (So the representation `G_C → S(C)` factors through
the image of `G_C` in `S(Ω(C))`.)

*Proof.*  Let `t = t_Ω` be the common size of the labels (`G` is transitive, so there is
one orbit, Theorem 10.5.1 (c)).

* If `t = 0` then every label is empty, so `Ω(C) = Ω`, and an element fixing `Ω` pointwise
 is the identity.
* If `t ≥ 1`, let `T ⊆ C` be any `t`-set.  By Theorem 10.5.1 (e) (`Babai.exists_Tpoint_eq`)
 there is a `u ∈ Ω` with `T(u) = T`; then `T(u) ⊆ C`, so `u ∈ Ω(C)` and `u^σ = u`, and
 Eq. (54) gives `T = T(u) = T(u^σ) = T^{σ^ϕ}`.  So `σ^ϕ` fixes every `t`-subset of `C`
 setwise.  Now fix `γ ∈ C`.  Since `4t < m < 2|C|` we have `t < |C|`, so there are a
 `t`-set `T ⊆ C` with `γ ∈ T` and a point `δ ∈ C ∖ T`; put `T' = (T ∖ {γ}) ∪ {δ}`, again
 a `t`-subset of `C`.  Both are fixed setwise by `σ^ϕ`, hence so is
 `T ∩ T' = T ∖ {γ}`, and therefore so is `{γ}`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 10.5.1 (Main Structure Theorem) (PDF p. 88) — §12, proof of Cor. 12.0.10: **an element of `G_C` that fixes `Ω(C)` pointwise has a `ϕ`-image that fixes `C` pointwise.**  (So the representation `G_C → S(C)` factors through the image of `G_C` in `S(Ω(C))`.)

decls.name: hasHint_designSel_eqv
decls.docstring:
§9.7, Case 3a1.  *"If color class selected is greater than `3n₂/4`, this color class is
equipartitioned; apply Procedure ImprimitiveCase."*  (The original, `babai-gi.tex`,
lines 3981-3992.)

When Procedure Reduce-Part2-by-Color selects a part that is a single class `S` of the
**refined** coloring of Prop. 7.1.3 and that class is larger than `3n₂/4`, the restricted
input carries the hint.  The structure is `Babai.eqvConfig`: the blocks of the colored
partition that lie inside `S` all have one common size `m`, which is what the refinement
buys; `m ≥ 2` is admissibility (Def. 7.1.1), and there are at least two of them because
`ρ(Π) ≤ (3/4)n₂ < |S|`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 7.1.1 (PDF p. 62) — §9.7, Case 3a1.  *"If color class selected is greater than `3n₂/4`, this color class is equipartitioned; apply Procedure ImprimitiveCase."*  (The original, `babai-gi.tex`, lines 3981-3992.)

decls.name: homogeneous_trichotomy
decls.docstring:
§9.4, step 9.  *"We need to consider the following cases: (i) `X₂` is imprimitive;
(ii) `X₂` is the clique configuration; (iii) `X₂` is uniprimitive."*  (Version 2.5, lines
4166-4171.)

The three cases are exhaustive for a homogeneous configuration: either it is imprimitive,
or it is primitive, and then it is the clique configuration (rank `≤ 2`) or uniprimitive
(rank `≥ 3`, Def. 3.2.1).

decls.name: hugeM_of_line2
decls.docstring:
§15, lines 2 and 4b: the test of line 2, `m > ℓ = (log₂ n)³`, gives the numeric
hypothesis `m ≥ max{16, 4 + 2 log₂ n}` of Cor. 12.0.10.

*Proof.*  Write `L = ⌊log₂ n⌋ ≥ 6`.  Then `m > L³ ≥ 6·6·L ≥ 216`, so `m ≥ 16`, and
`4 + 2 log₂ n < 2L + 6 ≤ L³ < m`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Corollary 12.0.10 (TopAction4) (PDF p. 99) — §15, lines 2 and 4b: the test of line 2, `m > ℓ = (log₂ n)³`, gives the numeric hypothesis `m ≥ max{16, 4 + 2 log₂ n}` of Cor. 12.0.10.

outcome category.

colored partitions from the outcome at `z` to the outcome at `z^σ`: `F(z^σ)^Γ` is

object is unique (`Babai.Cat.eq_of_transport`), so it **is** `σ^ϕ • X(z)`.

§10.3, proof of Lemma 10.3.1: "This is a system of imprimitivity on which `G` acts as a
primitive group."

Proof: a block of imprimitivity `𝒞 ⊆ ℬ` for `G^ℬ` has union `⋃₀ 𝒞` a block of
imprimitivity for `G` containing any `B₀ ∈ 𝒞`, so by the maximality of the blocks of `ℬ`
either `⋃₀ 𝒞 = B₀`, and then `𝒞 = {B₀}`, or `⋃₀ 𝒞 = Ω`, and then `𝒞 = ℬ`.  The group
`G^ℬ` has order at least `2` because `G` is transitive on the at least two blocks.

decls.name: isSplitOutcome_extendOutcome
decls.docstring:
§13.2, §14.1: **the extension of an outcome on `D` is an outcome on `Γ`**, at a
threshold that the Align core accepts.

`D` is the canonical subset Theorem 13.2.1 works on, with `|D| > 4m/5`.  In the
colored-partition case nothing is lost: `ρ` of the extension is at most
`max(α|D|, |Γ ∖ D|) ≤ max(αm, m/5) ≤ αm`, so `β = α` serves.  In the Johnson case the
vertex set of the scheme has at least `α|D| > (4α/5)m` points, so `β = 4α/5` serves.

Both values meet the three conditions `Babai.nonempty_alignCore_of_versions` asks of its
threshold, `1/2 < β`, `0 ≤ β` and `5β ≤ 4`, when `3/4 ≤ α ≤ 4/5`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 13.2.1 (AggregateCertificates) (PDF p. 108) — §13.2, §14.1: **the extension of an outcome on `D` is an outcome on `Γ`**, at a threshold that the Align core accepts.

decls.name: isSplitOutcome_extendOutcome_of
decls.docstring:
§13.2, §14.1: **the extension of an outcome on `D` is an outcome on `Γ`**, with the two
thresholds given separately.

The Align core asks of its threshold only `1/2 < β`, `0 ≤ β` and `5β ≤ 4`, and which value
of `β` the extension reaches depends on the summand the outcome lands in.  So the two values
are two parameters here:

* a Johnson scheme inside `D` has at least `α|D|` vertices, so `βJ` serves as soon as
 `βJ·m ≤ α|D|`;
* a colored `α`-partition of `D`, extended by `Γ ∖ D` as one block of its own color, has
 `ρ ≤ max(α|D|, m − |D|)`, so `βP` serves as soon as `α|D| ≤ βP·m` and `m − |D| ≤ βP·m`.

`Babai.isSplitOutcome_extendOutcome` is the case `βJ = 4α/5`, `βP = α` of a set `D` with
`4m < 5|D|`.  Outcome (2b) of Theorem 13.2.1 needs the general form: there `D` is `C ∖ S`
with `|C| > 4m/5` and `|S| = d − 1 ≤ 4`, which gives only `|D| > 4m/5 − 4`, and that is not
above `4m/5` (take `m = 100`, `|C| = 81`, `d = 5`: then `|D| = 77 < 80`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 13.2.1 (AggregateCertificates) (PDF p. 108) — §13.2, §14.1: **the extension of an outcome on `D` is an outcome on `Γ`**, with the two thresholds given separately.

decls.name: isTransitive_stabOn_omegaOf
decls.docstring:
§12, the step the proof of Cor. 12.0.10 leaves out: **`G_C` is transitive on `Ω(C)`**,
which is what Cor. 12.0.8 needs of the group acting on the window.

*The argument*.  Let `u, v ∈ Ω(C)`, i.e. `T(u) ⊆ C` and `T(v) ⊆ C`,
and write `T = T(u)`.

1. `G` is transitive on `Ω`, so there is a `τ ∈ G` with `u^τ = v`.  By Eq. (54)
  (`Babai.theorem_10_5_1_c_eq54`), `T(v) = T^{τ^ϕ}`.
2. The correction is made inside `G_u`.  Put `D = (τ^ϕ)^{-1}(C)`.  Then `|D| = |C|`, and
  `T ⊆ D` because `T^{τ^ϕ} = T(v) ⊆ C`; also `T ⊆ C`.  By Theorem 10.5.1 (a) we have
  `4|T| < m`, and `m ≥ 9`, so `|Γ ∖ T| ≥ 3`.  Hence there is an **even** permutation `α`
  of `Γ` fixing `T` pointwise with `α(C) = D`
  (`Babai.exists_alternating_fixing_image_eq`).
3. Theorem 10.5.1 (a), Eq. (52), gives `(A(Γ))_{(T(u))} ≤ G_u^ϕ`, so `α = ρ^ϕ` for some
  `ρ ∈ G_u`.
4. Then `σ = τρ` (Lean: `σ = τ * ρ`) has `σ(u) = τ(ρ(u)) = τ(u) = v` and
  `σ^ϕ(C) = τ^ϕ(α(C)) = τ^ϕ(D) = C`, so `σ ∈ G_C` and `σ` carries `u` to `v`.

The hypothesis `|C| > m/2` of Cor. 12.0.10 is not needed for this step; it is kept in the
statement because that is the situation in which the step is used.

The earlier version of this argument went through the standard blocks (transitivity of
`G_C` on the blocks `B_T` with `T ⊆ C`, then inside one block).  The route above avoids
both the block transitivity and Theorem 10.5.1 (e), (f); see the corrected paper.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Theorem 10.5.1 (Main Structure Theorem) (PDF p. 88) — §12, the step the proof of Cor. 12.0.10 leaves out: **`G_C` is transitive on `Ω(C)`**, which is what Cor. 12.0.8 needs of the group acting on the window.

decls.name: le_add_two_of_involved_GL
decls.docstring:
**`A_k` involved in `GL(s,p)`**, §10.2, inside the proof of Lemma 10.2.5 (Case 1, the
affine case).

Quoted from the paper:

> Moreover `A_k` is involved in `GL(s, p)`.  It is shown in [BaPS, Prop. 1.22] that if
> `A_k` is involved in `GL(s, p)` then, combining a result of Feit and Tits [FeT] with
> [KlL, Prop. 5.3.7], for `k ≥ 9` it follows that `k ≤ s + 2`.

**Citation.** `[BaPS, Prop. 1.22]` = László Babai, Péter P. Pálfy, Jan Saxl, *On the
number of `p`-regular elements in finite simple groups*, LMS J. Comput. Math. **12**
(2009), 82–119, Prop. 1.22 — itself a rendering of `[FeT]` = Walter Feit, Jacques Tits,
*Projective representations of minimum degree of group extensions*, Canad. J. Math. **30**
(1978), 1092–1102, combined with `[KlL, Prop. 5.3.7]` = Peter Kleidman, Martin Liebeck,
*The Subgroup Structure of the Finite Classical Groups*, LMS Lecture Note Ser. 129, CUP
1990, Prop. 5.3.7.  The acknowledgments of the paper confirm that `k ≤ s + 2` is the
paper's rendering of that result.

**Used where.** Lemma 10.2.5, Case 1, to reach the contradiction
`k ≤ s + 2 ≤ 2 + log_p n < k`.

**"Involved".** The paper never defines the word; `Babai.Involved A B` is the standard
usage, "`A` is a quotient of a subgroup of `B`" (`A` is a *section* of `B`), here stated
as "some subgroup of `B` admits an epimorphism onto `A`".

**Warning (consistency).** `p` is a prime and `GL(s,p)` is over the field with `p`
elements (`Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup (Fin s) (ZMod p)`); the hypothesis `p.Prime` is the
paper's context (`N ≅ ℤ_p^s`, `G/N ≤ GL(s,p)`), not an addition.  For `s = 0` the group
`GL(0,p)` is trivial, so no `A_k` with `k ≥ 9` is involved and the axiom is vacuous
there.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Lemma 10.2.5 (PDF p. 84) — **`A_k` involved in `GL(s,p)`**, §10.2, inside the proof of Lemma 10.2.5 (Case 1, the affine case).

decls.docstring:
**Lemma 10.1.1** (Simple quotient of subdirect product), §10.1.

> Let `G ≤ K₁ × ⋯ × K_m` be a subdirect product; let `Mᵢ` be the kernel of the `G → Kᵢ`

> simple group.  Then `(∃i)(Mᵢ ≤ ker ϕ)`.  In particular, one of the `Kᵢ` admits an
> epimorphism onto `S`.

decls.name: lemma_10_2_5
decls.docstring:
**Lemma 10.2.5**, §10.2 — the result of the section.

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be primitive.  Assume `ϕ : G → A_k` is an epimorphism where
> `k > max{8, 2 + log₂ n}`.  Then `ϕ` is an isomorphism; hence `G ≅ A_k`.

The paper's proof: let `N = Soc(G) = R₁ × ⋯ × R_s` (Fact 10.2.2).  Case 1, `N` abelian:
then `N ≅ ℤ_p^s` is regular, `n = p^s`, `G/N ≤ GL(s,p)` and `A_k` is involved in
`GL(s,p)`, so `k ≤ s + 2 ≤ 2 + log_p n < k`, a contradiction.  Case 2, `N` nonabelian:
`s ≤ log₅ n < k`, `Pker(G)/N ≤ Out(R₁) × ⋯ × Out(R_s)` is solvable by Schreier's
Hypothesis and `G/Pker(G) ≤ S_s` does not involve `A_k`, so `G/N` does not involve `A_k`
and `ker ϕ ≱ N`; a minimal normal subgroup `M ≠ N` would force `n ≥ |A_k| > 2^k > n`, so
`M = N` is the unique minimal normal subgroup and `ker ϕ = 1`.

The proof depends on the CFSG through Schreier's Hypothesis (`Babai.schreierHypothesis`,
`Workspace/Cited/AltQuotients.lean`).

decls.name: lemma_10_2_5_socle_not_abelian
decls.docstring:
§10.2, **Lemma 10.2.5, Case 1** in the paper's own form.

> Case 1.  `N` is abelian (the "affine case") and therefore regular … a contradiction, so
> this case cannot occur.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 10.2.5 the socle of `G` is **not** abelian, so Case 1 does
not occur.  The paper leaves one step implicit, which is supplied here: `ϕ(N)` is an
abelian normal subgroup of `A_k`, and `A_k` is simple and nonabelian for `k ≥ 5`, so
`ϕ(N) = 1`, i.e. `N ≤ ker ϕ`; this is what makes `A_k` a quotient of `G/N ≤ GL(s,p)`, which
is the paper's "`A_k` is involved in `GL(s,p)`".  See the entry on Lemma 10.2.5, Case 1 in
the corrected paper.

`Babai.lemma_10_2_5_affine` is the weaker form used in the proof of Lemma 10.2.5.

decls.name: lemma_10_3_1
decls.docstring:
**Lemma 10.3.1**, §10.3.

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a transitive permutation group and `ϕ : G → A_k` an epimorphism where
> `k > max{8, 2 + log₂ n}`.  Then `G_x^ϕ ≠ A_k` for any `x ∈ Ω`.

The paper's proof, an induction on `|G|`: let `B` be a maximal block of imprimitivity
containing `x`, let `Ω'` be the system of its `G`-images (on which `G` acts primitively,
`Babai.isPrimitive_onBlocks`) and `K` the kernel of the action on `Ω'`.  Since `ker ϕ` is
a maximal normal subgroup of `G`, either `K ≤ ker ϕ` or `K^ϕ = A_k`.

In the first case `ϕ` factors through the primitive group `G^{Ω'}`, so Lemma 10.2.5 makes
that factor injective, `ker ϕ = K`; as `G_x ≤ G_B` we get `G_B^ϕ = A_k` and hence
`G = K G_B = G_B`, so `Ω'` has one block, contradicting its definition.

In the second case `K` is a subdirect product of its restrictions to its orbits, so by
Lemma 10.1.1 `ϕ|_K` factors through the restriction `K^Δ` to one orbit `Δ = z^K`, and
`|K| < |G|` lets the induction hypothesis apply to `K^Δ`: `K_z^ϕ ≠ A_k`.  As `K ⊴ G` we
have `K_z ⊴ G_z`, so `K_z^ϕ ⊴ G_z^ϕ = A_k` and therefore `K_z^ϕ = 1`.  Then
`|A_k|` divides `|K : K_z| = |z^K| ≤ |B| < n < 2^{k-2} < |A_k|`, a contradiction.

decls.docstring:
**Lemma 10.3.1**, §10.3, as an induction on `|G|` over all domains at once.

The paper's proof is an induction on `|G|`, and the inductive step passes from `G ≤ S(Ω)`
to the restriction of a normal subgroup of `G` to one of *its* orbits, so the domain
shrinks as well; the statement is therefore quantified over the domain too.

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a permutation group and `ϕ : G → A_k` an epimorphism.  Assume

decls.name: lemma_7_2_1a
decls.docstring:
Lemma 7.2.1(a).  *"the size of each color class in `Φ` is `≤ (2/3)|Φ|` with the
possible exception of one of the `k` sets `(Δᵢ choose t)`."*

The exceptional color classes are those whose color vector has `vᵢ = t` for some `i`; such
a class is contained in `(Δᵢ choose t)` (`tupleClass_subset_powersetCard`).

Proof.  The paper proves this by induction on `k`, the case `k = 2` being Prop. 7.2.3.  We
reduce to the case `k = 2` directly, by grouping all classes other than `Δ_{i₀}` into one
(see the corrected paper why the paper's induction step is replaced): if `vᵢ ≠ t` for all
`i` and the class is non-empty, pick `i₀` with `v_{i₀} ≥ 1`; then
`∑_{i ≠ i₀} vᵢ = t - v_{i₀} ≥ 1`, and
`∏ᵢ C(mᵢ,vᵢ) ≤ C(m_{i₀}, v_{i₀}) · C(∑_{i≠i₀} mᵢ, ∑_{i≠i₀} vᵢ) ≤ (2/3) C(m,t)`
by `prod_choose_le` and Prop. 7.2.3.

decls.name: lemma_9_1_2
decls.docstring:
Lemma 9.1.2 (Intact Johnson subscheme), repaired.  *"Let `G ≤ Aut(J(m,t))`.  Assume
`m!/|G| < C(m, r+1)` for some `r < m/2 - 1`.  Then `G ≥ A⁽ᵗ⁾_{m-r}` where `A⁽ᵗ⁾_{m-r}` acts
on a `J(m-r,t)` subscheme of `J(m,t)` corresponding to a subset of size `m-r` of `[m]`."*
(Version 2.5, lines 3940–3951.)

Paper's proof: *"Let us view `G` as a subgroup of `S_m`, so `G⁽ᵗ⁾ ≤ S_m` is the subgroup of
`Aut(J(m,t))` in question.  Then, by the Jordan–Liebeck Theorem (Thm. 10.4.2) we have that
`G ≥ (A_m)_(T)` for some `T ⊂ [m]`, `|T| ≤ r`.  Let `Γ = [m] \ T`.  This means that
`G⁽ᵗ⁾ ≥ A⁽ᵗ⁾(Γ)` where `|Γ| ≥ m - r`."*

Since `Theorem 10.4.2` is false as the paper prints it, the
conclusion here is the true conclusion of `Babai.theorem_10_4_2` for `K = S_m` and
`r + 1` in place of `r`: either the paper's conclusion — a set `T` with `|T| ≤ r` whose
pointwise stabilizer in `A_m` lies in `G` (this is the paper's `G ≥ (A_m)_(T)`, and the
induced action on the `t`-subsets of `Γ = [m] \ T` is the Johnson group `A⁽ᵗ⁾_{m-r}` of the
`J(m-r,t)` subscheme) — or the exceptional alternative (ii) of the cited source.  The
alternative (iii) of Theorem 10.4.2 cannot occur here because it requires
`K = A(Ω)`, while `K = S_m`.  The hypothesis `m ≥ 9` is the one Theorem 10.4.2 carries.

`G` is a subgroup of `S_m = S(Γ)`; the paper's `G⁽ᵗ⁾` is the induced action on the
`t`-subsets, which is the same abstract group, so the statement is about `G ≤ S(Γ)`.

decls.name: lemma_9_3_1_transfer
decls.docstring:
Lemma 9.3.1(ii), the transfer clause: *"a solution to each part of Theorem 9.2.2 for
`X̄` is also a solution to the corresponding part of Theorem 9.2.1 for `X`"*.

In the paper's proof, `W = C₂` is the first part of `X̄`, `V` is the vertex set of the
UPCC, and `α = βn/d₂`, so that `α|W| = βn = β|V|`; a colored `α`-partition of `W` becomes
a colored `β`-partition of `V` by adding `V \ W` as one block of a new color (of size
`|V| - |W| ≤ (1-β)|V| ≤ β|V|`, which is where `β ≥ 1/2` is used), and an embedded Johnson
scheme on a subset of `W` of relative size `≥ α` has absolute size `≥ α|W| = β|V|` already.

The hypothesis is the paper's equality `α|W| = β|V|`, not an inequality: the two branches
need it in opposite directions (see the note on `IsUPCCToBipOutcome`).

Lemma 9.3.2.  *"In at least one of `X₁` and `X₂`, the symmetry defect of `V₁` is at
least `(n₁ - 1)/2`."*  (Version 2.5, lines 4085–4090.)

Here `X_j = X[V₁, C_j]` for a partition `V₂ = C₁ ∪ C₂`, and `X` has no twins in `V₁`,

Paper's proof: *"Assume for a contradiction that for `j = 1, 2` there exists a twin
equivalence class `D_j ⊆ V₁` of size `|D_j| ≥ 1 + (n₁/2)` in `X_j`.  It follows that

`C_j`; therefore all vertices in `D₁ ∩ D₂` are twins in `X`.  Since `X` has no twins, we
infer `|D₁ ∩ D₂| ≤ 1`, a contradiction."*

Lemma 9.6.1.  *"Under the assumptions stated in 'Case' above, we can either return a
canonical colored `1/2`-partition of `V₁` at a multiplicative cost of `< n₂`, or return, at
only additive polynomial cost (no multiplicative cost) a canonical bipartite graph
`Y = (V₁, W₂; F)` such that `|W₂| ≤ |V₂|/2` such that the symmetry defect of `V₁` in `Y` is
`≥ 1/2`."*  (Version 2.5, lines 4190-4193.)

The statement is in the wider category of §9.4-§9.8: a vertex of `V₂` is a block, so `n₂`
is the number of blocks, and the graph `Y` returned in the second branch is an object of
`Babai.VColBlkGraphs`.  This is what lets step 2(ii) return the contracted graph; see the
entry for Lemma 9.6.1 in the corrected paper.

**The cost bound is `≤ n₂`, not `< n₂` and not `0`.**  The lemma's wording does not match
its own Procedure ImprimitiveCase: step 1 *individualizes* a point of `V₂`, which costs
exactly `n₂`, and step 2(i) says *"This involves choosing `i` at a multiplicative cost of

the procedure cost `n₂` (step 1), `m ≤ n₂/2` (step 2(i)) and `1` (step 2(ii)), so `n₂`
bounds them all; `FindsAtMultCost` takes one cost function of the input object, and the
branch is not a function of the object alone (it depends on the color `j` and the block
system chosen inside the procedure), so the single bound `n₂` is what is stated.  See the
entry for Lemma 9.6.1 in the corrected paper.

The additive polynomial cost is a running-time claim and is pending.

decls.name: line4a_multiplicities_not_sufficient
decls.docstring:
§15, line 4a: the paper's parenthetical *"isomorphism only depends on the multiplicity
of each letter in the strings `x, y`"* is false for `G = A(Ω)`.

Take `Ω = Σ = {0,1,2}`, `x` the identity string and `y = x^{(0 1)}`.  Every letter occurs
once in each of `x` and `y`, so the multiplicities agree; but the only permutation carrying
`x` to `y` is the transposition `(0 1)`, which is not in `A(Ω)`, so `Iso_{A(Ω)}(x,y) = ∅`.
(For `G = S(Ω)` the comment is correct, and it is correct for `G = A(Ω)` as soon as some
letter occurs at least twice.)

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure String-Isomorphism (PDF p. 113) — §15, line 4a: the paper's parenthetical *"isomorphism only depends on the multiplicity of each letter in the strings `x, y`"* is false for `G = A(Ω)`.

decls.name: line4a_nonempty_of_letterMult
decls.docstring:
§15, line 4a, the other half of *"isomorphism only depends on the multiplicity of each
letter"*, **as the paper's comment would have it**: for `G ≥ A(Ω)`, equal multiplicities
give an isomorphism.

This is false as stated; `Babai.line4a_multiplicities_not_sufficient` below is a
counterexample.  It becomes true once some letter occurs at least twice, which is the form
stated here.  See the entry "Sec. 15, line 4a" in the corrected paper.

*Proof.*  Equal multiplicities make the fibers of `x` and of `y` equinumerous, so a family
of bijections between them glues to a permutation `e` of `Ω` with `y(e u) = x u` for every
`u` (`Equiv.ofFiberEquiv`), that is `x^e = y`.  If `e` is even we are done.  If it is odd,
let `u ≠ v` be two positions where `x` has the same letter — they exist because `x` is not
injective — and replace `e` by `e·(u v)`: the transposition fixes `x`, so the product is
still an isomorphism, and its sign is the opposite one.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure String-Isomorphism (PDF p. 113) — §15, line 4a, the other half of *"isomorphism only depends on the multiplicity of each letter"*, **as the paper's comment would have it**: for `G ≥ A(Ω)`, equal multiplicities give an isomorphism.

decls.name: mapsOntoGiant_phiCFin
decls.docstring:
§12, proof of Cor. 12.0.10: the hypothesis *"the restriction of `Aut_G(x)^ϕ` to `C` is
a giant"* is exactly what Cor. 12.0.8 needs on the window, namely that `ϕ_C` maps
`Aut(x|_{Ω(C)})` onto a giant.

Given an even `δ ∈ A([|C|])`, transport it to `β ∈ A(C)` and extend it by the identity to
an even permutation `α` of `Γ` fixing `Γ ∖ C` pointwise.  The hypothesis produces a
`τ ∈ Aut_G(x)` with `τ^ϕ|_C = α|_C`; then `τ^ϕ` preserves `C`, so `τ ∈ G_C`, its
restriction to `Ω(C)` is an automorphism of `x|_{Ω(C)}`, and its `ϕ_C`-image is `β`,
i.e. its `phiCFin`-image is `δ`.

decls.name: masterStepOfFamily
decls.docstring:
§15, **one round of the Master Algorithm along a family of choices**.

`κ'` is the index type of the nodes the machine really has — a raw node, say.  `chOf r` is
what the machine picked at the node `r`, `p r` the typed hinted instance the node decodes
to, `lift' r J` the node the machine builds for the call `J`, and `top' I` the node it starts
from.

The two hypotheses say that decoding commutes with building children and with starting: the
node the machine attaches to a call decodes to the hinted instance the round of `chOf r`
attaches to that call, and the node the machine starts from decodes to the hinted instance
the round starts from.  The first is asked only for the calls the round really makes, which
is all `Babai.MasterStep.lift_inst` asks as well.

Every field is then inherited pointwise from `Babai.sec15MasterStep Ω A (chOf r)` at `p r`.
That is possible because `inst`, `param`, `roundCost` and `top` of that round do not mention
the choice (`Babai.sec15MasterStep_inst` and the three lemmas beside it), so the four of them
are the same function of `p r` at every node, whatever the node picked.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure String-Isomorphism (PDF p. 113) — §15, **one round of the Master Algorithm along a family of choices**.

decls.name: ncard_le_alphaNew_mul_dominantClass
decls.docstring:
§9.4, step 5.  **The symmetry defect of the restricted instance.**  *"the symmetry
defect of `X` on `V₁` is at least `1 - α`"* is inherited by `X[W₁ ∪ V₂]` with the new
threshold: a set of twins inside `V₁` has at most `α n₁ = α_new |W₁|` points.

Two points of `W₁` that are twins in the restriction `X[W₁, V₂]` are twins in `X` — being
twins means having the same vertex color and the same set of neighboring blocks
(`Babai.VColBipBlk.isTwin_iff`), and the restriction changes neither — so a set of twins
of the restriction inside `W₁` is a set of twins of `X` inside `V₁`, and this bound applies
to it.  Since `1 - α_new = 1 - (α_new |W₁|)/|W₁|`, the defect of `W₁` in the restriction is
at least `1 - α_new`, which is the hypothesis of Theorem 9.2.2 for the restricted
instance.

The hypothesis is the twin condition of `Babai.VColBipBlk.isTwin_iff` written out — same
vertex color, same set of neighboring blocks — rather than `Babai.IsTwinSet`, because that

decls.name: nonempty_alignData_of_versions
decls.docstring:
§15, **lines 4d, 7 and 7a on the window**: Procedure Align (Sec. 14.1) applied to a
canonical family of versions of the structure, with everything the fields of
`Babai.Sec15Remaining` ask for.

This is the part of lines 4c–4d that comes **after** the canonical structure has been
found, so it is shared by line 4d (the structure comes from Theorem 9.2.3 at line 4c),
line 6a–7a (from Theorem 9.2.3 applied at line 6a to the structure Theorem 13.2.1
aggregated) and line 7–7a (the colored equipartition Theorem 13.2.1 returns).  What it
needs of the ambient data is Sec. 14's *"Situation"*: a transitive `G ≤ S(Ω)` with a giant
representation `ϕ : G → S(Γ)`, and the standard blocks `Φ = {B_T : T ∈ Γ^{(t)}}` of
Theorem 10.5.1, all labels of size `t`.

The threshold `α` is the one of the structure: `3/4` for Theorem 9.2.3 (line 4c, line 6a)
and `4/5` for Theorem 13.2.1 (line 7).  The three numeric conditions on it are the ones
Sec. 14.2 uses: `1/2 < α` (line 6's *"dominant color"* is a real dichotomy), `0 ≤ α` and
`5α ≤ 4` — Eq. (72) at the threshold of `Babai.MakesProgress`, through
`Babai.five_mul_card_tupleClass_le_of_le`.

**`1 ≤ t` is enough.**  Lemma 7.2.1 (b) gives `|Ω(Δ)|/n ≤ (|Δ|/m)^t ≤ α^t ≤ α` for every
`t ≥ 1`, so a color class that carries no structure gives a window of at most `αn ≤ 4n/5`
points, which is the window alternative of `Babai.MakesProgress`.  This is what lines 5–7
need, where `t = 1` is not excluded; see the corrected paper entry on Sec. 15 lines 5–7a
and Sec. 14.2 Eqs. (72)–(73).

**The reduction is a function of the data** (`Babai.AlignShape.red`).  The two cases of
line 6 differ only in the field `dom`: when there is no dominant color class the call of
the Chain Rule on the first window stands, and when there is one it is expanded by the
round of lines 7–11.  See the corrected paper entry on Finding 1 of the audit of
Secs. 14–15.

§15, **lines 4c and 4d on the window**: the branch, with everything the fields of
`Babai.Sec15Remaining` ask for.

The hypotheses are the data lines 1–4 leave: the group `G` induced on the window is
transitive with a giant representation `ϕ : G → S(Γ)`, the window is the set of standard
blocks labelled by the `t`-subsets of `Γ` (`Babai.PrimitiveCaseId`), the Johnson parameter
is at least `217` — the test of line 2 has failed (`Babai.le_param_of_line4c`) — and the
relative symmetry defect of `H(x)` is at least `1/2` (`Babai.LargeDefectData` at
`α = 3/4`).

Line 4c is Theorem 9.2.3 (`Babai.exists_canonicalVersions_of_uniform`); line 4d is
Procedure Align, which is `Babai.nonempty_alignData_of_versions` with `α = 3/4`.

**The reject exit of lines 4c–4d.**  When the family `Vers y` is empty, Eq. (71) is a union
over nothing and `Babai.AlignShape.red` answers `∅` with no call.  That is right, and it is
not a way of writing the answer down: Theorem 9.2.3 makes `Vers z` empty *exactly* when
`Babai.LargeDefectData` fails at `z` — `Babai.exists_canonicalVersions_of_uniform` gives
both directions, `hne` for nonemptiness under the test and `hoff` for emptiness outside it —
and that test reads `z` alone.  The test holds at `x` here, by the failure of line 4b, so a
failure at `y` says that `x` and `y` have different relative symmetry defects; the defect is
canonical, so `Iso_G(x,y) = ∅`.  This is the same shape as the two reject exits of
lines 5–7 (`Babai.Line57Data.rejectDefect`, `Babai.Line57Data.rejectCase`).

decls.name: not_Align_G1_image_as_printed
decls.docstring:
The printed second clause of Eq. (70) is false.

Counterexample: `Ω = Γ = [5]`, `G = A(Γ)` acting on itself, `ϕ` the inclusion (a giant
representation, `G^ϕ = A(Γ)`), and `X(z)` the constant structure (all of `Γ` one color, no
additional structure), which is canonical.  Then `Aut(X(x)) = S(Γ)`, so
`G₁ = ϕ⁻¹(S(Γ)) = G` and `G₁^ϕ = A(Γ)`, which does not contain the transposition
`(0 1) ∈ S(Γ) = Aut(X(x))`.

What is true is `G₁^ϕ = Aut(X(x)) ∩ G^ϕ` (`Babai.Align_G1_image`), which in the
counterexample reads `A(Γ) = S(Γ) ∩ A(Γ)`.

links.rationale: The printed second clause of Eq. (70) is false.

decls.name: not_Remark_12_0_7_as_printed
decls.docstring:
Remark 12.0.7 is false as printed.

Counterexample: `Ω = Γ = [20]`, `G = S(Ω) = ⊤`, `ϕ` the identity representation, `m = 20`.
Then `G` is transitive, `ϕ` is a giant representation and `m ≥ max{9, 2 log₂ 20}`, while
`N = ker(ϕ) = 1`, so every `N`-orbit is a singleton and `n/k = 1`.  But `1 ≤ t < m/4 = 5`
forces `t ≤ 4`, and `(20 choose t) ≥ 20 > 1` for every such `t`.

What item (e) of Theorem 10.5.1 does give is that `N` fixes every standard block setwise,
so each `N`-orbit lies in one standard block; `G` is transitive on the `(m choose t)`
standard blocks and normalizes `N`, so every block contains the same number of `N`-orbits,
whence `(m choose t)` *divides* `k` — which is `Babai.Remark_12_0_7_statement`.  In the
counterexample the standard blocks are the singletons, `t = 1`, and `(20 choose 1) = 20 = k`.
See the corrected paper.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 12.0.7 (PDF p. 98) — Remark 12.0.7 is false as printed.

decls.docstring:
§13.2, case (3).

> Our current assumption is that the objects in `𝓛` are not full in our sense, i. e.,
> `Aut(T,i) ≤ M_i(T)` where `M_i(T) ≱ A(T)`.  In particular it follows that the objects in
> `𝓛` are not full in the sense of Prop. ??, i. e., `Aut(T,i) ≠ S(T)`.

`Aut(T,i) ≤ M_i(T)` is `Babai.compareIso_mem_outStage_H`: a `G`-automorphism of the
truncated, colored string `(x_i)_T^{W_i(T)}` stabilizes `T` and respects `x_i` on the
window, so it lies in `H(W(T))`, whose image in `S(T)` is `M(T)`.  `M_i(T) ≱ A(T)` is the
certificate of non-fullness of Theorem 13.1.3, i.e. Claim 13.1.7, applied to the test set
`T ⊆ D_i`, which is not full because it meets `D_i`
(`Babai.disjoint_fixedGamma_of_isFull`).  So if `Aut(T,i)` were all of `S(T)` we would get
`A(T) ≤ S(T) = Aut(T,i) ≤ M_i(T)`, a contradiction.

> Let `T, U ⊂ Ω`, `|T|, |U| < n/2`, where `n = |Ω| ≥ 5`.  Assume `A(Ω)_(T) ≤ S(Ω)_U`.

decls.name: param
decls.docstring:
§15, line 2: **the Johnson parameter `m`** of the hinted instance.

Outside the Johnson case there is no Johnson parameter, and the instance is given the value
`2n`.  This is not an arbitrary convention: `param` is the second component of the measure
of `Workspace/Master/Procedure.lean`, and `2n` is the top of its range, so an instance that
Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson has not processed yet ranks above every Johnson case on the same
window.  That is what makes line 1 of Sec. 15 *progress*: the Johnson case reached at the
end of Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (Sec. 11.3, step 6) has the same window, and its Johnson
parameter `m ≤ n` satisfies `2m ≤ 2n`, so the second component of the measure drops.  It is
also what recurrence (ii) of Sec. 11.4 says, `T_trans(x) ≤ m(T_Jh(x) + p(x))`: the cost of
a transitive instance is that of a Johnson case on the same window, times `m`.

decls.name: prop_9_1_1
decls.docstring:
Proposition 9.1.1.  *"Let `0 < ε ≤ 1/3`.  The multiplicative cost of a (relative)
canonical `(1-ε)`-partition of the Johnson scheme `J(m,t)` is `≥ (t/ε)^{εm/t}`."*
(Version 2.5, lines 3934–3936.)  *"Proof.  This is an immediate consequence of
Corollary 9.1.3 below."*

For any cost function and any canonical partition reduction with that cost bound,
the conclusion bounds `cost X` at each input `X` of parameters `(m,t)`. The bijection
`φ` and its coloring equation identify that input with `J(m,t)`. By Prop. 6.0.4,
`Aut(X,X')` has index at most `cost X` in `Aut(X)`. The strict form of Cor. 9.1.3
then forces a block larger than `(1-ε)|X|` whenever `cost X` is below the bound.

The passage from Cor. 9.1.3 to this statement is `Babai.prop_9_1_1_of_cor`
(`Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/ResilienceTransport.lean`), and the corollary is applied in its
strict form (`Babai.cor_9_1_3_strict`; the corrected paper).  The paper's proof of
Cor. 9.1.3 needs `m ≥ 9`, so the range `m ≤ 8` is done
separately, in `Babai.prop_9_1_1_small` (the small-degree repair, entry 92). These
repairs give the non-strict cost lower bound printed in the paper.

decls.name: prop_9_1_1_of_cor
decls.docstring:
Proposition 9.1.1 (version 2.5, lines 3934–3937) with the conclusion of Corollary 9.1.3
as a hypothesis: *"This is an immediate consequence of Corollary 9.1.3."*

Spelled out, the paper's one-line proof runs as follows.  Let `F` be a reduction of cost
`cost` and `G` a canonical `(1-ε)`-partition functor on `C^F`; take the given `X = J(m,t)` and any
`X' ∈ F(X)`. By Prop. 6.0.4 the group `Aut(X,X')` has index at most `|F(X)| ≤ cost X` in
`Aut(X) = S⁽ᵗ⁾_m` (`Babai.relIndex_aut_pairCat_le`), so Corollary 9.1.3 applies to it and
gives a subset `Δ` of `[m]` with `A⁽ᵗ⁾(Δ) ≤ Aut(X,X')` acting primitively on the
`C(|Δ|,t) > (1-ε)·C(m,t)` vertices lying in `Δ`.  The blocks of `G(X,X')` are
`Aut(X,X')`-invariant (a canonical embedding restricts automorphisms,
`Babai.Func.IsCanonicalEmbedding.autHom_apply`), hence `A⁽ᵗ⁾(Δ)`-invariant, so by
primitivity a block contains all those vertices
(`Babai.exists_ncard_block_ge_of_primitive_on`) and
`ρ(G(X,X')) ≥ C(|Δ|,t) > (1-ε)·n`, against `ρ ≤ (1-ε)·n`.
The strict corollary needed here is the repair recorded under Corollary 9.1.3 strictness
in the corrected paper; its small-degree companion gives the same strict bound. Thus the
cost lower bound remains non-strict.

decls.name: proposition_13_1_11
decls.docstring:
**Proposition 13.1.11** (Comparing local certificates), §13.1.

> For all test sets `T, T' ⊆ Γ` with `|T| = |T'| = t` and all strings `x, x' : Ω → Σ` we
> can compute `Iso_G(x_T^{W(T)}, (x')_{T'}^{W'(T')})` by making `≤ t!n²` calls to String
> Isomorphism problems on domains of size `≤ n/t` and performing `t! poly(n)` computation.

> Run procedure LocalCertificates simultaneously on `(x, T)` and on `(x', T')`,
> maintaining the variable `W` for `(x, T)` and the variable `W'` for `(x', T')`.  Further
> maintain the set `Q = Iso_G(x_T^W, (x')_{T'}^{W'})`.  On line 01 we shall have
> `Q = G_T σ` for any `σ ∈ G` that takes `T` to `T'`.  Change line 04 to "recompute `H(W)`
> and `Q`."

The mathematical content of the claim is that the procedure's output is the required set
of isomorphisms, i.e. that restricting `Q` to the initial coset `G_Tσ₀` of line 01 loses
no isomorphism of the final truncated strings. The separate-run bounds below do not
count the comparison calls. The paired reduction and its `2 * t! * n²` call bound are
proved in `ComparePaired.lean`. The exact printed constant and the `t! poly(n)` RAM
running time remain open.

The paper's proof sketch states an invariant that is false as printed, and the repaired
invariant is:

> `Q = {σ ∈ Iso_G(x^W, (x')^{W'}) | T^{σ̄} = T'}`

— the *plain* truncated strings together with the condition that `σ` carries the test set
`T` to `T'`.  At line 01 this is `{σ ∈ G | T^{σ̄} = T'} = G_Tσ`, which is what line 01 sets
(the printed invariant, without the condition on `T`, gives all of `G` there, since both
truncated strings are constantly `∗`).  The parallelism of the two runs (`W^σ = W'` for
`σ ∈ Q`), which line 04c0 needs in order to use `Q_old` as a coset of `H(W_old)`, is part
of the induction rather than an assumption: it holds at line 01, and conjugation by
`σ ∈ Q_old` carries `H(W_old) = Aut^{W_old}_{G_T}(x)` to `Aut^{W'_old}_{G_{T'}}(x')`
(using `T^{σ̄} = T'`), hence carries `Aff(H(W_old), ψ_T)` to `Aff(H'(W'_old), ψ_{T'})`.

The statement below is the step *from* that invariant to the set the proposition asks for,
which the sketch omits: the coloring of Notation 13.1.10 encodes the condition
`T^{σ̄} = T'` into the string, so that restricting to the initial coset `G_Tσ₀` loses no
isomorphism of the final colored truncated strings.  Its two ingredients are `Ω(T) ⊆ W(T)`
(Proposition 13.1.8 (i), `Babai.face_subset_windowOut`) and the injectivity of `A ↦ Ω(A)`
on `t`-subsets (`Babai.face_injective`), which comes from the labeling of the standard
blocks by *all* of `(Γ choose t_Δ)` (Theorem 10.5.1 (e)).

decls.name: proposition_13_1_8
decls.docstring:
**Proposition 13.1.8**, §13.1.

> As in Theorem 13.1.3, let a test set be a subset `T ⊆ Γ` with `|T| = t` elements where
> `max{8, 2 + log₂ n} < t ≤ m/10`.  For all test sets `T` we have
> (i) `Ω(T) ⊆ W(T) ⊆ Ω`
> (ii) `W(T)` is invariant under `Aut_{G_T}(x)`
> (iii) if `T` is full then `W(T) = Aff(Aut^{W(T)}_{G_T}(x))`
> (iv) if `T` is full then `K(T)` fixes all elements of `Ω ∖ W(T)`
> (v) the assignment `T ↦ W(T)` is canonical.

Item (v) is `Babai.canonical_windowOut` (in `Workspace/LocalCertificates/Canonicity.lean`).

Item (iv) is printed as "`K(T)^T` fixes all elements of `Ω ∖ W(T)`" in both versions of the
paper; `K(T)^T ≤ S(T)` is a group of permutations of `T ⊆ Γ`, which cannot fix or move
elements of `Ω`, so the superscript is a typo for `K(T)`.  In
`Aff(Aut^{W(T)}_{G_T}(x))` of item (iii) the second argument of `Aff` is left implicit by
the paper; it is `ψ_T`, as everywhere else in the procedure.

decls.name: proposition_localGuide
decls.docstring:
**Proposition (Local guide)**, §13.2 (`Prop. ??` of version 2.5; the statement is the
original's Proposition [Local guide], `babai-gi.tex:3236`, with version 2.5's symmetry
defect in place of the original's strong symmetry defect — see the module docstring).

> Let `C` be a category with two objects, `X₁` and `X₂`, with underlying sets
> `□(X_i) = Ω_i` where `|Ω₁| = |Ω₂| = n`.  Let `3 ≤ k ≤ n/4`.  Let the category `L` be a
> `k`-local guide to the category `C`.  Assume further that none of the sets
> `L ∈ (Ω₁ choose k)` is full for `i = 1`.  Then, in time `n^{O(k)}` we can either refute
> isomorphism of `X₁` and `X₂` [or] find a pair of canonical `k`-ary relational structures
> `X'₁` and `X'₂` with `□(X'_i) = □(X_i)` such that the [strong] symmetry defect of each
> `X'_i` is `≥ n − k + 1`.

The three conclusions are: the structures `𝔷_i` are `k`-ary (`isKAry_guideStruct`); they
are canonical, i.e. every morphism `X_i → X_j` of `C` is an isomorphism `𝔷_i → 𝔷_j`; and
either isomorphism of `X_i` and `X_j` is refuted (`morC i j = ∅`) or both structures have
symmetry defect `≥ n − k + 1`.  The running time `n^{O(k)}` is
covered inside the RAM proof of Theorem 1.1.1 (`Algo.theorem_1_1_1`) and not stated as a
separate RAM theorem.  The original's `3 ≤ k ≤ n/4` and its threshold `α` are not
needed for these conclusions; only `1 ≤ k` and, to state the bound in `ℕ`, `k ≤ n`.

Procedure Reduce-Part2-by-Color.  (Version 2.5, lines 4076–4084.)

> *Input:*  A colored bipartite graph `X = (V₁, V₂; E, f)` where `|V₂| < α|V₁|` such that

> color classes.
> *Output:* `j ∈ {1,2}` such that in the induced colored bipartite subgraph
> `X_j = X[V₁, C_j]` the symmetry defect of `V₁` is `≥ (n₁ - 1)/2` where `n₁ = |V₁|`.
> *"The procedure computes the symmetry defect of `V₁` in each `X_j`."*

The procedure is a function: it returns the part `C_j` selected (this is how the callers in
§9.7 and §9.8 use it — "if `V₂ \ C` is selected …").  It is total: the two hypotheses of
the input specification enter only in `reducePart2ByColor_spec`, which is Lemma 9.3.2.

it is what makes the selected part canonical.

decls.name: reduceToJohnson_step1
decls.docstring:
§11.3, Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, **step 1**.

> **if** `G ≤ Aut(x)` **then if** `x = y` **then return** `Iso_G(x,y) = G`, **exit**
> **else return** `Iso_G(x,y) = ∅`, **exit**

If every element of `G` fixes the string `x`, then `Iso_G(x,y)` is all of `G` when
`x = y` and empty otherwise.

links.rationale: Formalizes Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (PDF p. 94) — §11.3, Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, **step 1**.

decls.name: reduceToJohnson_step3
decls.docstring:
§11.3, Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, **step 3**.

> **if** `G` intransitive **then** apply Chain Rule

The orbits of `G` are `G`-invariant and cover `Ω`, so the Chain Rule
(`Babai.wIso_window_sUnion`, the identity behind Prop. 11.1.7) expresses `Iso_G(x,y)` as
the intersection of the window-isomorphism sets on the orbits.  The number of subproblems
is the number of orbits.

links.rationale: Formalizes Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson (PDF p. 94) — §11.3, Procedure Reduce-to-Johnson, **step 3**.

decls.name: remark_10_1_2_derivation
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.1.2**, §10.1, the derivation:

> Lemma 10.1.1 follows from this result [Lemma 10.1.3].  Indeed, observe that if
> `MᵢN = G` for all `i` then `R ≤ Mᵢ` for all `i` and therefore `R ≤ ⋂ᵢ Mᵢ = 1`,
> contradicting the equation `RN = G`.

Stated as an implication from the statement of Lemma 10.1.3 (which is cited, unused and has
no axiom) to Lemma 10.1.1, for a finite group `G`, as Lemma 10.1.3 requires.  `G/N` is
perfect because it is isomorphic to the nonabelian simple group `S`
(`Babai.commutator_quotient_ker_eq_top`).

The step "`R ≤ Mᵢ`", which the remark leaves to the reader, uses the uniqueness in
Lemma 10.1.3: since `Mᵢ` is normal, hence subnormal, and `MᵢN = G`, a subnormal subgroup
`R'` of least order among those with `R' ≤ Mᵢ` and `R'N = G` exists; it is minimal among
*all* subnormal subgroups with `R'N = G` (any smaller one also lies in `Mᵢ`), so `R' = R`
by uniqueness, and `R = R' ≤ Mᵢ`.

> Theorem 10.5.1) so the length of each orbit of `ker(ϕ)` contained in `∆` is
> `≤ |∆| / (k choose t_Δ)`.

*Proof*, the paper's: the `ker ϕ`-orbit of `y` lies in the standard block `B` of `y`,
since `ker ϕ` fixes `B` setwise (`Babai.ker_le_setwiseStab_standardBlock`).  The
`C(k,t_Δ)` standard blocks (item (e)) are the images of `B` under `G`, pairwise disjoint and

decls.name: sandwichSet
decls.docstring:
**Notation 10.4.3**, §10.4.

> Under the assumptions of Theorem 10.4.2 we write `T(H)` for the unique subset
> `T ⊂ Ω` guaranteed by the Theorem.  So we have
> `A(Ω)_(T(H)) ≤ H ≤ S(Ω)_{T(H)}`.  (51)

Outside the assumptions of Theorem 10.4.2 the notation is undefined; we make the
definition total by returning `∅`, and `Babai.sandwichSet_spec` (Sec. 10.4) records that
under those assumptions it is the set of Eq. (51).

links.rationale: Formalizes Notation 10.4.3 (PDF p. 87) — **Notation 10.4.3**, §10.4.

decls.name: sandwichSet_eq_empty_iff
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.4.4**, §10.4: "`T(H) = ∅` if and only if `A(Ω) ≤ H ≤ S(Ω)`."

(Under the assumptions of Theorem 10.4.2 and the sufficient condition `4r ≤ n` of
`Babai.sandwichSet_spec`; `H ≤ S(Ω)` is automatic.  The general form is
`Babai.sandwichSet_eq_empty_iff_of_exists`.)

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 10.4.4 (PDF p. 87) — **Remark 10.4.4**, §10.4: "`T(H) = ∅` if and only if `A(Ω) ≤ H ≤ S(Ω)`."

decls.name: sandwichSet_eq_empty_iff_of_exists
decls.docstring:
**Remark 10.4.4**, §10.4, in its general form: "`T(H) = ∅` if and only if
`A(Ω) ≤ H ≤ S(Ω)`", whenever `H` has a sandwich set at all and `n ≥ 5` (this is where
the uniqueness of Observation 10.4.1 holds).  `H ≤ S(Ω)` is automatic.  Under the

decls.name: schreierHypothesis
decls.docstring:
**Schreier's Hypothesis**, §1.2.2 and §10.2 (before Lemma 10.2.5).

Quoted from the paper:

> Another ingredient where we rely on CFSG occurs in the proof of Lemma 10.2.5 that
> depends on "Schreier's Hypothesis" (that the outer automorphisms group of a finite
> simple group is solvable), a consequence of CFSG.  (§1.2.2)

and at the point of use:

> The proof depends on the CFSG through "Schreier's Hypothesis" (a known consequence of
> the CFSG) which states that the outer automorphism group of every finite simple group is
> solvable.  (§10.2)

**Citation.** None given: the paper states it as a known consequence of the Classification
of Finite Simple Groups.  It is one of the two places (§16.1) where the paper relies on
the CFSG.

**Used where.** Lemma 10.2.5, Case 2: "`Pker(G)/N ≤ Out(R₁) × ⋯ × Out(R_s)` is solvable by
Schreier's Hypothesis" — and hence in everything that rests on Lemma 10.2.5: Lemmas
10.3.1, 10.3.3, Theorem 10.3.5, Theorem 10.5.1, Procedure LocalCertificates (§13.1).

Unlike Theorem 2.2.5 (b), which carries the hypothesis explicitly because the paper does,
Lemma 10.2.5 uses Schreier's Hypothesis unconditionally, so it is asserted here.
`Babai.SchreierHypothesis` (`Workspace/Prelim/SchreierHypothesis.lean`) is
`∀ (S : Type u) [Group S] [Finite S] [IsSimpleGroup S], IsSolvable (Out S)` with
`Out S = MulAut S ⧸ Inn S`.

**Warning (consistency).** The statement is usually quoted for *nonabelian* finite simple
groups; for the abelian ones, `Out(ℤ_p) = ℤ_{p-1}` is abelian, hence solvable, so the
statement as printed is true for all finite simple groups and needs no repair.  The axiom
is universe-polymorphic, which is no strengthening: `Babai.schreierHypothesis_iff` proves
that the statement at one universe implies it at every other.

links.rationale: Formalizes Remark 16.1.2 (PDF p. 116) — **Schreier's Hypothesis**, §1.2.2 and §10.2 (before Lemma 10.2.5).
Auxiliary declaration supporting the formalization with no standalone statement in the paper.

decls.name: small_index_subgroup_perm
decls.docstring:
**Subgroups of small index of `S_m` for `5 ≤ m ≤ 8`**, §9.1.

Under the hypotheses of Corollary 9.1.3 and `m ≤ 8`: either `|S_m : G| < m`, and then `G`
contains `A_m`; or `m ≤ |S_m : G|`, and then `G` fixes a point and contains its
pointwise stabilizer in `A_m`.  This is what replaces Lemma 9.1.2 in the range `m ≤ 8`, which the Jordan–
Liebeck theorem does not cover.

The proof is the cited theorem `[DiM, Thm. 5.2B]` (Dixon–Mortimer, *Permutation Groups*,
GTM 163, 1996, pp. 150–151; `Babai.dixonMortimer_5_2B`) at `r = 2`, which the project
already has for Theorem 10.4.2.  Write `n = |S_m : G|`.

*The index is small.*  Since `2 ≤ t` and `2t + 1 ≤ m ≤ 8` we have `5 ≤ m`.  The exponent
`εm/t` is at most `m/6`, and `(m/a)^a` grows with `a` up to `a = m/e`, so the bound of the
corollary is at most `6^{m/6}` (`Babai.cost_le_six_rpow`).  Hence `n < 5` for `m = 5`,
`n < 6` for `m = 6`, `n < 21` for `m = 7` and `n < 28` for `m = 8`
(`Babai.six_rpow_le_of_pow_le`).  In every case `n < C(m,2)`, the hypothesis of
`[DiM, Thm. 5.2B]` at `r = 2`.

*Case (i) of that theorem*: there is a set `Δ` with `|Δ| < 2` and
`A_{(Δ)} ≤ G ≤ S_{\{Δ\}}`.  If `Δ = ∅` then `A_m ≤ G`, so `n` divides `|S_m : A_m| = 2`,
and `n ≤ 2 < m`: the first alternative.  If `Δ = {a}` then `G` lies in the stabilizer of
the point `a`, whose index is `C(m,1) = m` by orbit–stabilizer
(`Babai.relIndex_setwiseStabilizer`), so `m` divides `n` and `m ≤ n`: the second
alternative, with `A_{(\{a\})} ≤ G`.

*Case (ii)*: `2n = C(m, m/2)`, that is `n = 5`, `10`, `35/2`, `35` for `m = 5, 6, 7, 8`.
Each contradicts the bound on `n` (for `m = 7` already because `35` is odd).

*Case (iii)*: the exceptional cases.  Those with `m = 6` blocks of size 2, `m = 7` and
`m = 8` require `3 ≤ r`, and `r = 2`.  The rest force `(m, n) = (5,6)`, `(6,6)` or
`(6,12)`, and again the bound on `n` excludes them.

decls.name: smul_versOf_subset_at
decls.docstring:
**One half of canonicity**: a `G`-shift of the string carries every version of `z` to a
version of `z^σ`.

*Proof.*  Let `f` be the morphism `Str z → Str (z^σ)` given by `ϕ σ`.  `F(f)` is a morphism
of tuples, so it is an isomorphism of *some* member of `F(Str z)` with *some* member of
`F(Str (z^σ))`; condition (ii) of Definition 6.0.1 (`Babai.TupleClass.cond_ii`) then makes
it an isomorphism of the given `X'` with some `Y' ∈ F(Str (z^σ))`.  The pair `(f, F(f))` is
therefore a morphism of `C^F`, and `G` of it is a morphism `G(Str z, X') → G(Str (z^σ), Y')`
which, `G` being a canonical embedding, is the restriction of `ϕ σ`.  So the second outcome
is the first moved by `ϕ σ`.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Definition 6.0.1 (Category of tuples) (PDF p. 59) — **One half of canonicity**: a `G`-shift of the string carries every version of `z` to a version of `z^σ`.

decls.docstring:
**Definition 10.2.1**, §10.2 (repeated in §11.2).

> The *socle* `Soc(G)` of a group `G` is the product of its minimal normal subgroups.

supremum; for a group with no minimal normal subgroup (only possible for infinite groups)
this is the empty product `⊥`.

§9.6, step 2.  **One of the two branches keeps the symmetry defect.**  This is
`Babai.case_9_6_1_step2` read for the candidates of step 2.

*The proof* is that lemma after a translation, in three pieces:

* the identification of `Babai.case_9_6_1_step2`'s data with the data here: `A` is `V₁`,
 `B` is `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.blocks` (a vertex of `V₂` is a block), `ι` is the set of
 groups and `blocks : B → ι` is `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.grpOf`; the graphs then match by
 `Babai.VColBipBlk.defect₁_toBip` (the object and its bipartite graph have the same
 symmetry defect on `V₁`, because `f` and `g` are constant) together with
 `Babai.BipGraph.defect₁_congr` (the second parts are in bijection: the blocks of a group
 versus the group itself, `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.groupBlkEquiv`, and the unions of the
 groups versus the groups, `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.grpUnionEquiv`); this is
 `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.defect₁_blkZ` and `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.defect₁_blkContr`;
* the hypothesis `hdj` of `Babai.case_9_6_1_step2`, *"for some `j ∈ J` we have
 `d_j > n₁/2`"*, which is the branch condition `¬ ImprimitiveSplits`
 (`Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.isBigColor_jColor`) together with
 `Babai.natColor_inDeg_eq_of_diag_eq'` (N7), which is what makes `d_j` independent of the
 vertex of `V₂` (`Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.inDeg₁_const`);
* the hypothesis `hEne`, *"`R_h` is not empty"*, which holds by the choice of
 `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.hColor` as a color that occurs on the link
 (`Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.isOtherColor_hColor`), and the hypothesis `hsr`, the
 semiregularity of the contraction (Cor. 3.4.9).  The latter is
 `Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.contractedBip_isSemiregular`, which is
 `Babai.natColor_contraction_degrees` (N8) read on the vertex set "points of `V₁` plus
 blocks" through `Babai.image_weakComponent_restrictColor`, which says that the blocks

decls.name: step6Config_isUniprimitive
decls.docstring:
§9.4, step 6, **the Claim**: *"`X₁` is uniprimitive."*  (Version 2.5, lines 4142-4146.)

On the branch of step 6 where `X₁` is primitive, `X₁` is a UPCC (Def. 3.2.1): it is
primitive by the branch condition (`Babai.step6Imprimitive_iff`), and it is not the clique
configuration, because it has at least two points and, were its rank `2`, the Large clique
lemma (Lemma 3.4.25) would make `W₁` a twin equivalence class of `X[W₁ ∪ V₂]`
(`Babai.claim_9_4_step6`), which the positive symmetry defect of the restricted instance
forbids (`Babai.not_twinClass_eq_step5Pts`).

The hypothesis `h` is the branch condition of step 4, *"the dominant vertex-color class has
size `> α n₁`"*, which is what step 5 runs on.

decls.name: step7Colors_nonempty
decls.docstring:
§9.4, step 7, the parenthetical: *"Such a `j` exists because otherwise `V₁` would be a
twin equivalence class in `X₁₂`."*

If every class `D_j` had a trivial link with `W₁`, then for any two points `x ≠ y` of `W₁`
and any block `B` the pairs `({x}, B)` and `({y}, B)` would carry the same color of the
configuration, hence — the refinement refining the edge relation — `x` and `y` would be
joined to the same blocks; with the equality of colors `f` that the homogeneity of `X₁`
gives, `x` and `y` would be twins of `X[W₁ ∪ V₂]`.  So `W₁` would be a set of twins, which
`Babai.not_isTwinSet_step5Obj_V₁` forbids.

The case is run on the instance `(W₁, V₂)` that step 8 leaves, at multiplicative cost
`n₂`.  Its outcome is either a colored `1/2`-partition of `W₁`, or a bipartite graph on
`W₁` with at most half as many blocks and symmetry defect at least `1/2`.  In the first
case objective (a) for `(α, V₁)` follows by extending the partition by the block
`V₁ \ W₁`; in the second, the graph is an admissible input of Theorem 9.2.2 for the
threshold `α_new` of step 5 (`Babai.isThm922Input_of_halved`) whose measure is smaller
(`n₂` has halved, and `n₂ ≥ 2` by `Babai.two_le_step8_numBlocks`), so the recursion `hrec`
applies to it and returns a solution for `(α_new, W₁)`.  Both cases end in

`α_new |W₁| = α n₁` (`Babai.alphaNew_mul_step8V₁`).  The cost is
`Babai.caseCost_mul_costRec_9_4_le` together with `Babai.cost_9_4_le_costRec_9_4`.

`V₁`: at most `n₁^{n₁} ≤ C₀^{C₀}`, a constant, which is why `Babai.cost_9_4` carries
`Babai.constFactor` (`Babai.pow_self_le_constFactor`).  The colored partition returned has
one block for each of the `n₁ - ⌊α n₁⌋ = ⌈(1-α) n₁⌉` individualized points and one block for
the `⌊α n₁⌋ ≤ α n₁` points that were not individualized, so every block has at most
`α n₁` points: this is objective (a) (`Babai.step1Outcome_isAlphaPartition`).  The symmetry
defect hypothesis is not needed for this step.

decls.name: step_9_4_2
decls.docstring:
§9.4, step 2.  *"If `n₂ ≤ c log n₁` for some specific constant `c > 0` then
individualize all vertices of `V₂`, apply naive vertex refinement, return colored partition
of `V₁`, exit.  Claim.  This is a colored `α`-partition.  Proof.  All vertices of the same
color in `V₁` are twins."*  (Version 2.5, lines 4120-4125.)

The Claim is `Babai.blkColor_eq_imp`: two vertices of `V₁` with the same refinement color
have the same vertex color and the same neighboring blocks, hence are twins
(`Babai.VColBipBlk.isTwin_iff`).  A color class is therefore a set of twins, so it has at
most `symmetricity₁ ≤ α n₁` points and the partition into the color classes is a colored
`α`-partition (`Babai.blkColor_class_le`, `Babai.symmetricity₁_le_alpha`).

The multiplicative cost is the choice of the individualization of `V₂`, that is of a
numbering of the `n₂` blocks: at most `n₂^{n₂}`, a little above the paper's `n₂!`.  On this
subcategory `n₂ ≤ C₀ log₂ n₁`, and `Babai.pow_self_le_cost_of_log_le` shows that
`n₂^{n₂} ≤ constFactor C₀ · costFun n n₂`, which is the cost charged here.  Note that
`(C₀ log₂ n₁)!` is *not* bounded by a constant, so the constant factor alone does not pay
for this step: the turns that the recursion still has do.  (The paper
adds that the method of §4.1.2 brings the cost down to `n₁^{O(1)}`; that refinement is not
needed for the bound proved here.)

decls.name: steps_9_4_3_to_9
decls.docstring:
§9.4, steps 3-9 together with the three cases of §9.6, §9.7 and §9.8.  This is the
body of Procedure Bipartite Split-or-Johnson on the instances that steps 1 and 2 do not
dispose of: `n₁ > C₀` and `n₂ > C₀ log n₁`.

*"3. Apply WL refinement to `X`. … 4. If all vertex-color classes in `V₁` have size
`≤ αn₁` then return the colored partition of `V₁`, exit. 5. Let `W₁ ⊆ V₁` be the dominant
color class … 6. If `X₁` is imprimitive, return the connected components of the first
disconnected off-diagonal color, exit … 7. If `X₂` is not homogeneous … 8. Let `i` be the
smallest index such that `Rᵢ` is involved in `X₁₂`.  Replace `X ← (V₁, V₂; Rᵢ)` … 9. We
need to consider the following cases: (i) `X₂` is imprimitive: Section 9.6; (ii) `X₂` is
the clique configuration … Section 9.7; (iii) `X₂` is uniprimitive: Section 9.8."*
(Version 2.5, lines 4126-4172.)

The absolute constant `C₀` of steps 1 and 2 is chosen here: it is the threshold above
which the estimates of steps 3-9 hold.  Its existence is part of the statement, which is
why `C₀` is bound here and not in `step_9_4_1` and `step_9_4_2`, where every value works.

The hypothesis `rec` is the recursive call allowed by §9.5: Theorem 9.2.2 may be applied to
instances of strictly smaller measure.

The pieces of the three cases that are already proved are: §9.4 itself
(`Babai.claim_9_4_step2`, `Babai.claim_9_4_step5`, `Babai.claim_9_4_step6`,
`Babai.claim_9_4_step7`, `Babai.claim_9_4_step8`), §9.6 (`Babai.lemma_9_6_1`, proved in
full, together with `Babai.imprimitiveCase_split`, `Babai.case_9_6_1_step2`,
`Babai.lemma_9_6_2`), §9.7 (`Babai.case_9_7_1`, `Babai.case_9_7_2`, `Babai.case_9_7_3a1`,
`Babai.case_9_7_3a2`, `Babai.case_9_7_3b_t_le`), §9.8 (`Babai.claim_9_8`), and
Lemma 9.3.2 (`Babai.lemma_9_3_2`, `Babai.reducePart2ByColor_spec`).

**Partly proved.**  Steps 3 and 4 are proved here (`Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor`,
`Babai.step_9_4_4`), and the case distinction of step 4 is what this theorem now is; what
remains is `Babai.steps_9_4_5_to_9`.

Steps 5-9 are a chain of *transformations* of the input, not a single
family of outcomes, so the proof is a composition of reductions, one per step.  The chain
below is the plan; each arrow is a `Babai.Func` together with a
`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.precomp` (a canonical embedding costs nothing) or a
`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases` (a branch), and the last arrow is a
`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.comp_dep` with the recursion hypothesis `rec`.

*The chain.*  Write `D₀` for the input category
`((BipBlockInputsAt Ω N).full ¬IsSmallPart₁ C₀).full ¬IsSmallPart₂ C₀`.

1. **Step 3 (WL refinement).**  *Proved*, in `Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/WLColor.lean`.  It
  needs no new category: the coloring `c = Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor` of the coherent
  configuration `X` on the vertex set *"points of `V₁` plus blocks"* is a **function of
  the object**, so step 3 adds no data and costs `1`.  The coloring is coherent
  (`Babai.VColBipBlk.isCoherentColoring_wlRaw`) and canonical
  (`Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor_map`, Eq. (26)), it refines the input
  (`Babai.VColBipBlk.f_eq_of_wlColor_eq`,
  `Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor_ne_of_part₁_blocks`), and its labels are natural numbers, as
  the categories of §9.6-§9.8 require.  Two points had to be arranged for that: the
  refinement runs a number of rounds fixed in advance for the whole ambient set
  (`Babai.wlRounds`), so that the color type does not depend on the input, and the colors
  are named by `Babai.WL.namedIter`, which ranks tags at each round. Isomorphisms preserve
  these tags and their ranks.
2. **Step 4 (branch).**  *Proved*: `Babai.step_9_4_4`, glued by
  `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases` on `Babai.AllClassesSmall` — *"all vertex-color classes in
  `V₁` have size `≤ αn₁`"*.  In the positive branch the outcome is the colored partition
  of `V₁` into the vertex-color classes of `c`, which is a colored `α`-partition by the
  branch condition; this is `Babai.kerPartition` with the coloring
  `Babai.VColBipBlk.wlDiag` and costs `1`.  In the negative branch
  `Babai.claim_9_4_step5` gives the dominant class.
3. **Step 5 (restriction to `W₁`).**  `Func D₄ D₅` onto the subset `W₁ ∪ V₂` of `□X`, with
  `α ← α n₁ / |W₁|`; `Babai.claim_9_4_step5` says the new threshold is again in
  `[3/4, 1)` and that `α_new |W₁| = α n₁`, which is what carries a colored
  `α_new`-partition of `W₁` back to a colored `α`-partition of `V₁` (Lemma 9.3.1's
  bookkeeping).  Cost `1`.
4. **Step 6 (branch).**  `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases` on *"`X₁` is imprimitive"*.  In the
  positive branch the outcome is the components of `Babai.blockColor` of the restriction
  of `c` to `V₁`, a colored `1/2`-partition by Prop. 3.4.4 and hence a colored
  `α`-partition; `Babai.claim_9_4_step6` is the Claim that the negative branch leaves a
  **uniprimitive** `X₁` (Large clique lemma).  Cost `1`.
5. **Step 7 (restriction of `V₂`).**  `Func D₆ D₇` onto `V₁ ∪ D_j`, for the smallest `j`
  with `X[V₁, D_j]` nontrivial; `Babai.claim_9_4_step7` is *"such a `j` exists"*.  Cost
  `1`.  `n₂` does not increase.
6. **Step 8 (one constituent).**  `Func D₇ D₈` replacing `c` by the constituent `Rᵢ` for
  the smallest `i` involved in `X₁₂`, followed by WL refinement again (same renumbering
  as in step 1); `Babai.claim_9_4_step8` is the Claim *"there are no `X`-twins in `V₁`"*.
  Cost `1`.  The objects of `D₈` are exactly the inputs of the three cases: `X₁` a UPCC,
  `X₂` homogeneous, `X₁₂` nontrivial.
7. **Step 9 (three cases).**  Two nested `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases` on *"`X₂` is
  imprimitive"* and *"`X₂` is the clique configuration"*, and then
  `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.precomp` with the forgetful functors `D₈ → BlkImprimitiveCases`,
  `D₈ → BlkBlockDesignCases`, `D₈ → BlkUPCCCases` into `Babai.lemma_9_6_1` (cost `n₂`),
  `Babai.case_9_7` (cost `n₂^{⌊(7/3) log₂ n₁⌋+1}`) and `Babai.case_9_8` (cost `n₂`).
8. **The recursive call.**  The outcome of §9.6 and §9.8 is
  `Babai.IsBlkImprimitiveOutcome`: either a colored `1/2`-partition of `V₁`, which is a
  colored `α`-partition because `α ≥ 3/4`, or a new object of `BipBlockInputs Ω` with
  `2 |W₂| ≤ n₂`, hence `measure_9_5 < N` (`Babai.measure_9_5`), and symmetry defect
  `≥ 1/2` on `V₁`.  The outcome of §9.7 is `Babai.IsBlkDesignOutcome`, which already
  carries `measure_9_5 < N`.  In both cases `rec` applies to the new object, and
  `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.comp_dep` composes; the transfer of a solution for the new `V₁`
  back to a solution for the old one is the bookkeeping of steps 5 and 7
  (`α_new |V₁_new| = α |V₁|`, `V₁_new ⊆ V₁`).
9. **The cost.**  Steps 3-8 cost `1` each, step 9 costs at most
  `Babai.turnCost □X` (`Babai.designCost_le_turnCost` for the §9.7 branch, and
  `n₂ ≤ □X` for the other two), and the recursive call costs
  `cost_9_4 C₀` at an object with `n₂_new ≤ n₂/2`, hence with
  `steps09 n₂_new + 1 ≤ steps09 n₂`.  So the product is at most
  `turnCost n · constFactor C₀ · turnCost n ^ steps09 n₂ = cost_9_4 C₀ X`, which is the
  cost claimed.  The absolute constant `C₀` is fixed here; `C₀ = 1` works for the
  estimates above, the constant of the paper's step 1 only having to be large enough for
  step 2.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Proposition 3.4.4 (Homogeneous connected components) (PDF p. 36) — §9.4, steps 3-9 together with the three cases of §9.6, §9.7 and §9.8.  This is the body of Procedure Bipartite Split-or-Johnson on the instances that steps 1 and 2 do not dispose of: `n₁ > C₀` and `n₂ > C₀ log n₁`.

decls.name: steps_9_4_5_to_9
decls.docstring:
§9.4, steps 5-9 together with the three cases of §9.6, §9.7 and §9.8: the body of
Procedure Bipartite Split-or-Johnson on the instances that steps 1, 2 and 4 do not dispose
of, that is on those for which `n₁ > C₀`, `n₂ > C₀ log n₁`, and some vertex-color class of
`V₁` has more than `α n₁` points.

The proof is `Babai.steps_9_4_5_to_9_at`, with the constant `C₀ = 1`; every value works
for the estimates of steps 5-9, the constant of step 1 only having to be large enough for
step 2.

## No new category is needed: everything is a function of the input

The earlier plan was to build a category of *(bipartite graph with blocks, threshold,
coloring)*, because from step 5 on the paper restricts the coherent configuration `X`
instead of refining the restricted graph again, so the coloring looked like data that has
to be carried.  It is not.  Every object that steps 5 to 8 produce is a **function of the
object of this category alone**:

* the coloring of step 3 is `Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor` of the input, a function of it;
* `W₁` is `Babai.dominantClass`, a function of the input
 (`Babai.dominantClass_image` is its canonicity), so the point set `W₁ ∪ V₂` of step 5 is
 `Babai.step5Set` and the restricted graph is `Babai.step5Obj`, both functions of the
 input, and the restricted *configuration* is the restriction of `wlColor` of the input;
* the color class `D_j` of step 7 and the constituent `Rᵢ` of step 8 are chosen by the
 colors of that same coloring, so they too are functions of the input; and the second WL
 refinement of step 8 is a function of the object it is applied to.

So steps 5 to 8 are one functor out of a full subcategory of *this* category, cut out by
the branch conditions of steps 6 and 7, into the input category of one of the three cases
of step 9, and the chain is `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.cases` for the branches and
`Babai.FindsAtMultCost.precomp` for the functor, exactly as steps 3 and 4 were.  This is
the cheaper of the two routes and it is the one taken here.

## What is proved of steps 5 to 9

Step 5 is **done** at the level of the objects:

* the update of the threshold, `α ← α n₁ / |W₁|`: `Babai.alphaNew`, with
 `Babai.claim_9_4_step5_at` for `2/3 ≤ α_new < 1`, `α_new |W₁| = α n₁` and `|W₁| ≥ 2`;
* the induced substructure `X[W₁ ∪ V₂]`: `Babai.step5Obj`, built with
 `Babai.VColBipBlk.restrictTo`, which is also what step 7 needs;
* `V₁ ← W₁` (`Babai.step5Obj_V₁_ncard`) and `n₂` unchanged
 (`Babai.step5Obj_numBlocks`);
* **the restricted instance is admissible**: `Babai.step5Obj_isThm922Input`.  The one
 delicate point, the symmetry defect, comes from
 `Babai.VColBipBlk.restrictTo_twin_imp` (a set of twins of the restriction is a set of
 twins of `X`) together with `Babai.ncard_le_alphaNew_mul_dominantClass`
 (a set of twins of `X` inside `V₁` has at most `α n₁ = α_new |W₁|` points).

What is missing is the rest of the chain:

* step 6 branches on the imprimitivity of `X₁`, and its Claim (the negative branch leaves a
 **uniprimitive** `X₁`, by the Large clique lemma 3.4.25),
* step 7 restricts `V₂` to the first vertex-color class `D_j` with `X[V₁, D_j]` nontrivial
 (the restriction is `Babai.VColBipBlk.restrictTo` again, with a different `s'`),
* step 8 replaces the coloring by the first constituent `Rᵢ` involved in `X₁₂` and refines
 again, with its Claim *"there are no `X`-twins in `V₁`"*,
* step 9 branches into `Babai.lemma_9_6_1`, `Babai.case_9_7` and `Babai.case_9_8` and
 composes the recursion hypothesis `rec` with `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.comp_dep`.

The cost accounting is item 9 of the docstring of `Babai.steps_9_4_3_to_9`.

## What is proved of step 9

The two pieces of bookkeeping that step 9 needs, and that do not depend on steps 6-8, are
proved in `Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/Step9.lean`:

* `Babai.isThm922Input_of_halved`: **the graph returned by §9.6 or by §9.8 is an admissible
 input of Theorem 9.2.2 for the threshold the procedure already carries.**  Those two
 cases keep `V₁` whole, so `α` does not change; `|V₂| < α|V₁|` survives because `n₂` has
 at least halved, and `1 - α ≤ 1/3 ≤ 1/2 ≤ defect₁` because `α ≥ 2/3`.  This is the only
 place in step 9 that uses the lower bound on the threshold.
* `Babai.caseCost_mul_cost_9_4_le`: **one turn pays for the recursive call it makes**, on
 `Babai.turnCost_mul_costFun_le` and `Babai.turnCost_mono`
 (`Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/Depth.lean`).  The cost of the §9.7 branch is below one turn
 by `Babai.caseCost_9_7_le_turnCost`, which is `Babai.designCost_le_turnCost` with the two
 extra factors `n₂` of `Babai.case_9_7` allowed for.

The `Y.car ⊆ X.car` that the cost accounting needs is **not** part of the outcome
predicates `Babai.IsBlkImprimitiveOutcome` and `Babai.IsBlkDesignOutcome`; it comes from
the composition itself.  `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.comp_dep` runs the second step on
`Babai.PairCatOf`, whose objects carry `sub_subset : sub ⊆ car`, so the recursive call is
made along `Babai.pairSndFunc`, a canonical embedding, and the instance handed to `rec`
lives on a subset of `□X`.  `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.comp` alone would not do: its cost
hypothesis quantifies over *every* `Y` with `Good₁ X Y`, and nothing there bounds `□Y`.

That the multiplicative cost of every branch is at least `1` is automatic: the `Case`
heading of §9.6, §9.7 and §9.8 contains `Babai.IsBipartiteCase.link_nontrivial`, which
makes `V₂` nonempty, so `n₂ ≥ 1` and `Babai.FindsAtMultCost.one_le_cost` is respected.

## Three obstacles

1. **Module layering.**  *Resolved.*  This is the module that was asked for: it stands
  above `Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/BlkCases.lean`, and holds the statements only.
2. **The threshold of `Babai.case_9_7`.**  *Resolved.*  `Babai.case_9_7` is now stated on
  `Babai.BlkBlockDesignInputs`, whose objects carry `α`.  Step 9 can supply what that
  category asks for: `α = Babai.alphaNew X` with `2/3 ≤ α < 1`
  (`Babai.claim_9_4_step5_at`) and `n₂ < α |V₁|`, because step 5 leaves `n₂` unchanged
  (`Babai.step5Obj_numBlocks`) and `α_new |W₁| = α n₁`, and steps 7 and 8 only shrink
  `n₂` and keep `V₁`.
3. **The transfer of a solution is stated for the wrong pair of sets.**  *Resolved.*
  `Babai.transfer_finds` (`Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/Sec92.lean`) carries a solution for a
  subset `W ⊆ □X` back to a solution for `□X`, because that is what Theorem 9.2.1 needs.
  Step 9 has to carry a solution for `V₁_new ⊆ V₁` back to a solution for `V₁`, and `V₁`
  is a proper subset of `□X` — the points of the blocks are in `□X` too.
  `Babai.transfer_finds_on` (`Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/Step9.lean`) is the same theorem
  with `□X` replaced by an isomorphism-invariant `V : Pt C → Set Ω` with `V X ⊆ □X`, and
  `Babai.transfer_finds` is its case `V X = □X`.

## The bridge from the coloring of step 3 to the configuration the three cases ask for

*Done*, in `Workspace/SplitOrJohnson/WLConfig.lean*.  The field
`Babai.IsBipartiteCase.coherent` asks for a `Babai.PartitionStructure` on the vertex set
`𝒱₁ ∪ 𝒞` whose `natColor` **is** the coloring the object carries.  It is
`Babai.VColBipBlk.wlConfig`, the ordered integer naming
(`Babai.PartitionStructure.ofNamedColoring`) of the named WL coloring on the vertices;
it is coherent (`Babai.VColBipBlk.wlConfig_isCoherent`), and
`Babai.VColBipBlk.exists_wlConfig` is the field `coherent` itself, once `X₁` and `X₂` are
homogeneous — which is what steps 5 and 7 arrange.  Three things were needed:

* Observation 3.3.4 (vertex-color awareness) and Observation 3.3.2 (*"a stable subset
 induces a coherent configuration"*) for *colorings* rather than for configurations
 (`Babai.WL.diag_fst_eq_of_eq`, `Babai.WL.isCoherentColoring_restrict`).  The second is
 also the restriction `X ← X[W₁ ∪ V₂]` of step 5 and `X ← X[V₁ ∪ D_j]` of step 7
 (`Babai.VColBipBlk.wlRestrictedConfig_coherent`);
* the vertex set is stable (`Babai.VColBipBlk.isStableSet_vtx`): the refinement refines the
 initial coloring, which already tells a vertex from a non-vertex;
* **the coloring the objects of §9.6-§9.8 carry is `Babai.VColBipBlk.wlCaseColor`, not
 `Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor`.**  The two differ by the shift `+ 1` that `wlColor` puts on
 the colors of pairs of vertices to keep them apart from the padding color `0`
 (`Babai.VColBipBlk.wlColor_eq_wlCaseColor_succ`), so they have the same color classes on
 the vertices.  A `natColor` cannot carry that shift: its values are the elements of
 `Fin rank` and every color is used (Def. 3.1.1), so the color `0` is attained.  With
 `wlCaseColor` the padding color `0` is also a genuine color, which costs nothing: every
 construction of §9.6-§9.8 reads the coloring on the vertex set only
 (`Babai.BlkImprimitiveObj.isIso_of_vertexColor`).

So what is left of steps 5-9 is steps 6, 7 and 8 at the level of the objects: the branch
conditions (*"`X₁` is imprimitive"*, *"`X₂` is not homogeneous"*), the two restrictions,
the replacement of the coloring by one constituent and the second WL refinement, and the

decls.name: subclaim_9_6_2
decls.docstring:
Subclaim of Lemma 9.6.2.  *"`Cᵢ × Bᵢ ⊆ R_j`."*

Paper's proof: *"The vertices of `Cᵢ` are twins in `Zᵢ`.  In other words, for each
`x ∈ Bᵢ` the set `Cᵢ × {x}` is monochromatic (has a single color), i.e.
`Cᵢ × {x} ⊆ R_ℓ` for some `ℓ ∈ J`.  It follows that `d_ℓ > n₁/2`.  Therefore `ℓ = j`,
proving the Subclaim."*

*What "twins in `Zᵢ`" means.*  `Zᵢ = X(V₁, Bᵢ; R_j)` is the **bipartite graph with edge set
`R_j`**, so twinness in `Zᵢ` is equality of the `R_j`-neighborhoods inside `Bᵢ`:
`c x y = j ↔ c x' y = j` for `y ∈ Bᵢ`.  This is `hCtwin`, and it is all that Procedure
ImprimitiveCase supplies.  (The paper's intermediate phrase *"the set `Cᵢ × {y}` is
monochromatic"* asserts more than twinness in a two-colored `Zᵢ` gives, and is not needed:
the argument below runs directly from the `R_j`-neighborhoods.)

Proof: if some `x ∈ Cᵢ` had `c x y ≠ j` for some `y ∈ Bᵢ`, then by `hCtwin` no vertex of
`Cᵢ` would be an `R_j`-neighbor of `y`, so the two disjoint sets `Cᵢ` and `R_j(y) ∩ V₁`
would have more than `n₁/2` elements each.

links.rationale: Formalizes Lemma 9.6.2 (PDF p. 77) — Subclaim of Lemma 9.6.2.  *"`Cᵢ × Bᵢ ⊆ R_j`."*

decls.name: surjective_domPsi
decls.docstring:
§14.1, **line 8, case (A)**: *"the natural epimorphism"* really is an epimorphism.

*Proof.*  `Babai.surjective_equipartitionPsi` realizes a permutation `β` of the blocks by a
permutation `σ` of the color class, glued from bijections between a block and its image;
the blocks have equal size because the partition is a colored equipartition.  Extend `σ` by
the identity outside the color class (`Equiv.Perm.ofSubtype`).  The extension preserves the
coloring — it moves the color class into itself and fixes everything else — and it preserves
the partition: inside the class two points are in the same block exactly when their blocks
agree, and `β` is injective; a block never meets two color classes, so no pair with one
point inside and one outside the class is in the same block.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure Align (PDF p. 110) — §14.1, **line 8, case (A)**: *"the natural epimorphism"* really is an epimorphism.

decls.name: surjective_equipartitionPsi
decls.docstring:
§14.1, line 8: the map of case (A) really is an **epimorphism**, provided the blocks all
have the same size — which is what *"equipartition"* means.

*Proof.*  Write `Δ` as the disjoint union of the blocks (`Equiv.sigmaFiberEquiv`).  A
permutation `β` of the blocks and a bijection from each block onto its image assemble into
a permutation of `Δ` that induces `β`; the bijections exist because the blocks have equal
size.

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Procedure Align (PDF p. 110) — §14.1, line 8: the map of case (A) really is an **epimorphism**, provided the blocks all have the same size — which is what *"equipartition"* means.

decls.name: surjective_johnsonPsiOf
decls.docstring:
§14.1, **line 8, case (B)**: the map really is an epimorphism.

*Proof.*  Every permutation `π` of `Γ*` acts on the `t*`-subsets, and that action is an
automorphism of the Johnson scheme (Prop. 3.2.11).  Read back through the identification
`Δ_j = (Γ* choose t*)` and extended by the identity outside `Δ_j`
(`Equiv.Perm.ofSubtype`), it is an automorphism of the outcome, because it carries `Δ_j`
onto itself and preserves the edge colors `|S ∖ T|`; and `ψ` sends it to `π`, because `ψ`
undoes `π ↦ π^{(t*)}` (`Babai.johnsonSchemePsi_tAction`).

links.rationale: Intermediate step or helper for Proposition 3.2.11 (PDF p. 32) — §14.1, **line 8, case (B)**: the map really is an epimorphism.

decls.name: theorem_10_2_4
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 10.2.4** (Extracted from `[DiM, Thm 4.1A]`), §10.2.

Formerly an axiom; it is now proved, with the statement unchanged (route: module
docstring).

Quoted from the paper:

> **Theorem 10.2.4** (Extracted from [DiM, Thm 4.1A]).  Let `G ≤ S_n` be a primitive group
> with socle `Soc(G) ≅ R^s` where `R` is a nonabelian simple group.  If `s ≥ 2` then
> either (a) `n ≥ |R|^{s−1}` or (b) there exists a proper divisor `d | s` and a primitive
> group `U` with socle `R^d` such that `n = ℓ^{s/d}` where `ℓ` is the degree of `U`.

**Citation.** `[DiM, Thm. 4.1A]` (Dixon–Mortimer, *Permutation Groups*, GTM 163, 1996),
summarizing `[Sco]`, `[AsS]` and `[LiePS]` = Martin W. Liebeck, Cheryl E. Praeger, Jan
Saxl, *On the O'Nan–Scott theorem for finite primitive permutation groups*, J. Austral.
Math. Soc. (A) **44** (1988), 389–396.  The paper says: "This result is an immediate
consequence of the 'summary' of the O'Nan–Scott–Aschbacher Theorem … given by Dixon and
Mortimer … as Theorem 4.1A.  We further compress the result to suit our purposes."  The
statement is Babai's compression, verbatim, not a verbatim theorem of `[DiM]`.

**Used where.** Proposition 10.2.3, which the paper proves from it.

**Warning (consistency).** A "proper divisor `d | s`" is `d ∣ s ∧ d < s`; the paper uses
`d < s` at the corresponding place in the proof of Prop. 10.2.3.  `s / d` is exact since
`d ∣ s`.  `|R|^{s-1}` uses truncated subtraction, harmless since `s ≥ 2`.  The group `U`
of case (b) is produced on a permutation domain `Ω'` in the same universe as `Ω`, which is
no strengthening: a permutation group can be transported along any bijection of its
domain, and Prop. 10.2.3 applies the theorem repeatedly to the groups it produces.  "Nonabelian" is
`¬ ∀ a b : R, a * b = b * a`.

**Universes.** The simple group `R` lives in an arbitrary universe `v`, as the paper's
"`R` a nonabelian simple group" has no universe attached.  This is not a strengthening:
for a *finite* group the statement at one universe implies it at every other, by
transport along `Finite.exists_type_univ_nonempty_mulEquiv` — the same argument that
`Babai.schreierHypothesis_iff` carries out for Schreier's Hypothesis.  The polymorphic
form is what the call sites in Lemma 10.2.5 need, where `R` is a socle factor of a
permutation group on `Ω : Type u`.

decls.name: theorem_10_3_5
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 10.3.5** (Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma), §10.3.

> Let `G ≤ S(Ω)` be a permutation group and `ϕ : G → S_k` a giant representation.  Assume
> `k > max{8, 2 + log₂ n₀}` where `n₀ = n₀(G)` denotes the length of the largest orbit of
> `G`.  Let `D` be the set of elements of `Ω` not affected by `ϕ`.  Then `G_(D)^ϕ ≥ A_k`.

The paper's proof: for `G^ϕ = A_k`, `D` is `G`-invariant and `G_(D)` is the kernel of the
restriction `G → S(D)` with image `P`; if `G_(D)^ϕ ≠ A_k` then `G_(D) ≤ ker ϕ`, so `ϕ`
factors as `G → P → A_k`, and Lemma 10.3.3 gives `x ∈ D` with `P_x^ψ ≠ A_k`, contradicting
that `x` is unaffected.  For `G^ϕ = S_k` apply this to `G₁ = ϕ⁻¹(A_k)` (the notion of
"affected" is the same for `ϕ` and `ϕ₁` because `A_k` has no subgroup of index 2).

links.rationale: Formalizes Theorem 1.2.1 (PDF p. 13) — **Theorem 10.3.5** (Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma), §10.3.
Formalizes Theorem 10.3.5 (Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma) (PDF p. 86) — **Theorem 10.3.5** (Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma), §10.3.

decls.name: theorem_10_3_5_aux
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 10.3.5**, §10.3, the paper's first case: `G^ϕ = A_k`.

> First assume `G^ϕ = A_k`.  The set `D` is `G`-invariant and `G_(D)` is the kernel of the
> restriction map `G → S(D)`.  Let `P ≤ S(D)` be the image of this map (restriction of `G`
> to `D`), so `P ≅ G/G_(D)`.  Since `G_(D) ⊴ G`, we have `G_(D)^ϕ ⊴ G^ϕ = A_k`.  Assume for
> a contradiction that `G_(D)^ϕ ≠ A_k`; it follows that `|G_(D)^ϕ| = 1`, i.e.
> `G_(D) ≤ ker(ϕ)`.  Hence `ϕ` factors across `P` as `G → P → A_k`.  It follows that
> `P^ψ = G^ϕ = A_k` so `ψ` is an epimorphism.  By Lemma 10.3.3 we have `P_x^ψ ≠ A_k` for
> some `x ∈ D`.  But `P_x^ψ = G_x^ϕ = A_k` (because `x ∈ D` is not affected by `ϕ`), a
> contradiction.

links.rationale: Formalizes Theorem 10.3.5 (Unaffected Stabilizers Lemma) (PDF p. 86) — **Theorem 10.3.5**, §10.3, the paper's first case: `G^ϕ = A_k`.

decls.name: theorem_10_4_2
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 10.4.2** (Jordan–Liebeck), §10.4, with the exceptional cases of the cited
source restored — the printed statement is false, see the corrected paper
"Theorem 10.4.2 (Jordan–Liebeck): the cited theorem is mis-transcribed".

> Let `A(Ω) ≤ K ≤ S(Ω)`.  Let `H ≤ K` and `1 ≤ r < n/2` where `n = |Ω| ≥ 9`.  Assume
> `|K : H| < (n choose r)`.  Then there exists a unique `T ⊂ Ω` with `|T| < n/2` such that
> `A(Ω)_(T) ≤ H ≤ S(Ω)_T`.  This unique `T` satisfies `|T| < r`.

Proved from the two cited theorems of the source, `Babai.dixonMortimer_5_2A` and
`Babai.dixonMortimer_5_2B` (`CITED.md`, C12): `A(Ω) ≤ K ≤ S(Ω)` forces `K = A(Ω)` or
`K = S(Ω)` (`Babai.eq_alternating_or_top`), and the two theorems cover the two cases.
All exceptional cases of the source have degree `n ≤ 9`, so for `n ≥ 9` only the case
`(9, 4, 120, PΓL₂(8))` of Theorem 5.2A survives, which needs `K = A(Ω)`.  Uniqueness of
`T` is proved from Observation 10.4.1, as the paper says.

For the paper's printed conclusion see `Babai.theorem_10_4_2_of_not_exceptional` and
`Babai.theorem_10_4_2_of_four_mul_le`.

decls.name: theorem_10_4_2_of_four_mul_le
decls.docstring:
**Theorem 10.4.2** (Jordan–Liebeck), §10.4, as the paper prints it, under a convenient
sufficient condition that covers every use of the theorem in §10.5: `4r ≤ n` and
`(n, r) ≠ (9, 4)`.

`4r ≤ n` excludes the exceptional case (ii) of the cited source: that case gives
`2|K : H| = (n choose ⌊n/2⌋) ≥ 2(n choose r) > 2|K : H|`
(`Babai.two_mul_choose_le_choose_half`), a contradiction; and it also excludes the
exceptional case (iii), whose `(n, r) = (9, 4)` violates `4r ≤ n`.  In Theorem 10.5.1 the
theorem is applied with `n = k ≥ 9` and `r = ⌊k/4⌋`, so `4r ≤ k`.
